en: The Fifteenth [Chapter]
Now begins the first chapter.
The Discrimination of the Inner Reality (*Pratyaktattvaviveka*).
The first chapter, titled "Discrimination of Reality.
Salutation to the lotus-feet of the venerable teacher Śaṅkarānanda.
To him whose sole function is to swallow the great delusion with its playful charms, like a crocodile seizing its prey. || 1 ||
This discrimination of reality is set forth for the easy understanding of those whose minds have been purified by service to the pair of his lotus feet. II.2.
In the waking state, sound, touch, and other objects of perception are distinct due to their diversity;
however, because they possess a uniform nature within the consciousness of that [subject], they do not differ from it.
Likewise, that which is perceived here in a dream is not stable, whereas in the waking state it is stable;
nevertheless, the distinction between these two does not affect their consciousness, which remains of a single form.

For one who has just awakened from sleep, there arises a memory consisting of the awareness of the deep sleep state; and that [memory] consists of the object previously experienced, as well as the awareness of that [experience] itself at that time.
The object is distinct from consciousness, but not from the act of being conscious, as in the case of the consciousness of a dream;
likewise, consciousness remains one throughout the three states, just as it is within a single day.
Through months, years, yugas, and kalpas, in various ways,
both past and yet to come, this single self-luminous consciousness neither rises nor sets.
This self is supreme bliss, because it is the object of supreme love; for one observes love toward the self in the form of the thought, "May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist. (8)
That love is for the sake of the Self and not so for the sake of anything else; it is not for the sake of another in the Self.
Therefore, it is supreme, because by means of it, the Self attains the state of supreme bliss.
Thus, by means of reasoning, the Self—which is consciousness, bliss, and supreme—is shown to be of such a nature;
and the identity of these two with the Supreme Brahman is taught in the Upanishads. (10)
When it does not manifest, there is no supreme love; when it manifests, there is no longing for sense objects.
Therefore, even while manifesting, it remains unmanifest because of its nature as supreme bliss.
Like the sound of a son's recitation occurring amidst a group of students, it is logical that there is a non-appearance of the appearance itself due to an obstruction of that appearance. (12)
There is an obstruction regarding an object that is fit for conventional usage as "it exists" or "it appears";
having set that aside, the production of its opposite is what is called [destruction]. (13)
The cause of that [error] is the confusion of similar [sounds], as in hearing the word "putra" (son);
here, beginningless ignorance alone is the sole basis for delusion. (14)
Endowed with the reflection of the Brahman consisting of consciousness and bliss,
that Prakṛti, possessing the qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva, is twofold.
Māyā and avidyā are considered to be the purity and impurity of the *sattva* [of buddhi].
By bringing that *māyā* under control, the Lord (*īśvara*) becomes omniscient, like a reflection in *māyā*. (16)
But another, under the sway of ignorance, becomes manifold through its various manifestations;
that [ignorance] constitutes the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra), wherein the Prājña resides with self-identification.
By the command of the Lord, for the sake of His enjoyment, the elements—ether, air, fire, water, and earth—were born from primordial nature (prakṛti), in which darkness (tamas) predominates. 18.
From those five portions of *sattva*, the five sense organs arise in sequence, known as hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell. (19)
By all of these together, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is twofold according to the distinction of its functions:
the mind (manas) consists of deliberation, while the intellect (buddhi) consists of ascertainment.
From five portions of rajas, the organs of action (karmendriyas) were produced from them in succession, namely those called speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
Together with all those, that vital breath (prāṇa) is fivefold due to the differentiation of its functions: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. Furthermore: || 22 ||

The subtle body, consisting of seventeen components—the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, the five vital breaths, the mind, and the intellect—is called the *liṅga* (the signifier). 23.
Through conceit therein, the wise one attains the state of Taijasa;
the Lord attains the state of Hiraṇyagarbha; these two constitute the individual and the collective.
The Lord is the totality (samaṣṭi) because of his realization of identity with his own self in all things;
others, however, are called by the designation of individuality (vyaṣṭi) due to the absence of that [realization].
For the sake of that enjoyment, and for the birth of further objects of enjoyment and the bodies that experience them,
the Blessed Lord quintuplicates each of the elements, beginning with ether.

Having divided each of these two into four parts, and then again dividing the first [of those] into four, they become five by each being joined with its own second part and the second part of the others. (27)
Therein, the Egg (Aṇḍa) arises as the locus for the enjoyment of the objects of experience in the world;
Hiraṇyagarbha exists within this gross body as Vaiśvānara. Those of the Taijasa nature attain the state of Viśva, such as gods, animals, humans, and so forth. (28)
They look outward and are devoid of the realization of the reality of the inward Self. || 29 ||
They perform actions for the sake of enjoyment, and they experience the results in order to perform further actions;
like insects in a river moving swiftly from one whirlpool to another,
they pass from birth to birth and never attain liberation.
Through the ripening of their past virtuous deeds, they have been rescued by that treasury of compassion;
having reached the shade of the tree on the shore, they rest at their ease. (31)
Having thus received instruction from a teacher who perceives reality,
they attain supreme bliss through the discernment of the five sheaths.
Food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss—these are the five sheaths;
enveloped by them, one's own Self goes to worldly existence through forgetfulness. (33)
The gross body, known as the *anna-maya*, arises from the five elements that have been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*).
Within the subtle body (*liṅga*), however, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) exists along with the *rājasa* vital forces and the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
Together with the sattvic organs of perception, the mind (manomaya) consists of deliberation;
together with those very same [organs], the intellect (vijñānamaya) consists of firm determination.
In the causal state, through the functions of bliss, joy, and so forth,
and by means of their respective sheaths (kośas), the Self becomes identical with each of them due to that identification.
Through the methods of positive and negative concomitance, by means of the discrimination of the five sheaths,
one extracts one's own self from them and attains the Supreme Brahman.
When the gross body is absent, that which is the manifestation of the self in a dream is its positive concomitance (anvaya);
its negative concomitance (vyatireka) is the non-manifestation of anything else during that manifestation.

In deep sleep, when the inferential mark (liṅga) does not appear, there is the appearance of the self; this is the positive concomitance (anvaya). Conversely, its non-appearance when that [the self] appears is called the negative concomitance (vyatireka). || 39 ||
Through the discernment of that [Self], the sheaths—vital breath, mind, and intellect—become distinct;
for they are differentiated there merely by the distinctions of qualities and states. (40)
The presence of the self during deep sleep while it is not manifest [in ordinary consciousness] constitutes its positive concomitance (anvaya) with meditative absorption;
whereas its absence when the self is manifest constitutes its negative concomitance (vyatireka) with deep sleep. (41)
Just as the tuft of grass is extracted from the Muñja reed, so too is the Self drawn forth by the wise through reasoning from the three bodies; thus it becomes the Supreme Brahman itself.

Thus, the identity between the higher and the lower selves, which has been established through reasoning, is indicated by statements such as "That art thou" (tattvamasi) through the abandonment of their respective parts. (43)
That which is the material cause (upādāna) of the world, taking recourse to the quality of darkness (tāmasī māyā),
while having the quality of pure goodness (śuddhasattva) as its instrumental cause (nimitta)— that is called "Brahman" by that term.
When that Supreme Brahman takes up that [individual soul] which is of impure nature and defiled by desire, action, and so forth, it is then designated by the term "Thou" (tvam-pada).
Having set aside even that triad which is mutually contradictory, the indivisible *saccidānanda* is indicated by means of the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*). (46)

Just as in sentences such as "this is that," due to the contradiction between the aspects of "that-ness" and "this-ness," a single substratum is indicated through the exclusion of those two parts. (47)
Thus, having set aside the limiting adjuncts of māyā and avidyā belonging to the Supreme and the individual soul,
only the Supreme Brahman— indivisible, being, consciousness, and bliss— is perceived.
If that which is conceptual were the object of definition, the object defined would lack reality;
the status of being an object of definition is neither seen nor possible for that which is non-conceptual. (49)
The conceptual construction (vikalpa) must belong either to that which is non-conceptual (nirvikalpa) or to that which is conceptual (savikalpa).
In the first case, there is a contradiction; in the other, there are faults such as infinite regress, circularity, and so forth. (50)
Let it be accepted that all this—namely, qualities, actions, universals, substances, relations, and entities—is in every respect the very nature of the self. (51)
In the reality of the self, which is untouched by conceptual construction and its absence,
such things as being conceptually constructed, being characterized, and their relationship are merely imagined.
Thus, the investigation of the meaning through these words constitutes *śravaṇa* (hearing);
whereas *manana* (reflection) is the investigation of its logical possibility.
When the mind has been established upon an object free from doubt, that state of one-pointedness is indeed called *nididhyāsana*. (54)
Having abandoned both the meditator and the meditation, when the mind gradually becomes focused solely on the object of meditation, like a lamp in a windless place, that is called samādhi. // 55 //
At that time, the mental modifications, though not consciously known, have the self as their object;
they are inferred from the recollection that arises in one who has emerged from samādhi.
The persistence of the mental modifications, however, may arise even from the first effort;
through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated practice, it becomes established after some time. (57)
In many ways, such as through the verse beginning "As a lamp in a windless place," the Blessed One explained this very same meaning to Arjuna. (58)
The millions of karmas accumulated here in this beginningless saṃsāra go to destruction by this means; pure dharma increases. (59)
Those most skilled in yoga call this the "Cloud of Dharma" samādhi,
because it rains down thousands of streams of the nectar of Dharma.
When this web of latent impressions has been completely dissolved, and the accumulation of karma known as merit and demerit has been uprooted from its very foundation; || 61 ||
When the statement is unobstructed, it produces a direct realization— like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand— regarding that which was previously perceived as indirect.
The indirect knowledge of Brahman, which is verbal and preceded by a teacher,
burns away all sin committed intentionally, just like fire.
The direct realization of the Self, preceded by the teacher and derived from scripture, is the fierce sun for the darkness of ignorance, which is the cause of saṃsāra. (64)
Having thus performed the discernment of reality and having properly composed the mind,
a person whose bonds to worldly existence have dissolved attains the supreme state beyond this world within no time.
Thus ends the *Tattvaviveka*. 1.
Thus ends the first chapter. || 1 ||
That non-duality which has been heard [in the scriptures] can be understood through the discrimination of the five elements; therefore, the five elements are now being analyzed. (1)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these are the qualities of the elements;
they possess one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively, starting from space (vyoman).
An echo is sound in the sky; in the wind, there is the whistling sound *vīsī*. The touch of fire is neither hot nor cold, and its sound is *bhugubhugu*.
Its touch is hot, and its form is light; in water, there is the bubbling sound *bulu-bulu*.
Cold touch, white color, and sweetness are said to be the taste.
On earth, the sound *kaḍakaḍā* and hardness are considered its touch.
Blue and other colors constitute variegated form, while sweet, sour, and other flavors constitute taste.
The two qualities of fragrance and pleasant scent have been correctly distinguished. || 3 ||

The five sense organs—ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—are located within the spheres of the ear and so forth; they apprehend their respective objects, such as sound, in succession. Due to their subtlety, they are to be inferred from their effects; generally, they tend to flow toward external objects. (4)
Sometimes, when the ears are closed, an internal sound is heard;
likewise during the movement of the vital breath, the digestive fire, the drinking of water, and the eating of food.
Indeed, at the end of the oblation, there are internal sensations of touch, and upon the closing of the eyes, there is internal darkness.
In vomiting, there is the internal perception of both taste and smell; such is the case for the senses. || 5 ||
The five activities— speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing bliss— in fact,
all [other] activities such as agriculture, commerce, and service are included within these five.
The production of those respective actions occurs through the organs of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals;
this pentad of action organs resides within the physical spheres of the mouth and so forth. (7)
The mind is the presiding lord over the ten sense organs, situated within the sphere of the heart-lotus;
it is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), for without the [external] senses, it lacks independence regarding external objects.
When the senses are directed toward their objects, this [mind] deliberates upon their merits and defects;
for its qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are indeed modified by them.
Dispassion, patience, magnanimity, and so forth, arise from *sattva*;
desire, anger, greed, effort, and so forth, arise from *rajas*;
and laziness, delusion, drowsiness, and other such distortions arise from *tamas*. (10)
Through those characterized by *sattva*, merit is produced; through those characterized by *rajas*, sin arises;
through those characterized by *tamas*, neither occurs, but rather there is merely the wasting away of life.
In this regard, the worldly convention is that the one who possesses the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyayin*) is the agent. (11)
In things such as sound that possess clarity and so forth, their material nature is extremely evident;
this should also be understood regarding the sense organs and the like through both scripture and reasoning. (12)
Through reasoning with the eleven sense organs and also through the scriptures, it is understood that whatever may exist—this entire world denoted by the word "this"—is such. (13)
"Before creation, all this was indeed one alone without a second;
it existed as Being (sat), for name and form did not yet exist"—such is the word of Āruṇi. (14)
The internal differentiation of a tree consists of its leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth;
it is homogeneous with other trees and heterogeneous with stones and the like. (15)

In this way, the threefold division that might accrue to an existing entity is precluded, respectively, by the three [means]: the determination of oneness, the restriction [to that], and the negation of duality. (16)
It cannot be suspected that *sat* has parts, because no such constituent part can be defined;
name and form are not its parts, since they have not yet arisen at this stage. (17)
Since creation is precisely the arising of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), there was no arising of those two prior to creation; therefore, it exists as partless, like space.
That which is different from Being is not of the same class, because it would lack the quality of being distinct;
for there is no division of Being itself except through the differences of the limiting adjuncts of name and form. (19)
Indeed, it is understood that the dissimilar does not exist at all; therefore, it cannot be the counter-correlate [of non-existence]. How, then, could there be a distinction from the dissimilar? (20)
In this matter, however, some who are bewildered maintain that while the Existent alone is established as non-dual, this world was previously only non-existent. (21)
Just as the senses become overwhelmed in the great ocean, so too is his intellect;
having heard of the unbroken, single flavor, it becomes motionless and fears this [reality]. (22)

The Gauḍa masters declared that those practitioners of other yogas who are devoted to meditation with mental images (sākāra-dhyāna) feel extreme fear regarding non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi).
This is called the yoga of the intangible, difficult to perceive by all yogis;
for yogis fear this which is fearless, seeing danger where there is no danger.

And the venerable teacher Bhagavatpūjyapāda has said that these people, who are clever at dry logic, are Mādhyamikas who have gone astray regarding this ever-present Self, which is inconceivable. (25)
Disregarding the Śruti out of folly, these wretched Buddhists,
who possess inference as their sole eye, have arrived at the state of being bodiless (nirāmatva).
You claim that it was empty, whether as being associated with existence or as having existence as its nature;
however, neither of these two is logically consistent with emptiness from the perspective of ultimate reality.
The sun is not joined with darkness, nor is it composed of darkness;
since existence and emptiness are contradictory, tell me, how could there have been emptiness? (28)
If name and form are imagined through *māyā* in the case of space and so forth, and likewise in the case of the Void, then may you live long! (29)

If it is argued that even though name-and-form exist, they are both imagined, then tell me: where could an error occur without a substratum? An error is never observed anywhere in the absence of a basis.
If there were a difference between the word "was" (sadāsīt) and its meaning, a doubling [of the referent] would result;
if there were no difference, it would be a tautology. Let it not be so, for such is observed in the world. (31)
"It performs what ought to be done, speaks words, and maintains what is to be maintained"—such was the declaration addressed to one possessed by such latent impressions (vāsanā). 32.
The mention of "previously" (pura) in the absence of a specific time is due to the latent impression (vāsanā) of time;
it refers only to the disciple, and therefore a second [time] is not to be suspected here.
Whether it be an objection or a resolution, let it be made in the language of duality;
in the language of non-duality, there is neither an objection nor its answer. (34)
Therefore, there remains a certain reality that is neither light nor pervasive darkness; it is unmoving and profound, unnameable, and unmanifest. (35)

If it is objected: "Granted that [entities] such as the earth may not exist down to the level of atoms due to their destruction; but how does the non-existence of space come to enter the intellect? (36)
Just as you have resorted to the intellect [viewing it] as an absolute void devoid of the world, why do you not likewise resort to the mind [viewing it] as truly spaceless? (37)
If a sky devoid of the world is seen without light and darkness, where has such a thing been seen? Moreover, in your own position, the sky is certainly not an object of direct perception.
A real entity is experienced by us who have reached certainty;
there is no state of emptiness in remaining silent, because the cognition of emptiness itself is abandoned. (39)
Even if true awareness does not exist, let it not; for because He is self-luminous, and because He is the witness of the state of mindlessness, pure Being is easily accessible to human beings. (40)
Just as the Witness remains undisturbed when there is no expansion of the mind, so too does that Reality remain undisturbed prior to the expansion of Māyā. (41)
Its power, which is devoid of reality and is to be inferred from its effects, is like the fire-potency of a magical illusion;
for a power is never perceived by anyone prior to its producing an effect.
A power is not an existent thing, for it cannot be the very nature of an existent, such as fire; if, however, power is distinct from the existent, then what is its true essence? (43)
If it is argued that "emptiness" means it is empty, then it is said to be an effect of illusion;
yet it is neither non-empty nor existent. Therefore, let such a reality as this be accepted here.

At that time, there was neither non-existence nor existence; rather, there was only darkness (tamas). From the conjunction with darkness, existence (sattva) arose, not from itself, because it is negated as being self-originated.
Therefore, its secondness is not reckoned as being like that of emptiness;
nor in the world is the life of Caitra and his power reckoned separately.
If life increases due to an increase in capacity (*śakti*), then it is that [life] which effects the increase there;
it is not the capacity itself, but rather its effects, such as battle, agriculture, and so forth.
In no case is there ever a separate calculation for mere capacity alone.
But since there is no effect of power whatsoever, how can a second [power] be suspected? (47)
That power does not reside throughout the entire Brahman, but rather occupies only a single part;
just as the capacity for a jar exists in the earth only where the clay is moist. (48)
"One foot of His consists of all beings; three feet are the self-luminous [Brahman] itself"—thus the Śruti declares that Māyā exists as a partial locus. (49)
"Pervading this entire universe, I stand with but a single portion," thus Kṛṣṇa said to Arjuna, [implying] that the world constitutes but one part [of himself]. (50)
Having encompassed the entire earth on all sides, He stood ten fingers' breadth beyond it;
and regarding this, there are the words of the authors of the Śruti and the Sūtras concerning the absence of transformation.

Even though [the Self] is partless, the Śruti— desiring the welfare of the listener— provides an answer in the language of the questioner, who asks whether [it exists] "in the whole" or "in a part," by superimposing parts upon that which is partless.
The Power, resting upon the seven principles, brings about transformations within that which exists,
just as a painting of various kinds appears on a wall based on the support of the colors.
The first transformation is space (ākāśa), which has the nature of providing room;
the reality of existence (sattva) follows even into space, such that one says, "space exists. (54)
The reality of existence has a single nature, while space possesses a dual nature; there is no room [for space] when existence is present, yet both of these likewise abide as a pair.
Alternatively, the echo is not perceived as a quality of space;
for there are two real sounds in space, and thus space, though one, possesses a double quality.
That power which might conceive space would, having brought about the non-difference of existence and space,
conceive the relationship of attribute and substrate through their reversal.
Ordinary people and logicians perceive the existence of space as having attained the state of being from the existent; for that is indeed appropriate for Māyā.
In whatever manner a thing exists, its being thus appears through valid cognition;
its being otherwise appears through delusion—this is a principle common to all the world. (59)
Thus, just as an object appears prior to the investigation of scripture, it is subverted by that very investigation; therefore, let that [object] be considered as being like space.
Even when [the ether] is divided, existence remains in the sky because of the difference in words and the difference in cognition;
however, there is no such cognition of difference regarding the air and other elements, as they do not persist as "existent" in the same way that the sky does.
Because it exists as something additional to an existing entity, space is a property (dharma) while the substratum (dharmin) is the existent thing;
yet, when the existent is mentally separated [from its properties], tell me, what is the nature of that space? (62)
If that which consists of space is non-existent, then let it be considered as such;
if you say that the non-existent is not different from the existent, then you are contradicting yourself. (63)
If it is argued that it appears, let it indeed appear; for that which is an ornament of the illusory is unreal, appearing as such, and is false like an elephant in a dream. (54)

Just as genus and individuality, the embodied soul and the body, or quality and substance exist separately, so too let there be a distinctness between space and existence; what wonder is there in this? (65)
If even the notion of "Buddha" as a distinction does not attain firm establishment in the mind, then tell me:
is that due to a lack of one-pointedness or due to doubt? For in such cases, there is an absence of its firm establishment. (66)
Be vigilant; perform an investigation of the first meditation and the others by means of valid cognition and reasoning, and thereby you shall become most firmly established. (67)

Even through meditation, reasoning, or logical argument, the distinction between space and existence is never established; for the real entity that is existence is not like a void, nor is it like a hole in space.
To the knower, space always appears as devoid of any trace of objective reality;
even the existent thing appears to him as being preceded by its own flawlessness.
Seeing one who asserts the reality of space when latent impressions have increased, and who is devoid of the realization of pure Being, the wise man is struck with wonder. (70)
Thus, when the falsity of space and the reality of existence have been established by this reasoning, let the real entity of air and the other elements be discerned in the same manner. (71)
Illusion (māyā) resides in one part of that existent reality; space is conceived as residing in one part of that [illusion];
and wind is conceived as residing in one part of that [space]. (72)
Dryness, touch, motion, and velocity—these are considered the attributes of air.
Furthermore, the three natures of existence, māyā, and space are also said to reside within air.

The existence [of the thought] "the wind exists" is the reality within the wind; when separated from that which is real, it is a state devoid of essence—a sound moving in space, whose nature is illusion.
It was previously stated that the persistence of the conscious self exists everywhere, whereas that of space does not;
how then can your current statement regarding the persistence of space not contradict what was said before? (75)

The previous statement was "the persistence of the defect is not [there]," whereas this one now states merely "the persistence of the word"; how, then, can there be a contradiction in the speech? (76)

If it be argued that [the world] is non-existent because it is distinct from an existent entity, then how could there be even the absence of being composed of māyā, due to the inequality of unmanifested māyā? (77)
In this context, the very state of lacking an essential reality (niṣtattvarūpatā) is the cause of its being illusory (māyātva).
That [state] is equal in both the power (śakti) and its effect (kārya), which are distinguished by being manifest (vyakta) or unmanifest (avyakta). || 78 ||

Since the discrimination between existence and non-existence is the subject at hand, let that be reflected upon; as for the internal subdivisions of the non-existent, what is the use of considering them here? (79)
The portion of air remaining after the real entity of Brahman has been discarded is false, just like the sky;
having dwelt for a long time within the air, one should abandon that false air.
One should likewise contemplate the fire and the wind as being situated below;
regarding these coverings of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there is an investigation into their relative deficiency or excess.
Fire is conceived as being less than one-tenth of air;
such is the gradation among the five elements according to the tenfold proportions mentioned in the Purāṇas.
Fire consists of heat and light, and its prior continuity is present here as well;
fire exists as a real entity, possessing both sound and touch. (83)
Of fire, which is composed of the elements of earth, water, ether, and air, its own inherent quality is form;
there, let everything else belonging to the existent [earth] be mentally separated. (84)
When the fire has been separated by means of mindfulness, and falsehood has been perfumed, one should contemplate that the waters have been conceived as being less than one-tenth [of the total]. (85)
These waters exist as the essence of emptiness, endowed with sound and touch; they possess form through the persistence of other qualities, while their own specific quality is taste. (86)
When the water has been mentally separated and its falsity has been instilled, one should contemplate that the earth is conceived as being less than ten parts within the water. (87)
There exists an element whose essence is voidness; sound and touch are its intrinsic natures, while taste and smell belong to subsequent elements. Let its true existence be discerned. (88)
When existence is separated [from its essence], false earth remains;
the cosmic egg, situated within that earth, is less than one-tenth of the extent of the earth. (89)
Within the cosmic egg reside the fourteen worlds;
within these worlds dwell the bodies of living beings, each according to its kind.
When the real entity has been distinguished from the bodies of the worlds within the cosmic egg, even if those unreal eggs and so forth appear, what harm is there in that appearance? (91)
When the elements, their derivatives, and māyā have been thoroughly permeated by the realization of their non-identity,
this cognition that "the existent reality is non-dual" never undergoes subversion.

Just as the performance of various purposeful actions is observed in the world regarding duality— which, though distinct from absolute non-duality, takes the form of the earth and other elements— so too is it [the case] here.
In whatever manner the diversity of the world is conceptualized through various arguments by the Sāṃkhyas, the Kāṇādas, the Buddhists, and others—let it be so in that very way. (94)
Since the reality of non-duality is disregarded by other proponents who are free from doubt, what loss is there for us who likewise disregard that duality? (95)
If the disregard for duality is well-established, the non-dual intellect will become firm;
when that [intellect] is stable, this person is said to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 96 ||
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Abiding in this even at the time of death, one attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman. 97.

When there is the perception of mutual identity between the real non-duality and the unreal duality, that very cognition of their distinction is the end of that [perception of identity], and nothing else. 98.
Or rather, let there be the separation of the vital breath at the time of death as is well known;
even at that time, there is no returning for one who has gone beyond delusion. 99.
Whether healthy and seated, or diseased and rolling on the ground, or even unconscious, he may give up his life; there is no doubt whatsoever about this.
Even if it is forgotten, what has been studied day by day during dreaming and deep sleep does not remain unstudied on the following day; thus, the knowledge of reality is never lost.

Knowledge produced by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) does not perish without a more powerful means of valid cognition; nor does it perceive any means of valid cognition more powerful than the Vedānta. || 102 ||
Therefore, the non-duality of Being established by the Vedanta is not sublated;
thus, even at the time of death, liberation remains established through the discernment of the elements.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Discernment of the Elements."
The Third Chapter, titled "Discrimination of the Five Sheaths.
That Brahman which is hidden in the cave [of the heart] can be understood through the discrimination of the five sheaths; therefore, the five sheaths are now analyzed in detail. (1)
Within the body is the vital breath (prāṇa), within the vital breath is the mind (manas);
beyond that is the agent, and beyond that the enjoyer—this is the succession of the cave (guhā). (2)
Born from the semen produced by the food consumed by the father, the body grows through that very food;
it is composed of food (annamaya), not the Self, because prior to birth and after death, such food is absent. || 3 ||
If there were no self in a previous birth, how could that birth have been accomplished? If there were no self in a future birth, why would one not experience here the karma accumulated in this life?
The vital air (vāyu) consisting of prāṇa, which bestows strength upon the body and is the activator of the senses, is not the Self, because it is devoid of consciousness. || 5 ||
He who, deluded by states such as desire, conceives of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" in the body, the home, and so forth, is not the self consisting of mind.
In the states of dissolution and sleep, [the intellect] remains latent; upon the awakening of the body, it pervades it as far as the tips of the nails.
The intellect, when endowed with the reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā), is not the Self, though it bears the designation "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya).
The internal organ undergoes modification through its functions as agent and instrument;
these two, consciousness and the mind, exist internally and externally with respect to one another.
A certain inward-turned state of consciousness, which bears the reflection of bliss,
dissolves in the form of sleep during the enjoyment of merit or when that enjoyment has ceased.
Because it is occasional, even this self consisting of bliss cannot be the [ultimate] Self;
for that bliss which serves as the archetype is the Self, since it exists at all times. (10)
Now, one might object: "Granted that from the body up to the objects ending with the bliss of sleep, there may not be the nature of the Self; yet, no other [Self] whatsoever is experienced. (11)
"Granted, sleep and all the rest are experienced, but nothing else;
nevertheless, who can deny that by which these very things are experienced? (12)
Because it is self-experienced, it possesses no state of being an object of experience;
because there is no other knower or knowledge, it is unknowable, yet not due to non-existence. (13)

For those whose intrinsic natures consist of sweetness and so forth, which impart their own qualities to other things, there is no need for them to receive those [qualities] back from themselves, nor do they require anything else to bestow them upon others. (14)

Even in the absence of another object of cognition, these [cognitions] possess that very nature; let there be no such thing as being experienced by another, yet their essence as consciousness is never lost. (15)
He becomes self-luminous; he shines before all this universe. Following him alone as he shines, the world shines by his light.
By what other means could they know that by which all this is known?
By what could one know the knower? For a means of knowledge is effective only with respect to an object to be known. (17)
He knows all that is to be known; there is no other knower than him.
He is distinct from both the known and the unknown, being the very nature of pure consciousness.
How can a scripture awaken one in whom no experience of awakening arises by any means? It is like a clod of earth in human form.
Just as the statement "I have a tongue" serves only to cause shame, so too is the thought "I must understand the understanding that is to be understood"—it is likewise [shameful]. (20)
In whatever exists in the world, by disregarding that very thing, the realization that "that which is pure awareness alone is Brahman"—such an intellect is the ascertainment of Brahman. (21)
Upon the abandonment of the five sheaths, when nothing remains but the consciousness of the witness, that very self becomes its own true nature; for it is impossible for that [self] to be a void.
First of all, there is indeed that which is called "self" because it is not an object of dispute.
If there were dispute even regarding the self, who could be the opponent in that case? (23)
However, non-existence is not pleasing to anyone except through delusion;
for this very reason, the Śruti declares the sublation of those who maintain such non-existence.
If one knows Brahman to be non-existent, one would oneself become non-existent;
therefore, let it not be an object of knowledge for him, but let its own existence be admitted. (25)
If one should ask, "What then is it like?", [the answer is: "It is not like anything there at all. Therefore, determine its true nature as that which is neither 'like this' nor 'like that'. (26)
Such an object of the senses is said to be "indirect" (parokṣa) in that manner;
however, an object that is not an object of the senses lacks indirectness because it is [by nature] internal. || 27 ||
Therefore, although it is not an object of cognition, this [Self] is immediate and self-luminous.
"Truth, Knowledge, Infinite"—this is the definition of Brahman found here. (28)

Truth consists in being free from sublation; yet for that which is the sole witness to the sublation of the world, tell me, by what witness is its own sublation known? For it is not accepted that there can be a sublation without a witness. (29)
When all material forms have been removed, the immaterial ether alone remains;
when all that is capable of being sublated has been sublated, that which remains at the end is indeed that [Reality] itself.
If, when all things are negated, there is nothing at all, then that very "nothing" is precisely what remains.
Only the linguistic expressions differ here; for that which is beyond negation certainly exists.

For this very reason, scripture sets aside what is to be sublated and leaves behind that which remains, in the form of the negation of what is not the Self: "This is the Self—'not this, not this. (32)
If this form could indeed be abandoned entirely, then that Self—which is devoid of such form and free from affliction—would be impossible to reach. (33)
The reality of Brahman is established, while its nature as knowledge has already been explained clearly by such statements as "because it is itself self-experience" (svayamevānubhūtitvāt). || 34 ||

Because it is all-pervasive, Brahman has no end in terms of space; because it is eternal, it has no end in terms of time; and because it is the self of all, it has no end in terms of substance—thus, infinity exists in Brahman in three ways.
Since space, time, and other entities are imagined through illusion (māyā), there is no end produced by space and the like; therefore, the infinity of Brahman is manifest.
That which is Brahman—truth, knowledge, and infinite—is that very reality;
its state as the Lord (Īśvara) and its state as the individual soul (jīva) are both imagined through two limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
There exists a certain divine power that governs all things;
beginning with that which consists of bliss, it is hidden within all objects. (38)
If the properties of entities were not constrained by their own inherent capacities, then indeed the world would fall into disorder due to the mutual confusion of those properties. (39)
Through the entry of its reflection, that power shines as if it were conscious;
through union with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of that power, Brahman itself attains the state of the Lord (Īśvara).

When there is an intention to express the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the sheath (kośa), Brahman itself attains the state of being a living soul (jīva), just as one and the same person becomes a father and a grandfather in relation to his son and grandson respectively. 41.

Just as when sons and others are not intended to be expressed, there is neither "father" nor "grandfather," so too, when the treasury of power (śakti) is not intended to be expressed, there is neither Īśvara nor the individual soul (jīva).
He who thus knows Brahman becomes Brahman himself;
since there is no birth for Brahman, he is not born again. || 43 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Discrimination of the Five Sheaths."

The Fourth Chapter, titled "Discrimination of Duality. Even by the Lord, duality is projected through the individual soul (jīva). When discrimination arises, bondage—which must be abandoned by the soul—becomes clearly manifest. (1)
"One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, but the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā (Māyin).
He, the wielder of Māyā, creates"—thus say the followers of the Śvetāśvatara branch. (2)
"In the beginning, the Self alone was this [universe]. He thought, 'Let me create.
By his volition, he created these worlds"—thus say the Bahvṛcas.
Space, air, fire, water, earth, herbs, food, and bodies—all these have arisen in succession from that Brahman; indeed, all these have emerged from this very Self.
"May I be many; may I procreate"—with this desire, having performed austerity, he created the entire world; thus says the Taittirīya.
"In the beginning, this was indeed Being alone; then it thought, 'May I become many,' and it created fire, water, food, and the egg-born and other beings—so the chanters of the Sāman say. (6)
"Just as sparks arise from a fire, so do various conscious and insentient entities arise from the Imperishable"—thus says the Śruti of the Atharvaṇikas. (7)
The world was previously unmanifest;
now it is being manifested through the two visible factors of name and form, which are clearly evident in Virāṭ and the others.
[From him came] Virāṭ, Nārāyaṇa, Manu, cows, donkeys, horses, goats, and sheep.
The Vājasaneyins state that the conflict extends as far as the ant.
"Having assumed another form, the Lord entered the body as the individual soul (jīva). Thus those Śrutis declare that the state of being a jīva arises from the maintenance of the vital breaths.

That which is consciousness as the substratum, that which is the subtle body (liṅgadeha), and the reflection of consciousness residing in the subtle body—the conjunction of these is called the individual soul (jīva). || 10 ||
The Māyā belonging to Maheśvara possesses a power of delusion, just like its power of creative manifestation;
it is this [Māyā] that deludes that individual soul (jīva).
Having fallen into a state of powerlessness through delusion, one who is immersed in the body grieves;
all this duality has been briefly described as created by the Lord. 12.
In the *Saptānnabrāhmaṇa*, duality created by the individual soul (*jīva*) is elaborated;
the Father produced the seven foods through knowledge and action. (13)
One part of food is for mortals, two parts are for the gods, and the fourth is for animals;
this threefold application of foods is for the sake of the self.
Rice and other grains, the new- and full-moon sacrifices, milk, as well as the mind, speech, and breath—let it be understood that these are the sevenfold nature of food. (15)
Although these were created by the Lord in their essential form,
nevertheless, through knowledge and action, the individual soul made them its food.
The world, which is the work of the Lord and the object of enjoyment for the individual soul, is endowed with both;
it should be understood in this way, just as a woman is born of her father but is enjoyed by her husband. (17)
The volition of the Lord, consisting of the activity of *māyā*, is the means for the birth of beings;
the volition of the individual soul (*jīva*), consisting of the activity of the mind, is the means for experience. (18)
When a single kind of object, such as a jewel created by the Lord, exists, its enjoyment is held to be manifold because of the diversity of the mental states of the enjoyers. (19)
One rejoices upon finding a jewel, while another becomes angry at not having found one;
but the dispassionate person merely observes this and neither rejoices nor feels anger.
The three forms residing in the jewel—namely, the pleasant, the unpleasant, and the indifferent—are created by living beings; the form created by the Lord is common to all three.

Whether she is a wife, a daughter-in-law, a sister-in-law, a mother-in-law, or a mother— though a woman is divided in many such ways by the cognition of her various correlates, she does not differ in her essential nature.
Surely, let the cognitions differ, but the form does not differ; for no excellence produced by a living being is seen in the body of a woman. (23)
Let it not be so; for while one woman consists of flesh, another consists of mind. Even though there is no difference in the case of the one made of flesh, the one made of mind differs here.

If it is argued that while the mental nature [of objects] may exist in cases of error, dreams, daydreams, and memories, it does not apply to the object of cognition as measured by waking perception, [we reply: 25.
When there is sublation, however, the cognition assumes the form of the object due to its connection with the object of knowledge;
this point has been illustrated by both the author of the Bhāṣya and the author of the Vārttika. (26)
Just as copper poured into a mold takes on its likeness, so too the mind, pervading forms and other objects, is certainly seen to take on their likeness. (27)
Or, just as the world becomes the form of the manifested object through the manifestor, so too cognition, because it manifests all objects, appears to possess the form of the object. (28)
The manifestation of the cognition of the mother [of consciousness] reaches the object once it has been established;
and that [cognition], being conjoined with the object, attains the appearance of the object. (29)
This being so, there are two objects: the earthen jar and the one consisting of consciousness.
The earthen one is the object of measurement, while that which consists of consciousness is to be manifested by the witness.
Through positive and negative concomitance, it is understood that the intellect is the cause of the living being's bondage:
when this [intellect] exists, pleasure and pain exist; when it does not exist, neither of the two exists. (31)
Even in the absence of an external object, a person is bound in dreams and the like;
yet, even when such an object exists, one is not bound during meditative absorption, deep sleep, or fainting.
When his son has gone to a distant land, the father remains alive there,
yet, believing him dead due to the words of a deceiver, he weeps.
Even when that person has died, one does not weep as long as news of it has not been heard;
therefore, for every living being, the world is a mental construct that creates bondage.

If it is argued that the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda) follows here because external objects are useless, we say no; for an external object is required in order to impart its form to the mind. (35)
Or let there be external uselessness; we are not able to prevent it.
For such is the established rule: that means of knowledge do not depend upon a [previously established] purpose.
If bondage is mental duality, it is pacified by its cessation;
therefore, one should practice yoga itself—tell me, what is the use of the knowledge of Brahman? (37)
"Even when duality is momentarily stilled, the destruction of future births does not occur without the knowledge of Brahman; such is the drumbeat of Vedānta. (38)
Even while the duality created by the Lord has not ceased, one who asserts the unity of reality is able to realize non-dual Brahman by understanding that this duality is illusory in nature. (39)

But at the time of dissolution, when that [duality] has ceased, because of the absence of teachers, scriptures, and so forth, it is not possible to realize the non-dual, even though opposing duality is absent. (40)
Duality, created by the Lord, is both non-obstructive and conducive [to liberation], and it is impossible to remove; let this be so—why then should it be hated? (41)
The non-duality of the living self (jīvadvaita), however, is twofold: scriptural and non-scriptural.
One should adopt the scriptural [form] until the realization of reality (tattva) occurs. (42)
The scriptural mental world known as the inquiry into the Self and Brahman must also be abandoned once Reality is realized; such is the instruction of the Śruti. (43)
Having studied the scriptures and having practiced them again and again, the wise man,
having realized the supreme Brahman, should cast them aside like a firebrand.
Having studied the scriptures, the wise man, intent upon knowledge and realization, should discard the scripture entirely, just as one seeking grain discards the straw. (45)
Having understood that very [Self], the wise Brahmin should cultivate wisdom;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is a weariness of speech.
"Know that One alone; indeed, abandon other words," and "That which is beyond speech and mind is the Wise One"—such scriptural passages are clear. (47)
Even non-scriptural duality is of two kinds: intense and mild;
the intense consists of desire, anger, and so forth, while the other is the kingdom of the mind (mental fantasies). 48.
Both [passion and aversion] must be warded off prior to the realization of reality for the sake of attaining that realization;
for it is heard in the scriptures that one should be equanimous toward all means of attainment and maintain a state of composure. (49)
And after enlightenment, that [residual karma] must be abandoned for the sake of attaining liberation while living (jīvanmukti);
for one who is bound by the afflictions such as desire and the like, there is indeed no liberation.
"If this liberation while living (jīvanmukti) were not enjoyed, then I would be successful upon the absence of birth;
however, since you still have birth, you are successful merely by [attaining] heaven. (51)

When heaven is to be abandoned because of the defects of decay and excess, then why is this [worldly] desire and so forth—not being of the nature of the most extreme defect—not abandoned of its own accord? (52)
Even if you have realized the truth, if you do not abandon desire and the like entirely,
you will act according to your whims as one who transgresses the scriptures of action.

If there is such a thing as acting according to one's own will based on the non-dual reality of the Buddha, then what difference is there between dogs and those who perceive the truth in their consuming of impurities? (54)
Previously, before awakening, you were afflicted merely by mental defects;
now, moreover, there is the censure of the entire world—oh, the majesty of your awakening!
Do not desire to be like a village pig or similar [lowly beings]; being a knower of reality, abandon all defects of the intellect and be honored by the world like a god.
The perception of defects such as desire and the like are well-known in the scriptures on liberation as the causes for abandoning desire; seek these out and be happy.
"Let this desire and the rest be abandoned; for what loss is there in the realm of the imagination?
Yet, because it is the seed of all defects, the Blessed One has declared that it is indeed a loss. (58)
As a person dwells upon sense objects, attachment to them arises;
from attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger is produced;
from anger, delusion arises; and from delusion, the confusion of memory occurs.
From the loss of mindfulness comes the destruction of the intellect; from the destruction of the intellect, one perishes. || 59 ||
The kingdom of the mind can be conquered through non-conceptual meditative absorption; even that is easily accomplished through gradual stages by means of conceptual meditative absorption. (50)
By means of the reality of Buddhahood— empty of intellectual defects and dwelling in solitude—
one conquers the kingdom of the mind after uttering the long *praṇava*.
When that [intellect] is conquered, the mind remains devoid of activity like a mute person;
this state was described at great length by Vasiṣṭha to Rāma. (62)

When the cleansing of the mind's objects of perception is accomplished through the realization that "the visible does not exist," then the supreme bliss of Nirvana has arisen. Enough with this study of the scriptures; enough with long and mutual recitations.
For one whose latent impressions have been abandoned, no supreme state exists apart from silence.
Sometimes the intellect is distracted by karma that yields experience;
yet it may become concentrated once again through the proficiency gained from practice. (64)
The sages who have seen the further shore declare that he in whom there is no distraction does not even consider himself a knower of Brahman; they say, "This one is Brahman itself. (65)
O Brahmin, he who stands by himself in his own absolute form, having abandoned both seeing and not-seeing, is indeed Brahman; he is not merely a knower of Brahman.

The supreme pinnacle of liberation while living is attained through the abandonment of duality regarding the living self; therefore, this discrimination between the Lord and duality is presented here.

The Fifth Chapter, titled "Discernment of the Great Sayings" (Mahāvākyaviveka). That by which one sees, hears this [world], smells, articulates, and discerns what is sweet and what is not sweet—that is declared to be *prajñāna* (pure consciousness). || 1 ||

In the four-faced Indra and the gods, and among humans, horses, cattle, and so forth, consciousness is the one Brahman; therefore, even in that which consists of the intellect (prajñā), it is Brahman. || 2 ||
The Supreme Self, fully complete, abiding in this body as the witness of the intellect within one qualified for knowledge, manifests and is designated as "I. (3)
The Supreme Self, which is inherently full, is described here by the word "Brahman.
Through the reflective awareness of oneness expressed as "I am," I become that Brahman. (4)
That which is one alone, without a second, devoid of name and form, and which existed before creation—its very same nature is said to persist even now. (5)
In this context, the word "thou" (tvam) denotes a reality that transcends the body and senses of the listener;
by the word "art" (asi), oneness is expressed—let that identity be realized.
Its self-luminous immediacy is understood from the statement "this [is it]";
it is celebrated as the inner self (pratyagātman) that extends from the ego (ahaṅkāra) to the body. || 7 ||
The reality of this entire visible world is designated by the word "Brahman"; that Brahman has the nature of the self-luminous Self.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Great Sayings."
The Sixth Chapter, titled "The Lamp of the Painting.
Just as the four states are seen in a painted cloth, so too should the fourfold state be understood within the Supreme Self. (1)
Just as a cloth is washed, beaten, marked, and dyed, so too is the Self— the Virāj— impelled by the threads of the inner controller, consciousness.
In this context, it is "naturally white" (svataḥ śubhra) when washed; it is "polished" (ghaṭṭita) by being rubbed with an ointment of rice-flour paste;
it is "marked" (lāñchita) by being engraved with the forms of letters; and it is "colored" (rañjita) by the filling in of the colors. || 3 ||

By his own nature he is the conscious inner controller; as the wielder of *māyā*, he is the *sūtrātman* due to subtle creation, and this supreme one is called *virāj* for the sake of gross creation. (4)
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, living beings here— even the insentient—
exist in a state of superior and inferior, like figures in a painted cloth.
The various appearances of clothing on the figures depicted in a painting are fashioned as if they were identical to the actual garments that served as the basis for the painting.

These individual manifestations of consciousness, which are superimposed upon the body by means of pure awareness, are called "living beings" (jīva) at the end of a kalpa; they transmigrate in manifold ways.

Just as the ignorant say that the colors situated in the appearance of a cloth reside in the supporting cloth itself, so too do they perceive the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva) as residing within consciousness (cit).
Just as the reflection of cloth is not depicted for mountains and such things situated in a painting,
so too the reflections of consciousness are not [depicted] for clay and such things situated in the world of manifestation.
"This saṃsāra is the ultimate reality, firmly attached to the substance of one's own self"—this delusion is ignorance (avidyā), and it is removed by knowledge (vidyā). || 10 ||
The transmigratory existence belongs to the individual soul (jīva), which is a reflection of the Self, and not to the reality of the Self;
such understanding constitutes knowledge (vidyā), and it is obtained through inquiry. 11.

Therefore, one should always investigate the world, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self; when the notions of the individual soul and the world are sublated, only one's own Self remains. || 12 ||
It is not a lack of cognition that constitutes the sublation of those two, but rather the ascertainment of their falsity;
otherwise, people would be liberated effortlessly even during deep sleep, fainting, and the like. (13)
Even when only the Supreme Self remains, there must be a firm conviction in its reality;
otherwise, if the world were not forgotten, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) would be impossible.
Knowledge born of inquiry is twofold: indirect and direct.
Among these, this inquiry is concluded upon the attainment of direct knowledge. || 15 ||
If one knows that "Brahman exists," that is merely indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna).
If one knows "I am Brahman," that is called direct realization (sākṣātkāra). || 16 ||

For the sake of accomplishing the direct realization of that [reality], the true nature of the self is analyzed, by means of which one is immediately liberated from the entire cycle of transmigratory existence. (17)
The immutable, Brahman, the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord (īśa)— thus consciousness is fourfold,
just as there are the space within a jar, the great space, the space in water, and the space in a cloud.
The water contained within the space delimited by a jar reflects the sky along with its clouds and stars; this is what is called the "water-sky. (19)
In the midst of the great space, that circle of clouds which is perceived exists as a reflection; therein, the cloud-space is situated within the water. (20)
The water, which has the form of a portion of a cloud, exists in the shape of ice;
therein, this reflection of the sky is inferred because of its lack of liquidity. (21)
As the presiding principle, the consciousness delimited by the two bodies remains unchanging like a peak; thus it is called the "unchanging one" (kūṭastha).
The intellect is superimposed upon the immutable; therein lies the reflection of consciousness.
Through the support of the vital breaths, it becomes the individual soul (jīva) and is joined with the cycle of transmigration. || 23 ||

Just as the space within a jar is entirely concealed by the [limited] space of the water, so too is the immutable Self concealed by the individual soul (jīva); this is called mutual superimposition (anyonyādhyāsa). || 24 ||
This living self never distinguishes itself from the immutable [Self];
let it be understood that this beginningless non-discrimination is root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā). || 25 ||
Ignorance (avidyā) is conceived as being twofold, by way of its forms as distraction (vikṣepa) and concealment (āvṛti).
Concealment is the imposition that "the immutable (kūṭastha) neither shines nor exists. (26)
An ignorant person, when questioned by a wise man, does not awaken to the immutable;
even having understood it, he says, "The immutable does not shine, nor does it exist. (27)
"How can there be ignorance in that which is self-luminous? Without it, how can there be obscuration?"—this very direct experience devours such webs of reasoning as these. (28)
If there is no confidence in one's own experience and reasoning is also unstable, how could one who considers himself a logician attain certainty regarding reality? (29)
If reasoning is required for the ascent of the intellect, then let it be reasoned in accordance with one's own direct experience; do not engage in fallacious reasoning.
One's own experience has been demonstrated regarding both ignorance and its concealment;
therefore, let it be reasoned that the immutable consciousness is not in contradiction [with them]. || 31 ||
If that [ignorance] is indeed the obstacle, by what could this obscuration be experienced?
Let it be seen, however, that the obstacle is actually the failure of discrimination, which exists in one who possesses knowledge of reality. (32)

Consciousness, which is immutable and veiled by ignorance, is superimposed upon the two bodies—just as silver is [superimposed] upon a mother-of-pearl shell; for this is indeed the superimposition of projection (vikṣepādhyāsa).
The reality of this "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) is observed in the silver located in the mother-of-pearl;
likewise, selfhood and substantiality are observed as belonging elsewhere within the mental projection.
Just as the blue surface and triangular shape are concealed in mother-of-pearl, so too are non-attachment, bliss, and other qualities concealed within the immutable Self (kūṭastha). || 35 ||
Just as in the example of superimposition there is that which is called "silver," so too is the conviction "I" the name for the projection superimposed upon the immutable [Self]. (36)
Perceiving this "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) by itself, one conceives it as "silver";
likewise, perceiving the self (sva) by itself, one conceives it as "I. (37)

But this [self-nature] is described as distinct; likewise, let it be observed that "mineness" and "I-ness" are seen in both cases, as both the universal and the particular are understood therein. (38)
"Devadatta himself should go; you yourself should observe likewise;
I myself am not able"—thus it is used in common parlance. (39)
Just as one thinks, "This is silver" or "This is a cloth," so too,
in relation to these [notions] such as "that," "you," and "I," one conceives of them as being "self."
Since "I-ness" is distinct from the immutable [Self], what does that have to do with you?
It is my view that this very meaning of the word "self" is the immutable one. (41)
If it is argued that selfhood is the exclusion of otherness, then the exclusion of otherness would indeed be exactly what the speaker intends as the immutability of the Self. (42)

"Self" (*ātman*) is a synonym for "one's own" (*sva*); therefore, in common usage, the two are not employed together. Consequently, being one's own (*svatva*) and being a self (*ātmatva*) exclude each other. (43)
If it is observed that "the jar does not know by itself," and thus selfhood is seen in insentient things like jars, then let it be so observed on the basis of the existence of the Self. (44)
The distinction between the conscious and the unconscious is certainly not created by the immutable Self;
rather, it should be understood as being produced solely by the reflection of the intellect (buddhi). 45.
Just as the appearance of consciousness is imagined through delusion within the immutable [Self], so too are insentient things such as jars imagined within that very same [Self]. (46)

If it is argued that, just as "selfhood" (svatva) persists even when the body ends, so too the notions of "you" and "I" persist everywhere; therefore, these two [the body and the ego] must also be the Self. (47)

Even though "selfhood" (ātmatva) persists through both [the self and the non-self], it does not constitute their true essence; therefore, just as with correctness (samyaktva) and the like, selfhood cannot possibly belong to them. (48)
In this world, it is well known that "self" and "other," as well as "end" and "non-end," exist in a state of mutual opposition; of this there is no doubt. (49)
Let it be accepted that the Self is itself immutable, being the direct opposite of otherness;
this "I" is imagined within the Self as the counter-correlative to finitude.

Although the difference between "I-ness" (ahantā) and "belonging-to-me-ness" (svatva) is as clear as that between "this" (rūpya) and "that" (idanta), people have fallen into delusion and have asserted their identity.
In this context, it is precisely the superimposition of identity that has been produced by the previously mentioned ignorance;
when ignorance ceases, its effect is also withdrawn. (52)
The identity with the veil of ignorance perishes through knowledge alone;
however, the nature of the projection (vikṣepa) is seen to persist until the exhaustion of prārabdha karma.
"Even when the appropriation has perished, the effect awaits for a moment"—so say the logicians; why should that not be possible for us as well? (54)
By those [threads] numbering as many days, such a moment is described;
let it be understood here that this is a moment suitable for a delusion spanning countless kalpas. (55)
Without a measure that withstands scrutiny, they conceptualize things in vain;
for those who speak in accordance with scripture, reason, and experience, what indeed is difficult to accomplish? (56)
Let the dispute with wicked logicians rest; I shall speak of the subject at hand:
O friend, the identity of the immutable and the transforming is established.
All those worldly logicians who consider themselves wise wander about in delusion;
out of folly, they disregard the Śruti and rely solely upon mere reasoning.
There, some who lack the comprehension of what precedes and follows shamelessly apply mere semblances of sentences to their respective positions. (59)
The Lokāyatas and the common folk, relying on fallacious perception, assert that the self is the aggregate beginning from the immutable [primordial matter] and ending with the body. (60)
In order to establish their own position as Vedic, they accepted the treasury consisting of food as the authoritative proof for Virocana’s doctrine.
Because the death of the body is observed here upon the departure of the living self (jīvātman),
others— the Lokāyatas— assert that the self is indeed distinct from the body.
I maintain that the cognition "I," which is regarded as being perceptible, leads to the conclusion that the self is distinct from the body, based on such linguistic usages as "I speak. (63)
The quarrel among the sense organs, such as speech and the rest, is heard in the Vedas;
therefore, consciousness belongs to them, and for that very reason, they possess the nature of the Self.
The followers of Hiraṇyagarbha, who maintain that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the self, have declared as follows:
"Even when the senses such as sight are lost, one continues to live as long as the vital breath exists. (65)
The vital breath (prāṇa) remains awake while others sleep; the preeminence of the prāṇa and other qualities have been heard in the Śruti.
The sheath consisting of prāṇa has thus been fully explained in detail. || 66 ||
People devoted to meditation consider the mind to be the self;
thus, the non-enjoyership of the vital breath (prāṇa) is evident, and consequently, the mind possesses the quality of being the enjoyer.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
since it is heard in scripture that the sheath consisting of mind (manomaya-kośa) is the Self, the mind is thus called the Self.
Proponents of momentariness claim that consciousness is the self, because it is clearly understood that the mind has consciousness as its root. (69)
The internal organ (antahkarana) is twofold: the function of "I" (aham-vrtti) and the function of "this" (idam-vrtti).
The function of "I" would be consciousness (vijñāna), while the function of "this" would be the mind (manas).
It is clear that this state of the mental modification (vṛtti) is the seed of the notion of "I";
for without knowing one's own Self, one never knows anything external.

Since the occurrence of birth and destruction happens at every moment within the scope of cognition, consciousness is therefore momentary; it is self-luminous by virtue of its own direct apprehension.
The scriptures declare that this sheath consisting of consciousness is the individual soul (jīva), and all of saṃsāra—including birth, death, pleasure, and so forth—belongs to it. (73)
Consciousness is momentary and not the self, like a flash of lightning or the blinking of an eye;
because no other [self] is perceived, the Mādhyamikas have declared it to be empty. (74)
In such passages as "this was indeed non-existent," it is precisely this [world] that is heard;
therefore, the entire world, consisting of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, is constructed by delusion. (75)
The existence of the self follows from the absence of a groundless delusion;
furthermore, even that which is empty possesses a witness, otherwise your statement regarding it would not be possible.
Different from that which consists of consciousness is the one consisting of bliss, which is more internal;
"it exists"—thus indeed it should be perceived—such is the Vedic vision. 77.
In that regard as well, proponents dispute in many ways—whether [the self] is minute, large, or intermediate—relying respectively upon scripture and reasoning. (78)
Those who know the intermediate spaces say it is minute because of its movement through the subtle channels;
it moves within those [channels] that are equal to a thousandth part of a hair. (79)
"This Self is subtler than the subtlest and more minute than the minute."
The sacred scriptures declare its atomic nature by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Furthermore, another Śruti declares: "The individual soul (jīva) should be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again into a hundred parts. (81)
The Digambaras assert the state of being "middle" (madhyamatva) from the feet to the head,
because of the observed pervasion of consciousness and because of the scriptural authority extending even to the tips of the nails.
The movement within the subtle channels occurs through subtle constituent parts, just as one puts on a bodice with both hands from the gross body. (83)
Furthermore, by means of going and coming, there is entry into bodies that are smaller or larger;
therefore, it is well-established that the soul possesses a medium size. (84)
If it were so that destruction occurs just as in the case of a jar once it has been praised, then who could prevent the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done? (85)
Therefore, the Self is indeed great; it is neither atomic nor of intermediate size.
Like space, it is all-pervading, partless, and thus accorded by the Śruti.
Having spoken thus, they fell into many disputes even regarding its specific nature:
"Is it of the nature of the insentient (acid-rūpa), or of the nature of the sentient (cit-rūpa), or even of the nature of both the sentient and the insentient (cid-acid-rūpa)? (87)
The Prābhākaras and the logicians assert its non-conscious nature:
"The self is a substance like space, and consciousness is its quality, like sound. (88)
Desire, aversion, effort, merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, as well as their latent impressions—these qualities of his are said to be like those of consciousness. (89)
Through the conjunction of the self with the mind, the qualities arise by the power of one's own unseen merit (adṛṣṭa); then they dissolve in deep sleep due to the cessation of that unseen merit.
Because it possesses consciousness, this [self] is sentient and endowed with desire, aversion, and effort;
it would be the agent of merit and demerit and the experiencer [of their results], due to its possession of suffering and so forth. (91)
Just as in this world the palate and other [organs] are produced by the power of karma, so too in another world, desire and the like are generated within the body by karma. (92)
And thus, even for that which is omnipresent, going and coming would be possible;
they said that the entire section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is the authority in this matter. (93)

That which remains in deep sleep, the sheath consisting of bliss, is the Self characterized by indistinct consciousness; it is the innermost sheath of these [others], and its qualities are those [of the preceding sheaths].

Observing that consciousness is latent and that the self possesses the nature of both cognition and non-cognition, the Bhāṭṭas declare this based on the recollection that arises from having previously perceived consciousness. (95)
The memory of dullness at that time, in the form "I slept then having become dull," is not possible in any way without the prior experience of dullness. (96)
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that the seer’s vision is not lost even during sleep;
therefore, this Self shines like a firefly by means of both non-manifestation and manifestation. (97)
The dual nature of that which is partless cannot be established in any way;
therefore, the discerning Sāṃkhyas declare that the Self is of the very nature of consciousness alone. 98.
The portion of inertia is the nature of Prakṛti; it is subject to transformation and consists of the three guṇas.
That Prakṛti proceeds for the sake of the experience and liberation of consciousness (cit). 99.
Bondage and liberation are attributed to unattached consciousness due to the non-apprehension of its distinctions;
this is for the sake of establishing the order of bondage and liberation, just as the ancient teachers [postulated] a distinction within consciousness.
That which is beyond the Great (mahat) is called the Unmanifest (avyakta), which is Prakṛti; likewise, the scriptural statement "for he is unattached" is clear [in its meaning]. 101.
For the Yogas declare that the Lord is the regulator of Prakṛti when it is active in proximity to consciousness; He is heard in scripture to be superior to the individual souls (jīvas). 102.
For the Śruti declares: "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas";
indeed, in the Āraṇyaka, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) has been established with great care.
Even here, disputants quarrel with their respective arguments; indeed, they cite even scriptural passages according to their own wisdom for the sake of strengthening their positions. (104)

Unconnected with afflictions, karma, and its fruition, as well as with the latent dispositions based upon them, the Lord would be a particular kind of person; like a living being (jīva), He too would possess unattached consciousness.
Nevertheless, because he is a particular kind of person, his status as a controller is logical;
otherwise, bondage and liberation would here fall into a state of lack of regularity. (106)
In passages such as "From fear of Him... and so forth, it is heard that the supreme Self is unattached; this is logical because of its lack of attachment to afflictions, karma, and the like.

For living beings as well, there is no affliction and so forth because they are unattached; nevertheless, afflictions, karma, and the rest were previously described [as existing] due to the non-apprehension of discrimination. (108)
The logicians maintain that the Lord possesses the qualities of eternal knowledge, effort, and desire;
however, they hold that it is illogical for one who is unattached to be a controller.
Even His status as a supreme Person is due solely to His qualities and not otherwise;
thus the Śruti declares, "He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true," and so forth.
If he possessed eternal knowledge and other attributes, creation would occur perpetually;
therefore, Hiraṇyagarbha is the Lord, conjoined with a subtle body (liṅgadeha).
In the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa, its greatness is described in great detail;
yet, despite possessing a subtle body (liṅga), it lacks the status of a living being due to the absence of karma and other such factors.
Without the gross body (sthūladeha), the subtle body (liṅgadeha) is never perceived anywhere;
therefore, the Vairāja body is the Lord, possessing a head and other limbs on all sides.
"Indeed, those who contemplate the Universal Form constantly recite from the Śruti: 'Thousand-headed,' and likewise, 'Eyes on all sides. (114)
If having hands and feet everywhere were the criterion for lordship, then even a worm would possess lordship;
therefore, the four-faced god alone is the Lord, and no other person.
Sitting there for the sake of a son, they spoke thus:
"The Lord of Creatures created progeny," and so forth; these people cite such scriptural passages.
From the navel of Viṣṇu arose the Creator, born from the lotus;
therefore, the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) say that Viṣṇu alone is the Lord in this world. (117)
"Since even the wielder of the Śārṅga bow is unable to seek out the feet of Śiva, Śiva is not Viṣṇu; thus say the Śaivas who hold the Āgamas as authoritative. (118)
He also worshipped Vighneśa in order to destroy the three cities;
those devoted to the Gāṇapatya doctrine call the Lord Vināyaka.
In this way, others, out of pride in their respective positions, have maintained various divergent views by relying on the mantras, arthavādas, kalpas, and other such texts. (120)
There are those who maintain that the Lord extends from the Inner Controller down to the level of stationary objects,
because they perceive the sacred fig tree, the sun, and other such entities as the family deities (kuladaivata) of their respective lineages.
For those who investigate through logic and scripture with the desire to ascertain reality, there should be only one mode of practice; that too is clearly stated here. (122)
