One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti (primordial nature) and Maheśvara to be the wielder of Māyā;
by its constituent parts, this entire universe is pervaded. 123.
Thus, according to the sacred revelation (śruti), the logical conclusion regarding the Lord is established;
in this way, there would be no contradiction for those who maintain that the Lord extends even to the level of immobile beings.
And this illusion (māyā) consists of darkness (tamas), because it is so described in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad];
regarding its experience therein, the Śruti itself provides the proof at the sacrifice.
The Śruti declares that it is insentient and of the nature of delusion; because this is evident even to children and cowherds, the scripture has declared its infinity.
The nature of things such as sourness, the self, or a jar is indeed insentient;
that wherein the intellect becomes blunted is what worldly people call delusion (moha). (127)
Thus, from the perspective of worldly experience, all this is experienced by everyone;
yet from the perspective of reasoning, it is inexpressible, according to the Vedic scripture: "Non-being did not exist. (128)
"Non-existence did not exist, because it was manifest; nor did existence exist, because it would be sublated.
From the perspective of knowledge, that which is heard [in scripture] as 'insubstantial' (tuccha) is eternally ceased. (129)
Māyā is to be known as threefold—void, indeterminable, and real—by means of the three types of knowledge: scriptural, logical, and worldly. (130)
This [Self] displays the existence and non-existence of the world, just as a painted cloth does through its expansion and contraction. || 131 ||
For illusion would be non-independent, since it is not perceived without consciousness;
yet even if it were independent, it would be the same, because there can be no alteration of that which is unattached.
She renders the immutable and unattached Self as if it were inert;
by means of the nature of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), she also fashioned both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). 133.
Without deviating from its immutable state, it brings about the world and so forth;
what wonder is there in Māyā, which accomplishes the utterly impossible? (134)
Fluidity in water, heat in fire, hardness in stone,
and the capacity for the impossible in māyā are established by their own nature, and not otherwise.
As long as the world does not recognize the deceiver, it maintains a sense of wonder in its mind; but once it realizes, "This is an illusion," it becomes tranquil.
For objections indeed proliferate against those who assert that the world is a real entity;
but one cannot object against illusion (māyā), because it is of the very nature of being subject to objection. 137.
If there were an objection even to my objection, then that objection would be raised by me against the objection; therefore, that objection must be refuted, and it should not be further contested.
Since Māyā, whose sole body is wonder, takes the form of an objection, its resolution must be sought with diligent effort by the wise. (139)
If you say that its very nature as illusion must be determined, then determine it: let the definition of illusion as it is well-known in the world be examined. (140)
"That which cannot be defined, yet appears quite clearly—that people have designated as 'illusion' (māyā) in cases such as Indra’s net. (141)
This world appears clearly, yet its true nature is impossible to define;
therefore, behold this world as consisting of illusion (māyāmaya) with an impartial mind. (142)
When all the scholars began to investigate, ignorance appeared before them in certain stages. (143)
How are entities such as the body and the sense organs produced by effort?
Or how is consciousness present therein? When this is asked, what is your answer? (144)
If this is the very nature of effort, how was it known by you?
For both positive and negative concomitance have been refuted due to the futility of effort. (145)
"I do not know what this is"—in the end, you alone are my refuge; for this very reason, the great ones proclaim her to be a magical illusion (indrajāla). 146.
What other illusion is there like this: that the semen, while still dwelling within the womb, perceives the positions of hands and head with various sprouts emerging,
and is subsequently encompassed by the many states of childhood, youth, old age, and disease in their turn?
It sees, eats, hears, smells, and likewise goes and comes. (147)

Just as in the case of a body, a banyan seed, and so forth, let it be observed after thorough investigation: where is the seed and where is the tree? Therefore, conclude that this is mere illusion (māyā). 148.
Those logicians and others who harbor pride regarding etymology have been well-instructed by Harṣamiśra and others in works such as the *Khaṇḍana*. (149)
Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be subjected to logical reasoning;
for the world, with its inconceivable structural form, is beyond even the mind. 150.
Determine that *māyā* is the seed of the power of inconceivable manifestation;
that very same single seed of *māyā* is experienced in deep sleep. (151)
The world of waking and dreaming is dissolved therein like a tree within its seed;
therefore, the latent impressions (vāsanās) of the entire world reside therein.
Consciousness is reflected in those mental impressions (vāsanās) of the intellect;
like the sky through clouds, let the indistinct appearance of consciousness (cidābhāsa) be inferred. 153.
That seed, possessing an appearance [of consciousness], sprouts in the form of cognition;
therefore, the reflection of consciousness appears clearly within the intellect. (154)
It is heard in the Śruti that [the Lord] creates the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) by means of the manifestation of Māyā;
these two are well-established like the space within a cloud and the space within water. 155.

Illusion functions like a cloud; the latent impressions of the intellect are like the frost within that cloud; and the reflection of consciousness remains like the sky situated within the frost. (156)

The reflection of consciousness is dependent on Māyā; in the Śruti, he is called the Illusionist (māyī), the Great Lord (maheśvara), the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), the Omniscient One, and indeed the Source of the Universe. 157.
Having introduced the state of deep sleep as consisting of bliss, the Śruti declares:
"He is the Lord of all. This is that very Lord spoken of in the Veda. (158)
One should not at all dispute his possession of omniscience and other such qualities, because the meaning of the scriptures is inconceivable and because everything is possible within illusion. (159)
No person whatsoever is capable of altering that which He creates as the universe; therefore, He is called the Lord of All. || 160 ||
The latent impressions (vāsanās) of the minds of all living beings without exception reside therein; everything is embraced by them, and for that reason he is called the Omniscient One.
Because latent impressions (vāsanās) are imperceptible, omniscience is not observed;
however, having seen that [omniscience] in all cognitions, let it be inferred from the latent impressions. (162)

Indeed, by abiding within the sheaths (kośas), primarily that consisting of consciousness and others as well, and by governing them from within, it attains the state of being the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin). || 163 ||
Abiding within the intellect, the inner self is not perceived by it; yet, having the intellect as its body, it controls the intellect from within—thus it is proclaimed by the Veda. (164)
Just as a thread exists within a cloth by way of being its material cause, so too does this [Self] abide everywhere, because it is the material cause of everything. || 165 ||
The thread is internal even to the cloth, and the fiber is internal even to the thread; let that wherein the rest of internality resides be inferred. (166)
Even when the inner, second, and third skins are visible, this innermost one is not seen; therefore, the determination [of its existence] is made through reasoning and scripture alone.
Just as a cloth is the body of the threads because it exists in the form of the cloth,
so too everything is his body because it exists in the form of everything.
Just as a cloth necessarily undergoes contraction, expansion, movement, and so forth,
there is not even the slightest degree of independence in the cloth.
Likewise, this inner controller (antaryāmin), by whatever latent impression (vāsanā) and in whatever manner it is transformed, necessarily becomes exactly so; of this there is no doubt. (170)
The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine. 171.
All beings consist of consciousness and reside within the heart;
indeed, it is the Lord, who is their material cause, who undergoes transformation therein.
The cage of the body and so forth is the machine; the mounting upon it is the sense of ego-identification. Engagement in what is prescribed and prohibited constitutes its wandering. (173)

By means of his own power, the Lord undergoes transformation through the form consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) and by way of the nature of its activity; for that is indeed a delusion produced by Māyā.
By the statement "He controls from within," the very same meaning heard in the Śruti is intended;
this principle should be applied with the intellect to all cases, beginning with the earth. (175)
I know what is dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is adharma, yet I have no aversion to it.
Whatever I am directed to do by whichever deity resides within my heart, that I perform.
One should not entertain the doubt that "there is no purpose served by human effort," because the Lord manifests even in the form of human effort. (177)
The activity of the Lord arising from such a cognition must not be obstructed;
nevertheless, through that cognition, there arises in the Lord the realization of His own self as being unattached. (178)
"To that extent alone is liberation," so say the Śrutis and the Smṛtis;
and it has been declared by the Lord Himself: "The Śruti and the Smṛti are My very commands. (179)
For it is heard in scripture that "from fear of Him," which establishes His command as the cause of fear;
this constitutes His status as the Lord of All, distinct from His nature as the Inner Controller. (180)
"Indeed, by the command of this Imperishable," so says the Śruti;
and "He has entered within as the ruler of these people," so too says the Śruti. (181)
He is the source of the world, since he is the cause of its origin and dissolution;
for manifestation and disappearance are considered to be birth and destruction. (182)
By the power of the karma of living beings, this [Self] manifests the entire universe that was dissolved within itself, just as a cloth is spread out. (183)
Furthermore, by the power of the exhaustion of the karma of living beings, He causes the entire universe to vanish into His own self, just as a rolled-up cloth is unrolled. (184)
Night and day are sleep and awakening; these two, creation and dissolution, are like closing and opening the eyes, or like silence and the kingdom of the mind. 185.
Because it possesses the power of manifestation and concealment, there is no possibility here for objections concerning creation, transformation, and so forth. (186)
In his aspect of insentience, the Lord may be the cause of insentient things;
however, through his aspect of the reflection of consciousness, he becomes the cause of living beings. (187)

Tamas predominates in the fields (kṣetra), while consciousness (cit) predominates in those whose nature is consciousness; through cultivation, knowledge, and action, it attains the state of being the supreme cause.
If it is argued that the author of the Vārttika has stated that the causality of both the insentient and the sentient belongs to the Supreme Self alone and not to Īśvara, then listen.

Sureśvara states this, taking for granted that mutual superimposition between Īśvara and Brahman is established here, just as it is between the individual soul (jīva) and the immutable witness (kūṭastha). 190.
"From that Brahman, which is truth, knowledge, and infinite, there have arisen space, air, fire, water, earth, herbs, food, and bodies"—thus says the Śruti. (191)
In that case, from the perspective of superficial observation, Brahman appears as the cause, and the cause appears as real; therefore, mutual superimposition is accepted. (192)
This [self] consists of mutual superimposition, like a cloth smeared with food;
through friction it attains oneness, and in that same way, it reaches a state of illusory unity.
Just as the cloud and the great sky are not distinguished by the ignorant,
so too do those who perceive only the surface see identity between Brahman and the individual soul.

Through the investigation of the intended meaning by means of indicators such as the opening statement and others, it is established that this Great Lord, the magician, creates the unattached Brahman. || 195 ||
Beginning with "Truth, knowledge, and infinite," and concluding with "from which words turn back," the determination of its non-attachment [to worldly qualities] is established. (196)
"The Illusionist creates the universe, being himself restrained therein by illusion";
thus another Śruti declares, and therefore the Lord would create. (197)
This Lord, consisting of bliss, willed, "May I become many";
He became the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, as if from deep sleep one were to enter a dream. (198)
This creation should be understood as occurring either successively or simultaneously, according to the scriptures;
for there exist two kinds of scriptural statements, and there are two kinds of dream visions. (199)
The essence of the Sūtra, known as the subtle body, consists of the aggregate of all individual souls;
because it sustains the "I-notion" (ahaṃkāra) of all, it possesses the powers of action, knowledge, and so forth. (200)
Just as this world appears indistinct when submerged in dull darkness at either dawn or dusk, so too is the universe perceived in that same way [at the time of dissolution]. (201)
Just as a cloth might be marked on all sides by being rubbed with ink,
so too is the body of the Lord marked everywhere by subtle forms.
Just as grain or a variety of vegetables sprouts from all sides,
so too is this tender sprout of the world delicate and soft.
Just as a cloth filled with colors becomes visible in the light of the sun,
or as grain becomes manifest when it has ripened into fruit, so too does the Virāj manifest its distinct form.
This chapter on the Universal Form has been declared even in the Puruṣasūkta; the wise know that all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass are His limbs. (205)
Īśa, Sūtra, Virāṭ, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and Agni;
Vighna, Bhairava, Mairāla, Mārikā, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas. || 206 ||
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; cows, horses, deer, and birds;
the Aśvattha, Vaṭa, and Āmra trees and others; barley, rice, grass, and so forth—[all these are likewise subject to the same principle]. || 207 ||
Water, stones, clay, wood, axes, spades, and so forth—all these are indeed lords; when worshipped, they bestow their fruits.

In whatever manner they worship Him, such is the fruit they obtain; for the excellence or deficiency of the fruit follows the excellence or deficiency of the worship of the object of veneration. (209)
Liberation arises only from the knowledge of the reality of Brahman and not otherwise;
for just as one's own dream does not cease without one's own awakening.
This entire world, consisting of sentient and insentient beings in the form of the Lord and the individual soul, is a dream within the non-dual reality of Brahman.
The Lord and the individual soul are these two, consisting of bliss and consciousness, who are imagined through Māyā; by them everything is imagined. (212)
The creation, beginning with the act of seeing and ending with the entry [into the body], is fashioned by the Lord;
the cycle of existence, beginning with the waking state and ending with liberation, is fashioned by the individual soul.

They do not know that non-dual reality of Brahman, which is free from attachment; thus, they engage in a futile quarrel between the individual soul and the Lord, both of whom are products of māyā. (214)
Having understood those who are always established in reality, we rejoice in them;
we indeed lament for others, yet we do not dispute with the deluded. (215)

Those beginning with the worshippers of grass and ending with the followers of Yoga rely upon the delusion of Īśvara; those beginning with the Lokāyatas and ending with the Sāṃkhyas rely upon the delusion of the individual soul (jīva). || 216 ||
When they do not know the non-dual reality of Brahman, then all of them are indeed deluded; for them, where is liberation, or where is happiness in this world? (217)
If there were a state of superior or inferior among them, let it be; what does that matter?
For a Buddha is certainly not affected by a kingdom or by begging in a dream. 218.
Therefore, those seeking liberation should not direct their minds toward the doctrines of the individual soul and the Lord;
rather, they should investigate the reality of Brahman and realize it.

If those two [theories] attain the status of being causes for the ascertainment of reality merely by way of being prima facie positions (pūrvapakṣa), let them do so; one does not fall under their control by that much alone.

If you argue that the individual soul (*jīva*) described in Sāṃkhya as the unattached, all-pervading consciousness is the same as the Lord (*īśvara*) described in Yoga, and that both are pure meanings of the word *tat* and *tvam*, then listen. (221)
The two meanings of "reality" (tattva) and "the great state" (aurabhāva) have not attained the status of our own established tenets;
rather, that particular stage is intended solely for the purpose of awakening one to non-duality (advaita). || 222 ||

Deluded by beginningless illusion, people consider the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) to be entirely distinct; therefore, for the sake of dispelling that notion, there is only the purification of those two.
For this very reason, the appropriate analogy previously correctly explained here consists of the space within a jar, the great space, the space within water, and the space within a cloud. (224)
Those two—the water and the sky-like cloud—depend upon the adjuncts of water and the cloud;
however, their supports, the pot-space and the great space, are perfectly pure.
Thus, Ānanda and Vijñānamaya are subject to Māyā and its presiding deity, Urvaśī; however, the two Brahmans, the immutable (kūṭastha) and the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), are perfectly pure.
If Sāṃkhya and Yoga are considered to be applicable to this "sheath" (kakṣa), then the body should be accepted as the Self because it is the sheath consisting of food (annamaya). (227)
If they maintain this triad— that there is a plurality of selves, that the world is real, and that God is distinct—
then they abandon the consensus of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Vedānta.

If it is argued that one has achieved the goal merely through the soul's state of non-attachment, then one would likewise achieve the goal merely through the permanence of garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth. (229)

Just as the permanence of things such as a garland is difficult to establish, so too is the non-attachment of the Self impossible to conceive while the individual soul and the Lord of the World both exist. 230.
Necessity would inevitably cause Prakṛti to bring about attachment as before; even the Lord would likewise restrain it. If that were so, what liberation could there be for him? (231)
If it is argued that attachment and restriction are caused by a lack of discrimination,
then the doctrine of Māyā has been forced upon the evil-minded Sāṃkhya.

If it is argued that "the plurality of selves must be accepted for the sake of establishing the distinction between bondage and liberation," we say no; for Māyā is capable of establishing that distinction.
Do you not see the contradiction in saying, "I shall effect that which is difficult to effect"?
Furthermore, the Śruti cannot at all tolerate the idea that bondage and liberation are real.
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor a practitioner, neither one seeking liberation nor one liberated—this is the ultimate reality. 235.
Jīva and Īśvara are both calves of the wish-fulfilling cow named Māyā;
let them both drink as they desire their duality, for the reality is indeed non-duality alone.
There is no difference between the immutable [Self] and Brahman except in name alone;
indeed, the space within a jar and the great space are never separated from one another. (237)
That very non-duality which was heard of before creation and likewise now and hereafter—even in liberation—this Māyā vainly deludes all people. (238)
Those who say, "Even these [beings] are thus deluded here by ignorance," are mistaken;
for their delusion here is not observed to be as it was before. (239)
"Therefore, the entire cycle of existence, pertaining to both this world and the next, is real;
neither the non-dual nor its absence shines forth"—such is the conviction of the ignorant. (240)
The opposite of this is clearly observed among the wise:
bound by their own respective convictions, they each think, "I am liberated. (241)
If non-duality is not directly perceived, it is because it does not appear in the form of consciousness;
if it has not appeared in its entirety, then what is it that appears as the whole of duality? (242)
Indeed, the mere indication of the general direction is equal for both;
for is not the establishment of non-duality achieved by this much, just as the establishment of duality is? (243)
Non-duality is devoid of duality; how then can this [non-duality] exist within the cognition of duality?
However, the manifestation of consciousness is not in contradiction with this duality; therefore, these two are unequal.
In that case, listen: duality is unreal because it consists of māyā;
therefore, by the process of elimination, non-duality shines forth as the reality.
The entire world is nothing but an illusion, its form being of an inconceivable construction;
having thus determined its true nature, let non-duality alone remain as the final residue. (246)
If, however, duality again appears as a real entity to you, then investigate it once more; tell me, what effort is required for that? (247)
If it is asked, "For how long?"—let this weariness be admitted in the case of duality;
however, it is not appropriate in the case of non-duality, because all misfortunes have been eliminated.

If it is argued that hunger, thirst, and so forth were observed in me previously, then let it be observed that these belong to the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) denoted by the word "I"; who would say they do not? (249)

If [the defects] were to follow even in the case of the nature of consciousness due to the superimposition of identity, then perform that superimposition; however, you must always maintain discrimination.
If it is argued that superimposition occurs instantaneously due to firm latent impressions (vāsanā),
then one must constantly cultivate discrimination (viveka) in order to firmly establish it.
One should not think that the falsity of duality is established through reasoning in solitude;
for the experience of its being an inconceivable construction is indeed self-evident.
If even consciousness possesses an inconceivable arrangement, then let it be so;
however, we call consciousness that which has a conceivable arrangement, because of its nature as eternal.
The prior non-existence of consciousness is not experienced because consciousness is eternal;
however, the prior non-existence of duality is experienced by consciousness. (254)
Duality, joined with prior non-existence, is indeed constructed like a jar or other objects; nevertheless, that construction must be considered illusory, like a magical illusion. (255)
Since consciousness is directly perceived and the falsity of anything other than it is experienced, how is it not contradictory to say that non-duality is not directly perceived? (256)
Having understood this, why are some still dissatisfied?
Tell me that. Even for the awakened Cārvāka and others, tell me, why is the self the body? (257)

If it is argued that there is no correct investigation of this [scripture] due to a defect in their intellect, then likewise, those who are dissatisfied with the meaning of the scripture do not perceive its specific excellence. (258)
"When all desires that dwell in his heart are liberated"—this scriptural fruit is indeed seen; if it is argued that it is not seen, it is nevertheless seen. (259)
"When all the knots of the heart are rent asunder"—by the remainder of the statement, desires are explained as being the very nature of those knots. (260)

Through non-discrimination, by not distinguishing between the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the conscious self (cidātman), the desires denoted by the word "kāma" arise in the form of thoughts such as, "May this be mine," and "May that be mine. (261)

Without entering into the conscious self (cidātman) and perceiving the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti) as separate, one may desire millions of objects; yet there is no obstruction once the knot [of ignorance] has been pierced.
Even when the knot [of ignorance] has been pierced, desires may still arise due to the fault of prārabdha karma;
just as your own dissatisfaction persists despite your realization, owing to the abundance of past sins.

What could desires arising from egoism, as well as bodily diseases and the like, or even the birth and destruction of trees and other things, possibly affect the Self whose nature is consciousness? (264)
If you argue that this was already so even before the breaking of the knot, do not forget this:
it is precisely this breaking of the knot that has occurred for you; therefore, you have become successful.
If the deluded do not know it thus, this is merely a knot and nothing else;
the difference between the deluded and the enlightened lies solely in the presence or absence of that knot. (266)

Whether in the state of worldly engagement or in the state of withdrawal, there is not the slightest difference between the ignorant and the enlightened regarding the body, senses, mind, and intellect. (267)
The distinction between a *vrātya* and a *śrotriya* is based on whether they have studied the Veda or not; there is no difference in their food. Let this same principle be applied here. (268)
He neither hates things that have arisen nor longs for those that have ceased; sitting like one indifferent, he is called the "breaker of knots. (269)
If indifference is to be practiced, then the word "child" (vatsa) would be meaningless;
for if you argue that the body and so forth are incapable [of acting], that is nothing but a disease.
Tell me, what is difficult for those of great intelligence to accomplish, whose wisdom is exceedingly clear, who regard the realization of reality as the destruction of disease? (271)
If you argue that the non-engagement [in worldly activity] of Bharata and others is stated in the Purāṇas, then have you not heard the Śruti which says: "Eating, playing, and finding delight"? (272)
For Bharata and others did not remain anywhere having completely abandoned food and the like like wood or stone; rather, fearing attachment, they remained indifferent. (273)
For one who is attached is oppressed in this world, while one free from attachment enjoys happiness;
therefore, attachment must always be abandoned by one who desires happiness. (274)
Not having understood the heart of the scriptures, the fool speaks in various ways;
let this be our established doctrine, which is the definitive conclusion for the ignorant. (275)
Dispassion, awakening, and cessation are companions to one another;
they generally exist together, though they are occasionally separated.
The causes, essential natures, and effects of these [categories] are distinct; their non-confusion must be understood exactly as they are through the discernment of the meaning of the treatise. (277)
The perception of defects, the desire for renunciation, and the absence of dejection regarding enjoyments—these three are the uncommon causes and so forth of dispassion. (278)
Likewise, the triad consisting of hearing and so forth, the discernment of reality as it is, and the non-recurrence of the knot—these three are considered to be the means for awakening. (279)

Yama and the others, as well as the cessation of the intellect (dhī) and the complete exhaustion of conventional discourse, are the causes and so forth for its cessation; thus, their non-confusion has been declared. (280)
The awakening to reality (tattvabodha) is primary because it directly bestows liberation;
both detachment (vairāgya) and cessation (uparama) are merely auxiliaries to that awakening.
If all three are completely ripened, they constitute the fruit of great austerity;
yet, sometimes, something may be obstructed by evil karma at some point.
For one in whom dispassion and cessation are complete, yet enlightenment remains obstructed, there is no liberation; by the power of austerity, he attains only a world of merit.
When full enlightenment is attained, the other two [aims] are necessarily bound to follow;
thus liberation is certain, yet the suffering already experienced does not perish.

The disregard for even the world of Brahmā is considered the limit of dispassion; when the firm realization of the Supreme Self arises, just as one views the body as the self, awakening reaches its completion. (285)
For forgetfulness, like sleep, constitutes the limit of cessation;
by this method, the internal gradations [of intensity] are to be determined. (286)
Because the Buddhas differ according to the variety of the actions they have undertaken, their modes of proceeding are diverse;
therefore, the wise should not be confused regarding the meaning of the treatise.
Let them proceed in whatever way according to their respective karma;
the established principle is that all-encompassing awakening is undifferentiated and liberation is equal. (288)
The world-picture is projected upon one's own consciousness as a painting on a canvas;
by means of *māyā*, let only that consciousness remain, having no dependence on anything else.
Those wise ones who constantly contemplate this "Lamp of Consciousness" are not deluded as before, even while perceiving the variegated world.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, named "The Lamp of Illusion."
The Seventh Chapter, titled "The Lamp of Satisfaction.
If a person were to know the Self as "This am I," desiring what and for whose sake would he suffer in this body? (1)
The intended meaning of this scripture is here correctly investigated; by means of it, that satisfaction which belongs to the one liberated while living is made clear. (2)

Since it is stated in the Śruti that [Brahman] creates the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) by means of the appearance of Māyā, both the individual soul and the Lord are indeed merely imagined; by them, everything is imagined.
The creation, beginning with the act of seeing and ending with the entry [into the body], is fashioned by the Lord;
the cycle of existence, beginning with the waking state and ending with liberation, is fashioned by the individual soul. || 4 ||
The Self, which is the substratum of delusion, has the nature of immutable, unattached consciousness;
through mutual superimposition, it becomes the individual soul (jīva) residing in the unattached intellect, known here as the person (puruṣa).
The individual soul (jīva), when accompanied by its substrate (sādhiṣṭhānaḥ), is qualified for liberation and the like;
however, it is not [qualified] alone, because a delusion without a substrate is nowhere established.
When it takes hold of the aspect of delusion conjoined with the aspect of the substrate, then the individual soul (jīva) conceives itself thus: "I am a transmigrating being. || 7 ||
When the delusory portion is set aside and the substrate becomes predominant, then one realizes: "I am the conscious self, free from attachment. (8)
If you ask how egoism is not appropriate regarding the Unattached One, listen:
the meaning of "I" (aham) is threefold—first, the primary; second and third, the secondary. (9)
Through the form of mutual superimposition, the bodies of the immutable and the reflection become unified; that which arises there is the primary [self], which is worshipped by the deluded.
In that regard, the knower of reality employs the word "I" alternately in both worldly and Vedic contexts for the two [states]: that which appears as distinct and that which is immutable and primary.
In worldly transactions such as "I am going," the wise person,
having clearly distinguished the reflection of consciousness from the immutable Self, intends to speak of that [reflection].
"Based on the scriptural vision that 'I am unattached' and 'I am the conscious Self,' the wise man employs the word 'I' with reference to the immutable and absolute [Self]. (13)
Knowledge and ignorance belong only to the reflection of the Self, and not to the Self itself;
and so, how could that reflection perceive, "I am the immutable"? (14)

This fault does not apply to the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), for it possesses the single nature of being immutable; since its status as a reflection is illusory, what remains is its immutability.
If even the cognition "I am immutable" were false, who could say it is not?
For the movement of a snake [seen] in a rope is certainly not accepted as real. (16)
Even by such an awakening, cyclic existence is brought to an end;
for worldly people say that the sacrificial offering must correspond to the nature of the spirit. (17)
Therefore, having distinguished that reflected person from the immutable one, the Śruti declared: "One ought to know, 'I am the immutable. (18)
An unambiguous and non-erroneous cognition of the body as the self is observed;
in order to determine that "it is not so" in this case, the word "this" (ayam) is employed. (19)

Just as the knowledge that the body is the self is sublated by the knowledge that the self is not the body, so too, he in whom this knowledge arises regarding the Self alone is liberated, even against his will.
If it is argued that "this" refers to immediacy, then let it be said:
for self-luminous consciousness is always immediate. (21)
This distinction between knowledge and ignorance— whether it be mediated or immediate—
may both exist even in that which is eternally immediate, just as in the case of the tenth [man].
At that time, his knowledge being obscured by the number nine, the tenth person—
due to delusion— did not realize, "I am the tenth," even though he was looking at those nine.
Thinking, "The tenth does not shine; it does not exist," one then regards oneself as the tenth; the wise know this to be an obscuration created by ignorance.
"He died in the river; he was my tenth!"—thus grieving, one weeps.
The wise know that weeping and the like are distractions caused by ignorance. (25)
Having then heard the word of a trustworthy person that "the tenth is not dead," one knows the tenth by way of being beyond the senses, like the worlds of heaven and so forth.
Having been shown by counting, "You yourself are the tenth," and having known this through direct perception, he rejoices indeed and does not weep.
Ignorance, veiling, and projection; the two kinds of knowledge and contentment; and the departure of sorrow—these are to be applied to the conscious self (cidātman). 28.
When the intellect-luminosity has its mind attached to saṃsāra, it never knows its own true nature, which is self-luminous and immutable. (29)
"It does not shine; it does not exist; it is unchanging"—thus one speaks by way of logical consequence.
Yet, thinking "I am the doer and the enjoyer," one falls into the delusion of distraction. || 30 ||
In such passages as "There exists the immutable one," one first knows [the Self] indirectly through hearsay;
subsequently, through inquiry, one knows: "I am indeed that immutable one. (31)

He casts off the multitude of sorrows such as "I am the doer" and "I am the enjoyer," and he is contented, thinking: "What was to be done has been done; what was to be attained has been attained. (32)
Ignorance is the veil, as is distraction, which is indirect cognition;
direct intuition is liberation from sorrow and unbounded contentment. (33)
These seven states belong to the reflection of consciousness; among them, bondage and liberation reside. Of these, three are traditionally held to be causes of bondage.
The cause of the indifferent behavior expressed as "I do not know" is ignorance (ajñāna), which is said to be conjoined with the prior non-existence of inquiry. || 35 ||
Having investigated by means other than the right path, one concludes: "This [object] does not exist, nor does it appear.
This erroneous practical behavior is held to be the effect of veiling (āvaraṇa).
The manifestation of consciousness in the form of the two bodies is said to be *vikṣepa* (distraction);
the entire sorrow consisting of agency and so forth, known as *saṃsāra*, is its binder.
Ignorance and veiling are established as occurring prior to projection;
nevertheless, even when they persist, they belong to projection alone and not to the Self.
Even prior to the arising of distraction, the latent impression (saṃskāra) of distraction certainly exists;
therefore, the state of being that [impression] is not contradictory with those two.
One should not suspect that these [states] exist in Brahman because they are superimposed upon it; for all [superimpositions] are indeed superimposed upon Brahman alone. || 40 ||

"I am transmigrating," "I am awakened," "I am free from sorrow," or "I am content"—if these subsequent states appear as belonging to the individual soul (jīva) and not to Brahman, [then one has not realized the truth]. (41)
"In that case, 'I am ignorant' and 'the manifestation of Brahman-reality does not appear from my perspective'—these two former states indeed manifest within the individual soul. (42)

They declare that Brahman is the substratum of ignorance by virtue of being its locus; I have stated that it is in the state of the individual soul (jīva) because of its identification with that ignorance. (43)
When this ignorance has been destroyed by the two-fold knowledge, the veil created by it—
which consists of the two kinds [of misconceptions] that "this does not appear" and "this does not exist"— is also destroyed.
Through indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), the state of being a cause for the persistence of non-existence is destroyed;
indeed, the state of being a cause for the persistence of non-appearance is destroyed by direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). (45)
When the obscuration of non-manifestation is destroyed through the cessation of the superimposition of the status of a living being,
the entire sorrow known as saṃsāra, consisting of agency and so forth, ceases.
When all saṃsāra has ceased, because the state of eternal liberation shines forth,
there shall be an unrestrained satisfaction, since sorrow no longer arises.
The Śruti states in the passage beginning with "If one knows the Self" that these two states—namely, immediate knowledge and the cessation of sorrow—reside within the individual soul. (48)
"This" refers to immediacy (aparokṣatva), which is of two kinds:
because the object is self-luminous, and because it is perceived in that same way by the intellect. (49)
Even at the time of indirect knowledge, the self-luminosity of the object remains the same up to Brahman, because of the realization that "Brahman exists as self-luminous. (50)
Not delineating "I am Brahman," but rather delineating "Brahman exists" in this manner, this is indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna); it is not erroneous, because no sublation is established. || 51 ||
If there were a cognition that "Brahman does not exist," it would certainly be sublated;
however, we do not perceive such a powerful cognition, and therefore it is not sublated.

If [a cognition] were erroneous merely because it does not mention an individual, then even the cognition of heaven would be erroneous, since it does not mention an individual and is seen to mention a universal. (53)
For that which is capable of being perceived directly, a cognition that is indirect is not an error;
for there is no mention of it as "indirect," and thus indirectness arises only by implication.
If it is argued that the non-apprehension of parts constitutes error, then the cognition of a jar would be an illusion;
for even that which is partless possesses the nature of having parts through the differentiation of its excluded portions. (55)
In that same way, the aspect of non-existence would be removed by means of indirect knowledge, while the removal of the aspect of non-appearance would be effected by direct cognition. (56)
The indirect knowledge that "the tenth exists" is observed to be unerring; likewise, the cognition that "Brahman exists" would be the same, as both are equally free from the veil of ignorance.
When the meaning of the statement "The Self is Brahman" has been investigated exhaustively, the [true] manifestation is revealed, just as in the case of the statement, "You are the tenth. (58)
When the question "Who is the tenth? is posed and [the answer] "You yourself" is rejected, one should count including oneself and remember that one's own self is indeed the tenth. (59)
The cognition arising from the statement "I am the tenth" is not sublated for the wise man;
there is no doubt regarding the state of being nine at the beginning, middle, or end. (60)
Having apprehended the existence of Brahman indirectly through such statements as "That [is] this," one should delineate its manifestation through statements such as "That thou art. (61)
This realization of one's own nature as Brahman does not waver in the beginning, middle, or end; therefore, it is firmly established as direct perception.
In ancient times, Bhṛgu, having first apprehended [Brahman] through the indirect definition known as being the cause of birth and so forth, then beheld its manifestation through inquiry.
Although the father of Bhṛgu did not utter the sentence "thou art this" here,
he nevertheless spoke of the subject matter for investigation, namely that food is the vital breath (prāṇa).
Having repeatedly investigated the sheaths (kośas) beginning with food and vital breath,
and having perceived the manifestation of bliss, he joined [the self] with the dissolution into the characteristic of Brahman.
Having thus stated the specific characteristic of Brahman as "Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," this [Brahman] is shown to be within the sheaths by virtue of being hidden in the cave. (66)
Having understood through indirect means that the Self is characterized by "I" and so forth, Indra,
desiring to realize it directly, went to his teacher four times.
In passages such as "The Self, indeed, this [was] in the beginning," Brahman is defined indirectly;
through the methods of superimposition and negation, Brahman is shown to be pure consciousness. (68)
Through an intermediate statement, there may arise a cognition of Brahman that is indirect;
however, through the inquiry into the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) everywhere, there arises a direct cognition.
The Great Sentence (mahāvākya) is thus declared for the purpose of achieving the direct realization of Brahman;
therefore, regarding the direct realization of Brahman through the function of the sentence, there is no disagreement.
That consciousness which, as the object of the notions "I" and "word," appears as inseparable from the internal organ, is designated by the term *sattva*. (71)

The source of the world, characterized by omniscience and other such qualities, having Māyā as its limiting adjunct, variegated by remoteness, and consisting of reality and so forth, is denoted by the word "That" (tat-pada). || 72 ||

Since being both manifest and unmanifest, as well as being accompanied by a second and yet being full, are contradictory in the case of a single entity, therefore figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) proceeds.
In sentences such as "That thou art," there is only partial indication (bhāgalakṣaṇā) as a secondary function;
it is not anything other than what occurs in the words of a sentence such as "This is that. (74)
Neither a relational connection (*saṃsarga*) nor a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is accepted here as the meaning of a sentence;
for the wise, the meaning of a sentence is held to be an indivisible, unitary essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasatva*). || 75 ||
That which shines as the inward consciousness is characterized by non-dual bliss;
and that which is of the nature of non-dual bliss is characterized solely by inward consciousness. (76)
When there occurs such a realization of mutual identity,
then indeed the non-Brahmanhood of the referent "thou" (tvamartha) is sublated,
as well as the remoteness of the referent "that" (tadartha). If this is so, hear what follows from it:
Only the inner consciousness remains, in the singular form of perfect bliss.
This being so, for those who maintain that parokṣajñāna (indirect knowledge) arises from the great sentence (mahāvākya),
their understanding of the established tenets of the scriptures shines all the more.

Let the established doctrine of the scripture stand; however, the cognition of an imperceptible object [arising] from a statement is not necessarily [valid] through reasoning alone, just as in the case of statements regarding heaven and so forth, because of the fallacy [of deviation] in the tenth [chapter].
For one who desires that the self-evident living being (jīva) be Brahman itself, its established state of being perceptible as something other would perish; oh, what a great logical consequence! (80)
"By your grace, this worldly proverb—'He who desires growth has lost even his root'—has become meaningful in its fulfillment. (81)

The individual soul (jīva), whose consciousness is conjoined with the internal organ, is capable of direct perception due to the existence of its limiting adjunct (upādhi); however, Brahman, being without such an adjunct, is not so. 82.
It is not so, because the realization of Brahman-hood has a conditioned object as its domain;
for as long as disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya) has not been attained, the conditioning adjunct (upādhi) cannot be removed.
The adjunct (upādhi) is distinguished by its association with or dissociation from the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
it is not otherwise [than this] that there exists the state of being a living soul (jīva-bhāva) or the state of being Brahman. 84.
Just as an affirmation may be a limiting condition, why should a negation not be so?
The nature of a chain is not differentiated by the distinction between gold and iron. (85)
"The activity of the Vedāntas is twofold: by way of the exclusion of what is not that (atadvyāvṛtti) and directly through affirmation (vidhimukha); thus it has been stated by the Teacher. (86)
From the abandonment of the referent "I," how could the cognition "I am Brahman" arise?
For such an abandonment of a part is not what is intended by the figurative indication based on a portion (bhāgalakṣaṇā). (87)
When the internal organ has been completely relinquished, Brahmanhood is perceived by the witness-consciousness through the statement "I am Brahman" within the remaining conscious self.
Although this witness is self-luminous, it is nevertheless pervaded by a mental modification (dhīvṛtti) just like other objects;
however, its being "pervaded by the fruit" (phalavyāpyatva) has been refuted by the authors of the scriptures.
Both the intellect and the reflection of consciousness residing within it pervade the jar;
therein, ignorance is destroyed by the intellect, while the jar is manifested by the reflection.
For the destruction of ignorance regarding Brahman, the pervasion by a mental modification (vṛtti) is required;
since Brahman is itself of the nature of self-luminosity, a reflection (ābhāsa) is not of use.
In the perception of a jar or similar objects, both the eye and a lamp are required;
however, in the perception of the lamp itself, only the eye is required. (92)
Even while remaining present, this reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) becomes one with Brahman in the highest sense;
it does not, however, produce any additional result within Brahman, just as a jar or similar object does not.
In this regard, it has been declared by scripture that [Brahman] is immeasurable and without beginning;
and by the statement "this is to be attained by the mind alone," its accessibility to the intellect is proclaimed. (94)
If one should know oneself through the statement "I am this," that awakening which delineates the manifestation of Brahman as the Self is what is designated [as such]. (95)
Granted that direct realization arises here from the Great Sentence (mahāvākya), nevertheless,
it is not yet firm, because the Teachers urge upon one further the practices of hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth.

Until the realization of the meaning of the sentence "I am Brahman" becomes firmly established, one should practice hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, accompanied by tranquility and other virtues. (97)
Indeed, there are causes for instability: the multiplicity of scriptural statements, the impossibility of the meaning, and contrary mental impressions. (98)

Just as ritual actions are heard differently due to differences in Vedic branches and differences in desires, one should not entertain such doubts here either; therefore, one should practice hearing [the scriptures]. 99.
The understanding that the purport of all the Vedantas, from their beginning, middle, and end, lies solely in Brahman as the Self, constitutes *śravaṇa*. (100)

This aphorism has been explained in the first chapter (the Samanvaya-adhyāya) by means of reasonings that produce mental composure; the second chapter is stated for the purpose of establishing the possibility [of such a Brahman]. 101.

Due to firm habituation over many births, the notion of a self with respect to the body and so forth arises again and again in an instant; likewise, the notion of the reality of the world also [arises]. (102)
This cultivation is erroneous; it ceases through one-pointed concentration.
This occurs even before the instruction on reality, through this very practice.
For this very reason, the meditations (upāstayaḥ) are also considered here in this treatise on Brahman;
for one who has not practiced them previously, they come to be through the subsequent practice of Brahman.
The wise know that practice of Brahman to consist of reflecting upon it, speaking of it, mutually awakening one another to it, and being solely intent upon it. 105.
Having understood that very [Self], the wise Brahmin should cultivate wisdom;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is a weariness of speech. 106.
For those people who worship Me, meditating on Me with undivided minds—
for those who are ever-devoted, I provide for their acquisition and preservation.
Thus, the Śruti and Smṛti constantly enjoin one-pointedness of the intellect upon the Self for the sake of destroying contrary mental impressions. 108.

When there is a cognition of something as being otherwise than its actual reality—having abandoned the true nature of that which exists in a certain way—that would be a distorted conception (*viparītabhāvanā*), just like the notion of an enemy toward one's father and so forth. (109)
This self is distinct from the body and so forth, and this world is false;
the cognition that regards the body and such as the self and regards them as real is the cultivation of error. (110)
Through the cultivation of reality, that [ignorance] perishes; one should likewise constantly cultivate the self as distinct from the body and the falsity of the world. 111.

In this context, is the cognition of the self as distinct [from the body] to be set aside—just like the recitation of mantras or the meditation on a [divine] form—and likewise the cognition of the world's falsity, or is it otherwise? (112)
Understand that it is otherwise, like eating, because its purpose is already perceived;
no one who desires to eat ever eats while reciting prayers, nor is anyone ever restricted by such a rule.
Whether he eats or does not eat, or whether he consumes according to his own will or otherwise, by whatever means possible he seeks to dispel his hunger.
One should perform the recitation according to the rule, for failure to do so results in sin;
otherwise, misfortune arises from the inversion of vowels and consonants. (115)
Just as hunger causes manifest suffering, so too is contrary cultivation;
it must be overcome by some means, for there is no sequential order of practice in this matter. (116)
The means—consisting of reflection upon that [reality] and so forth—has already been explained.
Even when one is solely intent upon this, there is no such insistence as there is in the case of meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Meditation is the continuous flow of mental cognition regarding a form, uninterrupted by anything else;
therein lies the intense application of the mind, which is by nature restless. (118)
For the mind is restless, O Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind. (119)
O virtuous one, even more than drinking the great ocean, or uprooting Mount Sumeru, or even consuming fire, the restraint of the mind is more difficult to achieve. 120.

There is no insistence on the beginning of the narration, as if one's body were bound by chains; rather, through infinite histories and the like, there is an entertainment for the intellect, just like a drama. (121)
Since the conclusion here is that consciousness alone is the Self and the world is illusory,
there can be no distraction from meditative absorption (nididhyāsana) caused by historical narratives and the like.
In agriculture, trade, service, and so forth, as well as in poetry, logic, and the like, the active intellect is distracted; because of that, the recollection of reality is impossible. (123)
Only by maintaining this continuity can one engage in activities such as eating;
for, due to the absence of extreme distraction, there is a rapid recurrence of memory.
Misfortune does not arise from the mere forgetting of reality, but rather from its inversion;
however, there is no time for it to be inverted for one who remembers it instantaneously at any moment. (125)
For one who possesses the practice of something else, there is no occasion for the recollection of reality;
on the contrary, because it is produced by that practice, reality is forcibly disregarded. (126)
"Know that alone as one; indeed, abandon other words.
Thus it is heard in scripture, and likewise elsewhere: "But [other speech] is merely a weariness of words. (127)

One may live even while abandoning food and such, but one cannot live by abandoning another scripture; why do you not live [otherwise], that you maintain such a stubborn insistence in this matter? (128)
If you ask how Janaka and others possessed a kingdom, it was due to their firm realization; if it were so for you as well, then study logic, or else engage in agriculture.
When the latent impression of false belief is firm, those who do not suffer strive according to their respective karma, out of a desire for the exhaustion of their prārabdha.
Let there not be an over-extension [of this argument] regarding those who are subject to their own karma;
or rather, tell me, who here would be able to ward off karma? (131)
In this world, both the wise and the ignorant are equal regarding their *prārabdha* karma;
yet the wise man suffers no affliction due to his fortitude, while the fool suffers because of his lack of fortitude.

On the road, even when two travelers are equally fatigued, one who knows they are not far from their destination should proceed quickly with fortitude, while the other remains behind with a dejected mind. (133)
One who has directly realized the Self, being perfectly established and free from subversion by error—desiring what, or for whose sake, would he allow his body to suffer? (134)
Because of the realization that the world is illusory, the seeker of pleasure and the object of desire are both sublated;
in their absence, suffering subsides like a lamp without oil. (135)
Knowing that nothing in the city of the Gandharvas is created by a magician’s trick, he desires it not; rather, smiling, he wishes to abandon it. (136)
Thus reflecting upon enjoyments that are pleasant only at first sight, he does not become attached to them; rather, seeing their faults, he desires to abandon them. || 137 ||
There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and likewise in its preservation;
there is pain in its loss and pain in its expenditure. Fie upon wealth, which causes such affliction! 138.
In this cage of limbs, which is a mere machine made of flesh-pañcālikā dolls, adorned with sinews, bones, and joints—what in a woman can truly be called beautiful? (139)
In such treatises as these, faults have been thoroughly elaborated;
reflecting upon them incessantly, how could one sink into sufferings? (140)
Even when tormented by hunger, one does not wish to eat poison; knowing that his thirst has been quenched by sweet food, a person who is not deluded does not desire to consume it.
If, due to the predominance of prārabdha karma, a desire for enjoyments should arise,
even then he experiences them only with distress, like one bound in forced labor.
Even those wise householders who eat them with faith continue to suffer incessantly, thinking, "Our ritual duty has not yet been fulfilled. (143)
This is not affliction here, nor is it the heat of saṃsāra; rather, it is detachment.
For the heat of worldly existence is known to have its cause in deluded cognition. (144)
One who is distressed by solitude finds satisfaction in even meager enjoyments;
otherwise, one is never satisfied even with infinite enjoyments. (145)
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. 146.
For when enjoyment is partaken of with full understanding, it leads to contentment;
and when a thief is served after being recognized, he attains the state of a friend and not that of a thief.
Even that slight enjoyment of play which belongs to the restrained mind, though it has not attained expansion,
is regarded as great because of its intensity.
A king who is bound [by his own desires] is satisfied with a mere village;
yet one who is neither bound by others nor oppressed by them does not hold even a kingdom in high regard. (149)
When discernment, characterized by the perception of defects, is awake, how can even the karma already set in motion produce a desire for enjoyment? (150)
This is not a fault, because prārabdha is seen to be of many kinds;
prārabdha is traditionally held to be threefold: that which arises from one's own desire, that which arises from lack of desire, and that which arises from the desire of another. (151)
Even thieves who indulge in negligence and those who take pleasure in the king's wives, though fully aware of their own ruin, still desire the results of the actions they have undertaken. (152)
And even by the Lord himself, this cannot be prevented here;
for the Lord himself said this to Arjuna in the Gītā. || 153 ||
Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature;
all beings follow their nature—what can restraint accomplish? (154)
If there were a remedy for things that are destined to happen, then Nala, Rāma, and Yudhiṣṭhira would not have been afflicted by sufferings. (155)
The lordship of the Lord is not diminished by that much, because even this inevitability was created by the Lord himself. (156)
This is understood precisely through the dialogue between Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa:
that there exists *prārabdha* (the momentum of past actions) even without one's own desire; listen to that. 157.
Then, by what impelled does this person commit sin, O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force? (158)
This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of passion (rajas);
it is gluttonous and most sinful—know this to be the enemy here in this world.
Bound by your own karma born of your very nature, O son of Kuntī,
you shall do that which you do not wish to do out of delusion, even against your will.

Neither those who do not desire it nor those who do desire it, even when constrained by the courtesy of others, experience pleasure and pain; for this is preceded by the desires of others and one's own past karma.
How, then, is desire negated by the phrase "desiring what"?
It is not a negation of desire, but rather a sublation of desire, like a roasted seed. (162)
But roasted seeds are incapable of producing their effects;
likewise, the desire of the wise, though it may be as one wishes, does not produce an effect because of the awakening of the [true] nature of reality. 163.
Just as a burnt seed, though incapable of sprouting, is still useful for consumption,
so too the desire of a wise man may result in little enjoyment but never in great calamity.
Because its purpose has been fulfilled through experience, the *prārabdha* karma is exhausted;
yet, due to the delusion regarding the reality of what is being experienced, attachment arises therein. (165)
"May this enjoyment not perish; may it increase further and further;
may obstacles not hinder it; I am fortunate because of this"—such is delusion. (166)
"What is not to be, will not be; and what is to be, cannot be otherwise.
This understanding, when immersed in such reflection, is the remover of delusion. (167)
Even when wealth is equal, the deluded man would go to ruin, but not the wise one;
for the deluded man suffers great calamity due to his resolve upon an unattainable object. (168)
Having realized that the object of enjoyment is composed of illusion, one withdraws attachment;
thus, even while enjoying, one forms no conceptual construction—how then could there be addiction?
Seeing the world as resembling a dream or a magician’s illusion, consisting of an inconceivable arrangement that vanishes as soon as it is seen—how could one be attached to it? (170)
Having seen one's own dream directly and perceiving one's own waking state, one should,
remaining vigilant, contemplate both of them repeatedly every day.
Having long reflected upon the complete equality of those two while awake,
and having abandoned the notion of their reality, he no longer feels attachment as before.
"This duality is a magical illusion because its arrangement is inconceivable"—for one who does not forget this, what loss can there be from the experience of *prārabdha*? (173)
The persistence of the knower of reality lies in remembering that all is a magical illusion;
the persistence regarding the jīva's experience of pleasure and pain lies in the non-attachment to what has already begun (prārabdha).
These two do not contradict each other when applied to knowledge, because their objects are distinct;
indeed, even by those who know [the truth], a magical illusion is seen as a mere diversion. (175)

If one were to establish the reality of the world and then experience the *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion), that would contradict knowledge (*vidyā*); yet, mere experience does not constitute reality. (176)
Just as enjoyment arises from imagined objects in a dream without deficiency, so too should enjoyment be understood to arise from waking objects, though they are likewise unreal. (177)

If knowledge were to negate the world by destroying its *prārabdha* (commenced karma), then it would be so; however, its negation does not occur through the mere realization of its illusory nature (*māyātva*). (178)
Without denying that this is a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), people know it as such;
likewise, without denying experience (*bhoga*), there is the cognition of its being an illusion (*māyātva*).
"But where one sees this universe as one's own Self, what could one see there, and by what?
What could one smell, or what could one speak?"—thus has it been proclaimed extensively in the Śruti. (180)
Therefore, by negating duality, knowledge arises, and not otherwise.
If it is asked how, then, there can be experience for the knower, listen: || 181 ||

Whether the scriptural passage concerns deep sleep or liberation, it has been stated very clearly in the Sūtra: "In the cases of deep sleep and union [with the Supreme], [the soul is one with Brahman]. (BrSū 4.4.16). || 182 ||
Otherwise, the status of Yājñavalkya and others as teachers would not be possible;
for if there were the perception of duality, there would be ignorance, and if there were no perception of duality, speech would not be uttered. (183)

If it is argued that non-conceptual samādhi is indeed "immediate knowledge" (aparokṣavidyā) because of the non-perception of duality therein, then why is deep sleep not likewise [considered such]? (184)
If you claim that one does not know the reality of the Self during deep sleep, then you must state that "knowledge" is simply the cognition of the Self, and not the forgetting of duality. (185)
If both [aspects] combined constitute *vidyā*, then jars and other such objects would possess half-vidyā, because they are entirely devoid of dualistic consciousness. (186)
Due to the multiplicity of distractions, such as the sound of mosquitoes and the like, the knowledge of reality would not be as firm as that regarding jars and other such objects. (187)
If you hold that the notion of a self is itself knowledge, then be happy!
If you would restrain the wicked mind, then restrain it as you please. (188)
Therefore, that which is desired should not be sought, because one perceives it to be composed of illusion;
for even though one desires, one should not desire like an ignorant person, as it is heard in the Śruti: "What is there to desire? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1).
"Passion is the mark of ignorance; let passion and the like exist in the wise.
These two scriptural statements are meaningful only when there is no contradiction [between them]. (190)
Because one perceives the non-attachment of one's own self, just as the world is perceived as illusory, the statement "for whose sake are desires? is intended to convey the absence of an enjoyer.
One does not desire one's husband, wife, and all else for their respective enjoyments, but rather for the sake of one's own enjoyment; this has been proclaimed extensively in the Śruti. (192)
Is the enjoyer the immutable consciousness-reflection, or is it of the nature of both?
In that regard, the immutable one cannot become an enjoyer because of its quality of being unattached. (193)
The modification known as the conceit of pleasure and pain is called experience (bhoga).
How is it not contradictory that the immutable (kūṭastha) should possess such a modification? (194)
Because it is dependent upon a transforming intellect, even when there is a transformation in the appearance,
a delusion without a substratum does not remain as something absolute.
Therefore, in the world, the enjoyer is said to be of a dual nature;
starting from such a self, the immutable one remains as the residue in the Śruti.
When asked, "What is the self?", Yājñavalkya, awakening [his interlocutor], began with that which consists of consciousness and concluded by describing it as non-attachment. (197)
In all instances such as "What is this self?", through the investigation of the self,
beginning with that which possesses both natures, the immutable (kūṭastha) remains as the residue in the Śruti.
Superimposing upon itself the immutability and reality of the Self through a lack of discrimination, the individual soul considers its own agency to be real and never desires to abandon it. (199)
The enjoyer desires a wife, husband, and so forth for his own enjoyment;
this worldly occurrence has been correctly restated by the Śruti. (200)
Since objects of enjoyment exist solely for the sake of the enjoyer, let there be no attachment to those objects;
therefore, he desires to instill that very attachment in the enjoyer, who is the primary factor.
May that unswerving affection which the undiscriminating feel for sense-objects never depart from my heart as I remember you. (202)
According to this principle, one whose mind is detached from the entire range of objects of enjoyment withdraws that affection and thus desires to know the enjoyer alone. (203)
Just as a common man remains vigilant regarding garlands, sandalwood, a wife, garments, gold, and the like, so too he does not become negligent toward the enjoyer. 204.
Just as one desiring victory practices poetry, drama, logic, and so forth continuously, so too should one desiring liberation investigate oneself. (205)
Just as one performs recitation, sacrifice, meditation,
and so forth with faith out of a desire for heaven and the like, in that same way, one should have faith in one's own [practice] out of a desire for liberation.
Just as a yogi might achieve one-pointedness of mind through great exertion out of a desire for powers such as *aṇimā*, so too should one who seeks liberation distinguish his own self.
Just as their skills increase through proficiency in practice, so too does this person’s discernment become clarified through cultivation. 208.

By one who discriminates the true nature of the enjoyer, its state of non-attachment throughout the states of waking and so forth is determined through positive and negative concomitance as belonging to the Witness. (29)
"Whatever is seen by the seer in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, that exists only there and not elsewhere; this is indeed the accepted experience. (210)
Whatever he perceives there, he remains unattached to it;
"having seen both merit and evil"—such is the proclamation in the Śrutis. (211)
Having realized that "I am that Brahman," by which the manifold world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, is illumined, one is liberated from all bonds. || 212 ||
The Self alone is to be contemplated as one and the same throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
for one who has transcended these three states, rebirth no longer exists.

Whatever may be the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoying within the three abodes—I am the witness distinct from them all, pure consciousness, the eternally auspicious Śiva. || 214 ||

When reality has been thus discerned, that which is designated as "consisting of consciousness"—the manifesting reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) which is subject to modification—is what remains as the experiencer. || 215 ||

This reflection of consciousness is illusory, according to both scripture and experience; for this world is said to be a magical illusion (indrajāla), and since this [reflection] falls within it, it too is such. (216)
Indeed, its disappearance during deep sleep and other such states is experienced by the witness;
thus, it repeatedly distinguishes this from its own true nature. (217)
Having discerned and ascertained his own destruction, he no longer desires enjoyment;
who, lying on the ground like one about to die, would desire marriage? (218)
He is ashamed to engage in worldly affairs, thinking "I am the enjoyer" as before;
like one whose nose has been cut off, he is robbed [of his identity] and, suffering, experiences the results of his past actions.
When he feels ashamed even to consider himself an enjoyer, then what need is there to mention that he would falsely attribute this state to the Witness? (220)
Intending this, he challenges the enjoyer without hesitation:
"For whose desires? For there is no subsequent fever for the body.
The body is traditionally known to be threefold: gross, subtle, and causal;
accordingly, there necessarily exists a corresponding threefold fever in each of those cases. (222)
Diseases born of wind, bile, and phlegm exist by the millions upon the body, as do foul odors, deformity, burning sensations, fractures, and the like. (223)

Lust, anger, and the like, as well as tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth—residing within the subtle body (liṅgadeha)—afflict a person through their attainment or non-attainment, respectively, even when one is free from fever. (224)
The self does not know itself or another, as if it were destroyed when its cause perishes; furthermore, it is the seed of future suffering—this has been demonstrated by Indra. (225)
These fevers are considered natural within the three bodies;
however, upon separation from the fevers, those very bodies do not remain.
Just as a cloth is not separated from its threads, nor a woolen blanket from its fibers, so too the body [is not separate] from the fevers; let this be observed. (227)
In the reflection of consciousness, there is no fever of its own accord, because the nature of consciousness is seen to be solely that of illumination and nothing else. (228)
Feverish afflictions are impossible even in the reflection of consciousness; what then to say of the Witness?
Thus indeed, through ignorance, the reflection of consciousness conceives of oneness.
Having superimposed the reality of the witness upon the three bodies assumed by himself,
he considers all of that to be his own true, real nature.
At this time of delusion, when these bodies are feverish,
he indeed thinks, "I myself am feverish," just like one who identifies with his family.
Just as a person falsely thinks, "I am satisfied" when his sons and wife are satisfied,
so too does the reflection (the individual soul) falsely imagine itself to be so.
Having discerned [the truth] and abandoned delusion, always disregarding even oneself, why should one who contemplates the Witness suffer on account of the body? (233)
The cognition of a snake or similar object when it is not actually present is the cause for fleeing;
once the notion of the snake is destroyed by the cognition of the rope, one regrets even that which was already done. (234)
In order to establish the expiation for the fault of a false accusation, he sought refuge with the witness, as if asking for forgiveness on his own behalf. || 235 ||
Just as one repeats ritual bathing and other acts for the sake of removing committed sins, so too,
being ever devoted to the Witness, one should practice meditation as if repeating it.
A courtesan afflicted with skin disease feels ashamed during amorous dalliances; likewise, one who appears as he is before those who know him feels ashamed regarding his own reputation. 237.
A Brahmin who has been captured by barbarians while performing penance is not at all defiled by those barbarians; likewise, one who merely appears so is not defiled by their bodies.
Just as a prince established in the position of crown prince acts in imitation of the king out of a desire for universal sovereignty, so too is this [reflection] to be imitated by the witness.
Having heard the Vedic revelation, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," one whose mind is focused solely on that knows Brahman and nothing else.
Just as those desiring divinity enter into fire and other elements, so too he desires his own destruction for the sake of remaining as a witness. (241)

As long as one does not abandon the human state until the burning of one's own body, so long will one remain with a body initiated by past karma; there is no liberation from the state of being a mere appearance.
Even when the rope is known [to be such], the trembling and other symptoms subside only gradually;
furthermore, in dim darkness, that rope may once again become a snake cast forth [by fear]. (243)
Even when enjoyment has thus begun, it subsides gradually and not by force;
yet at some time during the period of enjoyment, the thought "I am a mortal" may manifest.
The knowledge of reality is not destroyed by such a transgression;
this is not a vow for liberation while living, but rather the actual state of things.
Even when struck on the head for the tenth time, he wakes up and does not cry;
yet the wound on his head does not gradually heal for a month at that time.
Just as the joy born from obtaining the tenth nectar (immortality) eclipses the pain of a wound,
so too does the attainment of liberation obscure the suffering caused by one's past karma (*prārabdha*).
When there is superimposition due to the absence of vows, let it be further investigated:
just as one who indulges in flavors eats again and again throughout the day. (248)
Just as this tenth [type of person] heals his own wound with medicine,
so too, having exhausted this prārabdha through experience, he is liberated.
The liberation from sorrow mentioned in the statement "desiring what? has been declared;
for this is the sixth state of the reflection, while contentment is the seventh.
Satisfaction derived from sense objects is constrained by limits; this [spiritual] satisfaction is unrestrained.
One is truly satisfied only when thinking: "What was to be done has been done; what was to be attained has been attained. (251)

For the sake of accomplishing the multitude of goals pertaining to this world and the next, and for the sake of attaining liberation, there was much to be done by him in the past; all of that has now been accomplished.
Thus, by constantly reflecting upon this state of having accomplished all that was to be done in relation to its counterpart, he remains eternally satisfied in this manner.
Let those who are ignorant and suffering wander through saṃsāra at will out of attachment to sons and the like;
but I, filled with supreme bliss, wander through saṃsāra—what desire could I have? (254)
Let those who desire to go to the next world perform ritual actions;
why and how should I, who am the self of all worlds, perform them?
Let those who are qualified in this matter explain the treatises or teach the Vedas; as for me, however, there is no such qualification, because I am inactive.
"I have no desire for sleep, alms, bathing, or purification, nor do I perform them;
if observers nevertheless imagine them, what can that imagination of others affect me? (257)
A heap of gunja berries and the like would not be burned by a fire superimposed upon something else;
likewise, I do not partake in the worldly attributes superimposed upon another.
"Let those who do not know the truth listen; why should I, knowing it, listen?
Let those who are fallen into doubt reflect; I, being free from doubt, do not need to reflect. (259)
One who is deluded should practice meditative reflection; what need is there for meditation when there is no delusion?
I never entertain the delusion that the body is the self. (260)
The conventional usage such as "I am a human" and so forth is possible even without this misconception, due to the latencies of long-practiced habituation. (261)
When the prārabdha karma is exhausted, worldly activity ceases;
however, as long as that karma is not exhausted, this activity will not subside even through a thousand meditations.
If you desire that worldly activity be established as being illusory, then let your meditation be directed toward it;
observe that worldly activity is uncontradicted, for why should I meditate? (263)
Since there is no distraction for me, therefore I have no meditative absorption;
