for either distraction or meditative absorption can belong only to a mind that undergoes modification. (264)
For one whose nature is eternal experience, what separate experience could there be for me here?
The firm conviction is simply this: "What was to be done has been done; that which was to be attained has been attained. (265)
Whether it be worldly or scriptural, or even otherwise,
let my worldly affairs proceed as they have begun, for I am a non-doer and untainted.
Or rather, even though my purpose is accomplished, I shall proceed by the very path prescribed by the scriptures out of a desire to favor the world; what loss is there for me? (267)

Let the body be engaged in the worship of the gods, ritual bathing, purification, begging for alms, and so forth; likewise, let the speech chant the *tāra* (the syllable Om) and recite the crest-jewels of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). (268)
Let the intellect meditate upon Viṣṇu, or let it dissolve into the bliss of Brahman;
I am merely the witness here, performing nothing at all, nor causing anything to be done.
And thus, where could a conflict arise for me, an agent, since our objects are distinct, like the eastern and western oceans? (270)
The practitioner of ritual action exerts effort regarding body, speech, and mind, but not toward the Witness;
for the knower exerts effort toward the stainlessness of the Witness, and not toward anything else. (271)
Thus, like two deaf men ignorant of each other's affairs,
though they are intelligent, people surely laugh upon seeing them as they dispute.
The knower of reality perceives the witness within that very action which the agent does not recognize;
let Brahman-hood be understood there—what is lost for the agent? (273)
The body, speech, and intellect have been abandoned by the knower due to his realization of their unreality;
yet the agent acts through them—what is lost here for the knower? (274)
If activity is not useful, then where is cessation useful?
If cessation is the cause for awakening, then the other [activity] is likewise the cause for the desire to know.
If the Buddha were not desirous of knowing, he would not know again;
his cognition would persist without obstruction, and not through any other means. (276)
Neither ignorance nor its effect is able to subvert awakening, because both have already been subverted by the realization of reality. (277)
Let it be seen that [the object] is sublated by the senses; therefore, no sublation is to be suspected.
A living rat does not kill a cat; how could one that is dead do so? (278)
"Even if he were pierced by the Pāśupata weapon, if he did not die, what proof is there that he will perish when his body is merely perforated by a fruitless arrow? (279)
Having first fought against ignorance as it expanded through its various effects, consciousness has now emerged victorious; being so firmly established, how could it ever be overcome? (280)
Let those who have been killed by the lack of awareness of ignorance and its effects remain as corpses;
there is no loss for the Emperor, on the contrary, his fame increases because of them.
For one who is thus never separated from such supremely heroic awakening, what does it matter whether there is withdrawal or engagement pertaining to the body and so forth? (282)
For one devoid of awakening, it is entirely reasonable to be intent upon worldly activity;
for men must be directed toward either heaven or liberation. (283)
If a wise person should stand in the midst of such people out of compliance with them, he indeed performs all actions through body, mind, and speech. (284)
When he stands in the midst of those desiring to know, then,
for their sake, let him himself abandon all ritual actions while censuring them for the purpose of awakening them.
The conduct of a Buddha is appropriate according to the capacity of the ignorant, because a father acts in accordance with his suckling child. (286)
When his own son reviles or strikes him, a father at that time neither suffers nor becomes angry; instead, he treats the child with affection.
Whether reviled or praised by the ignorant, the wise man neither censures nor praises them; rather, he should act in such a way that they may attain awakening.
Whatever by means of which this [ignorant person] is awakened here to that very task must be performed;
for one who knows that, there is no other task here than the awakening of the ignorant. (289)
Satisfied by having accomplished what was to be done, and further satisfied by having attained that which was to be attained,
he thus continually reflects within his own mind.
Blessed am I, blessed am I, for I constantly and directly know my own Self;
blessed am I, blessed am I, for the bliss of Brahman shines clearly before me.
Blessed am I, blessed am I; today I no longer behold the suffering of worldly existence.
Blessed am I, blessed am I; my own ignorance has fled away to some unknown place. (292)
Blessed am I, blessed am I; there is nothing further for me to do.
Blessed am I, blessed am I; everything that was to be attained has been accomplished today.
I am blessed, I am blessed; may my satisfaction be beyond compare in this world.
I am blessed, I am blessed; blessed, blessed, blessed again and again. (294)
Oh, what merit! Oh, what merit! It has indeed borne firm fruit.
Oh, the attainment of this merit! Oh, who we are! (295)
Oh, the scripture! Oh, the scripture! Oh, the teacher! Oh, the teacher!
Oh, the knowledge! Oh, the knowledge! Oh, the bliss! Oh, the bliss! (296)
Those wise ones who constantly contemplate this Lamp of Satisfaction immerse themselves in the bliss of Brahman and remain perpetually satisfied. (297)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, named the Lamp of Contentment. 7.
The Eighth Chapter, titled "The Unchanging Lamp": Just as the light of the sun reflected in a mirror illuminates a wall already lit by the sun,
so too the body, illumined by the immutable [Self], is illuminated by the living self (jīva) residing in the intellect.
In the many junctions of the radiance of numerous mirrors and suns, one [light] is manifested;
yet even in the absence of those [mirrors], it shines forth.
Likewise, let it be discerned that this [Self], while illuminating the conjunction and the non-existence of various cognitions characterized by the reflection of consciousness, [is itself distinct].
The consciousness residing in the cognition of the single form of the jar would illuminate only the jar;
it is by the Brahman-consciousness that the "known-ness" (jñātatā) of the jar is illuminated. || 4 ||
Before the arising of the cognition, this jar was known by Brahman alone as being unknown; subsequently, however, it is known as being known—this is the distinction.
Knowledge is the mental modification ending in the reflection of consciousness, like an iron spear ending in metal;
ignorance is insentience. A jar, being pervaded by these two, is said to be twofold.
If the pot is known by Brahman, why is it not likewise manifest?
For the destruction of the reflection of consciousness occurs precisely through the production of the state of being known. (7)
By a cognition lacking manifestation, the state of being known is not produced at all;
what distinction, then, would such a cognition have from clay or other transformable substances? (8)
A jar smeared with clay is never said to be "known" [as such];
likewise, the state of being known is not accepted for a jar that is merely pervaded by cognition.
Thus, what is called "knowability" is the arising of the fruit of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) in the jar;
it is not the fruit of the Brahman-consciousness itself, because that exists even prior to the mind.
"That very consciousness which is accepted as the fruit in the case of external objects of knowledge is itself the object to be measured here, according to the authority of the Vedāntic statements"—
thus did the author of the Vārttika intend to express the identity of consciousness with the Self.
Since the distinction between the fruit of the Brahma-knowledge and the fruit [of ritual action] is renowned in the Sāhasrī. || 11 ||
Therefore, the manifestation that has arisen produces the state of being known in the jar;
yet that [jar] must be illumined by Brahman, just like its state of being unknown.
The collection of jars manifested through the modification of the intellect (dhīvṛtti) is illumined by consciousness;
because its result consists merely in the jar, it appears as a single unity from the perspective of manifestation.
Consequently, consciousness becomes twofold within the jar and manifests as the state of being known;
others call this, as has been described, "subsequent reflective awareness" (anuvyavasāya).
The statement "this is a jar" arises through the grace of the manifestation;
the statement "the jar is known" occurs through the grace of Brahman. (15)
Just as the appearance and Brahman were distinguished from the body externally,
so too should the appearance and the immutable reality (kūṭastha) be distinguished within the physical form itself.
The reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) exists pervading the function of the ego-sense as well as desire, anger, and the like,
just as fire exists pervading heated iron.
Just as heated iron illuminates only itself and never anything else, so too the mental modifications, accompanied by their own light, are self-illuminating. (18)
All mental modifications arise, being repeatedly interrupted in succession;
yet they all dissolve during sleep, fainting, and meditative absorption.
He by whom all the junctions of mental fluctuations and their absences are illumined,
while remaining himself changeless, is celebrated as the Immutable (Kūṭastha).
Just as there is double consciousness within a jar as there is on its exterior, so too it exists in the mental modifications;
therefore, clarity therein is even greater than at the point of contact.

The states of being known and being unknown do not exist anywhere in the cognitions themselves, as they do in the case of a jar; for a cognition cannot be apprehended by itself, and it is through those [cognitions] that ignorance is destroyed.
That which possesses consciousness doubled through the experience of birth and destruction is non-eternal; that which is other than it is eternal, due to its changelessness.
In various ways, such as "the witness of the internal organ and its modifications," it has been determined by the former teachers that the kūṭastha alone is present everywhere. (24)

And thus, the basis for the appearance of a self is understood through scripture and reasoning, just as the basis for the appearance of a face [is understood]; therefore, it has been described as an "appearance" (ābhāsa). || 25 ||
Tell me, how can the immutable Self, though delimited by the intellect, be capable of going to and returning from other worlds through its reflection, like the space within a jar? 26.
Indeed, the individual soul (jīva) does not become [the Supreme Self] merely through the absence of attachment due to limitation;
otherwise, that which is delimited by jars, walls, and the like would also possess the status of a jīva. (27)
If it is argued that consciousness is not like a wall because of its transparency, let it be so; however, what does that transparency accomplish for you in the matter of discernment? (28)
Indeed, the measurement of rice and other grains by a wooden or bronze *prastha* does not differ from that used by a seller. (29)

Even when there is a difference in size, the reflection is distinguished; if that were the case for bronze, then by the same logic, a reflection would necessarily appear in the intellect as well. (30)

A reflection (*ābhāsa*) is a slight manifestation; it is of such a nature that, though devoid of the characteristics of an original object (*bimba*), it appears as if it were that original object. (31)

Due to its being associated with attachment and subject to modification, it lacks the characteristics of a true reflection; nevertheless, the wise know that its manifestation as a form of radiance constitutes its appearance as a reflection.

If it is argued that "there is no appearance separate from cognition because the appearance exists only when cognition exists," then very little has been said; for in this same way, cognition itself [does not exist] apart from its own body.
If the intellect exists even when the body has died, as established by the scriptures,
then that which is heard of in the scriptures concerning "entry" must be the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) distinct from the intellect.
If it is argued that entry belongs to that which is joined with intelligence (*dhī*), then in the *Aitareya* [Upaniṣad], intelligence is not mentioned separately;
rather, it is stated that the Self, having formed the intention of entering, entered. (35)

"How indeed might this [world], together with its bodies, exist without me?"—from such a deliberation, having split open the suture of his own head, he entered and wanders through the cycle of existence. (36)
If he is unattached, how did he enter? Or tell me, how could there be creation for him? The nature of illusion (māyikatva) is equal for both, and the destruction of both is likewise the same. (37)
"Having arisen from the very elements, one perishes after them;
this is clearly so, O Maitreyī," for thus did Yājñavalkya say. 38.
"This Self is indestructible" thus it is determined to be immutable; "contact with the elements" thus declares its state of non-attachment. (39)
"The body indeed dies when deprived of the living soul, but not he [the soul]";
in this context, liberation is not the intended meaning, but rather movement to another world. (40)
If it is argued that one should not realize "I am Brahman" because [the self] is perishable, that is not so;
for grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible even when there is sublation [of the apparent meaning]. (41)
Just as the notion of a post is sublated by the cognition "this is a man," so too the residual sense of "I" is sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman. (42)
In the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi* as well, this has been clearly stated by the Teacher:
that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has the sense of sublation (*bādha*); therefore, let it be so. (43)

Just as there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between "the entire world is Brahman," so too there is coreferentiality between "I am Brahman" and the individual soul (jīva). || 44 ||

The view that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) has the purpose of negation has been refuted with great effort in the *Vivaraṇa*, with the intention of expressing [the Self's] immutability (kūṭasthatva). (45)
That purified meaning of the word which is the immutable [Self] is of the nature of Brahman;
its explanation has been stated here as well as elsewhere. (46)

The consciousness that serves as the substratum for the illusion of the individual soul (jīvābhāsa), which is associated with the body, senses, and so forth—that alone is intended here as the immutable (kūṭastha). 47.
That which is declared in the Upaniṣads (the conclusions of the three Vedas) to be the substratum of all the world's delusion—that is what is intended here by the word "Brahman. (48)
When the entire world is superimposed upon this very consciousness, what need is there to speak of the appearance of the individual soul (jīvābhāsa), which is but a single part of it? 49.

Due to the distinction between the superimposed [objects] known as the world and its parts, the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam* appear distinct; however, in reality, there is oneness of consciousness.
Because it manifests before one, assuming the attributes of the intellect such as agency and its own nature called "luminosity," this appearance becomes a delusion.

"What is the intellect? What is this appearance? Or what is the Self here, and how does the world come to be?"—from such lack of determination arises delusion, which is what is intended by the term "saṃsāra. (52)
He who discriminates the true nature of the intellect and the rest is the knower of reality;
he alone is liberated—such is the settled conclusion in the Vedāntas. (53)

This being the case, the mockeries arising from such fallacious reasoning—such as "to whom would there be bondage? and so forth—must be firmly refuted by means of the various methods of *khaṇḍana* (destructive critique). 54.
He exists as the witness of both the mental state and the prior absence of that state;
likewise, when there is a desire to know, He exists as the substrate of the ignorance that manifests as "I am ignorant."
He is real because he is not of the nature of an unreal object; for all that is insentient, however, he is real because he is their establisher.
He is of the nature of consciousness because he is always the locus of love. (56)
He whose nature is bliss, by virtue of being the accomplisher of all goals, and by virtue of possessing all connections, is complete and designated as Śiva. || 57 ||
Thus, in the Śaiva Purāṇas, Śiva has been analyzed as the immutable one—devoid of the states of being the individual soul (jīva) or the Lord (īśa), absolute, and self-luminous. (58)

Because it is stated in the Śruti that [Brahman] creates the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) through the manifestation of Māyā, both the jīva and the īśa are indeed products of Māyā; they are pure like a crystal jar.
Just as that which arises from food is clear compared to the mind and the body, so too those two,
though illusory, have attained a clarity greater than everything else.
And its nature as consciousness is conceivable, because it manifests precisely as thought;
for there is nothing difficult for Māyā, which possesses the power to conceive all things. 61.
Even our own sleep creates these two conscious beings, the individual soul and the Lord, as they wander in dreams;
that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) creates these two—what wonder is there in this for you? 62.
If one were to demonstrate [the probandum] by first postulating omniscience and so forth in the Lord, then who would find it a burden to postulate the subject (dharmin) for that [inference]? (63)

If it is argued that doubt might still arise even regarding the immutable (kūṭastha), let it be doubted; however, there exists no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the immutable being illusory (māyika).
All the Vedāntas proclaim its reality;
they do not tolerate any other entity here that would stand as its rival. (65)
We clarify the meaning of the Śruti; I do not utter any arguments based on logic (tarka).
Therefore, tell me, what occasion is there here for the doubts of logicians? 66.
Therefore, having abandoned fallacious reasoning, one who desires liberation should take refuge in the Śruti;
for in the Śruti it is demonstrated that Māyā brings about both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa).
The creation beginning with the act of seeing and ending with the entry [of the vital breath] is performed by the Lord;
the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) beginning with the waking state and ending with liberation has the individual soul (jīva) as its agent.
Being eternally unattached and immutable, he possesses no excellence whatsoever;
therefore, let it be reflected upon thus within the mind. (69)
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one bound nor a practitioner,
neither one seeking liberation nor one liberated— this is the ultimate reality.
Since that [Reality] is inaccessible to speech and mind, the Śruti always seeks to awaken one to it by resorting to the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), or even the world (jagat). || 71 ||
"By whatever means a person may attain realization of the inner self, that very method should be considered valid here; thus it has been declared by the Teacher. (72)
Without understanding the entire purport of the Vedas, the dull-witted person wanders in delusion;
but the man of discrimination, having understood it all, abides in the ocean of bliss. (73)
Just as this cloud of illusion rains down the water of the world, so too there is neither loss nor gain for the space of consciousness; such is the established state of affairs. (74)
He who continuously contemplates this immutable lamp shines himself continuously in the form of the immutable.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Lamp of the Immutable.
The ninth chapter, titled "The Lamp of Meditation":
Through the practice of meditation on the reality of Brahman, one is liberated, just as one is freed from an error that is consistent with reality (*saṃvādibhrama*).
Therefore, in the subsequent Tāpanīya Upanishads, there are various forms of scriptural meditation. || 1 ||

For two people who run toward a jewel and the light of a jewel-lamp respectively, both perceiving them with the cognition of a "jewel," although there is no difference in their false cognition, there is a distinction regarding purposeful action (arthakriyā). //2//
Just as the light of a lamp exists within an inner chamber yet is seen outside at the doorway,
so too is the radiance of a gem observed elsewhere.
Seeing two lusters from afar, both men run toward them with the thought that they are jewels;
however, the cognition of a jewel in what is merely a luster is false knowledge for both of them. (4)
The jewel is not obtained by one who runs toward the light of the lamp;
however, by running toward the light, the jewel of the lamp is necessarily obtained.

The error consisting of the mistaken perception of a lamp’s glow as a jewel is known as a non-corresponding error; the error consisting of the mistaken perception of a jewel’s glow as a jewel is called a corresponding error. (6)
Having perceived vapor as smoke and thereby inferred embers therein, one happens upon fire by chance; this is considered a "corresponding error" (saṃvādibhrama).
Thinking the water of the Godāvarī to be the water of the Gaṅgā for the sake of purification, one attains purity by sprinkling oneself; this is considered a "corresponding error" (saṃvādibhrama).
One who, having fallen into a state of delirium due to fever, remembers Nārāyaṇa and dies thereby attains heaven; this is considered "corresponding error" (saṃvādibhrama).
Within the scope of perception, inference, and likewise scripture, there exist here by the millions, according to the stated reasoning, concordant errors. (10)
Otherwise, how could clay, wood, and stone be deities?
Or how could women and the like be worshipped with the cognition that they are fire and so forth? (11)
When a desired result is obtained from a cognition that does not correspond to the actual state of things,
occurring by mere chance like the "crow and the palm fruit," this is called a "concordant error" (saṃvādibhrama).
Just as even a self-generated error, when it corresponds with reality, yields the correct result,
so too does the meditation on the principle of Brahman bestow the fruit of liberation.
Having understood from the Vedantas that the reality of Brahman consists of an undivided, single-flavored essence, they meditate upon it with the thought, "I am this. || 14 ||

Without delineating the inner individual self (pratyagvyakti), the mere general knowledge that "Brahman exists," derived from scripture—like the [general] forms of Viṣṇu and others—is indirect cognition (parokṣadhī). || 15 ||

Even when perceiving [Viṣṇu] as having four arms and so forth, if one does not delineate His form, then, like one possessing only indirect knowledge through the senses, one does not truly behold Viṣṇu at that time.

There can be no lack of knowledge of reality due to the fault of being beyond the senses, because that which has true form is revealed by the scripture itself, which is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). || 17 ||
Although that which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss is revealed through the scripture,
one who does not describe it as such does not directly perceive that Brahman within the individual self, the witness.
Because it is determined as Being-Consciousness-Bliss through the very path taught in the scriptures, that knowledge—even if indirect—is knowledge of reality and not an error. (19)
Although Brahman is described in the scriptures as being precisely the inner self through the Great Sayings (mahāvākyas), it remains difficult to understand for one who does not engage in inquiry.
While the delusion of identifying the body and so forth as the self persists during the waking state, a person of dull intellect is not able to realize [the self] as Brahman by force. (21)
Brahman alone is easily known by one who possesses faith and perceives the scriptures;
for such a person, the perception of duality as immediate ceases upon the perception of duality as mediate.
The perception of a stone as being directly present does not remove its status as a distant Lord;
for who would dispute that Viṣṇu resides in images and the like? (23)
It is not fit to be taught to one who lacks faith and has no conviction;
for only the faithful have the qualification for all Vedic matters. (24)
Through the instruction received once from a qualified teacher, indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna) arises;
for indeed, the instruction regarding the form of Viṣṇu does not depend upon Mīmāṃsā.
Ritual action and meditation are investigated here because their performance must be determined;
for what man is capable of discerning that which is scattered across many branches [of scripture]? (26)
The meaning determined by the Kalpasūtras is thus woven together; by that much alone, a believer is able to perform the ritual correctly even without further deliberation. (27)
The performance of meditations (*upāsti*) is described in the scriptures of the sages; and mortals who are incapable of critical inquiry, having heard that, practice them under a teacher. (28)
People who desire to determine the meaning of Vedic statements should engage in inquiry; for the performance of rites can only be possible through the instruction of a reliable authority. (29)
Indeed, for human beings, the direct realization of Brahman is not possible anywhere through mere instruction from a qualified teacher alone, without such inquiry. (30)
Lack of faith obstructs indirect knowledge, and nothing else;
lack of inquiry is the obstructer of direct knowledge. || 31 ||
If even through reflection one does not know the Brahman-Self as immediate, one should reflect again and again, because [the knowledge] culminates in immediacy. || 32 ||
If, while investigating, one does not find the self even unto death,
one will certainly find it in another birth once obstacles have been removed.
"The Sūtra-author has declared that this knowledge may be found either here or in the hereafter;
yet the Śruti says that many, even while hearing it, do not understand it. (34)
While still lying within the womb, Vāmadeva attained awakening through the investigation practiced in previous lives, just as one applies oneself to study and other such tasks.
If, even after studying many times, it does not come to him then,
the person may remember what was previously studied on another day without having studied it again.
Just as crops such as rice ripen in due time, so too the inquiry into the self matures gradually over time. (37)
"Even repeated reflection does not lead one to know the reality due to three kinds of obstacles; this has been correctly stated in the Vārttika. (38)
If it is asked, "Whence does that knowledge arise?", it is indeed from the complete destruction of bondage.
And that [destruction] is either past, future, or likewise present.
For this very reason, even one who has studied the Vedas and understood their meaning is not liberated;
indeed, this is demonstrated by the analogy of the hidden treasure of gold. (40)
"Even because of attachment due to past affection for a queen, a monk does not know reality"—thus is a verse sung in the world. (41)
Following his affection for the queen, the Guru spoke the truth;
thereafter, through the complete destruction of his obstruction, he understood it correctly according to the Vedas.
The obstacle present is characterized by attachment to sense objects, dullness of wisdom, fallacious reasoning, and a stubborn adherence to erroneous views. (43)

When this obstacle has been brought to destruction by means of tranquility and the like, as well as by hearing and the like, each being appropriate to its respective stage, one then attains one's own true nature as Brahman.
And the obstruction to future [liberation] that was proclaimed in the case of Vāmadeva was exhausted in a single birth, whereas for Bharata it was exhausted in three births. 45.
For one who has fallen from yoga, the destruction of obstacles is said to occur after many past births; thus, even inquiry is not useless. (46)

Having attained the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds through the inquiry into the reality of the Self, one who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous. (47)
Or else, he is born into a family of wise yogis; for such a birth, resulting from dispassion through inquiry into the reality of Brahman, is indeed difficult to attain. (48)
There he regains that same mental disposition belonging to his former body;
from that point he strives even more intensely, for this [attainment] is indeed difficult to obtain.
For by that very same previous practice, he is carried forward even against his will;
perfected through many births, he then attains the supreme goal.
If one truly desires the world of Brahmā, let that [desire] be completely ceased;
for one who investigates the self does not, however, directly realize it. (51)

"Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the higher knowledge of Vedānta"—according to the scripture, such a person is liberated together with Brahmā at the end of the kalpa in the world of Brahmā. || 52 ||
For some, even that inquiry is obstructed by karma, according to the Vedic scripture: "He who is not obtained even for hearing by many. (53)
One who does not obtain the opportunity for inquiry due to extreme dullness of intellect, or because of the impossibility of the necessary conditions, should meditate upon Brahman incessantly.

For there is no impossibility of meditation upon the reality of Brahman devoid of attributes (nirguṇa-brahma), because here too, as in the case of Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma), the repetition of mental impressions is possible. (55)

If it is argued that because That is inaccessible to speech and mind, It cannot be an object of meditation, then the knowledge of that which is inaccessible to speech and mind would also be impossible. (56)
If he knows it thus as having a form that is beyond the range of speech and other senses, why should he not worship it as "that which has a form beyond the range of speech and other senses"? (57)
If it possesses attributes because it is an object of meditation, then it must also possess them because it is an object of knowledge;
if it is an object of knowledge, let it be meditated upon as such, characterized through the function of indication (lakṣaṇā).

"If it be argued that the status of being an object of worship is denied of Brahman by the Śruti text: 'Know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which they worship as such' (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9)," [then we reply:]
Since the Śruti declares, "It is indeed other than the known," it cannot be an object of knowledge;
yet, just as that reality is to be known by the Śruti itself, so too should it be meditated upon by the Śruti.
If knowability is unreal, why is it not likewise [unreal] in the case of being an object of worship?
If knowability consists in the pervasion by a mental mode (vṛtti), that is the same even in the case of being an object of worship. (51)
If you ask what your devotion is toward worship, then declare what your aversion is;
one cannot say there is an absence of honor for this [worship], as it is seen in many scriptural texts (śruti). (62)
In the *Tāpanīya*, in the *Śaibyapraśna*, in the *Kāṭhaka*, and in the *Māṇḍūkya* and other such texts, the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) is taught everywhere. (63)
The method of its practice has been described as the "fivefold process" (pañcīkaraṇa).
If it is asked whether this is a means for attaining knowledge, the answer is "no"; by whom has this been stated here? (64)
If it is argued that no one practices this, let them not practice;
how can the worship be defiled by the fault of a person? (65)
Thinking that there is some excellence even in this, let the deluded mutter mantras that effect subjugation and the like; those even more deluded than they should devote themselves to agriculture.

Let the deluded remain aside; the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) is now being expounded. Due to the unity of knowledge, one should here synthesize all the attributes found in every Vedic branch (śākhā).
In this sūtra, "Ānandādayaḥ," the withdrawal of the entire collection of qualities such as bliss and the rest, which are to be enjoined, was described by Vyāsa. (68)

The collection of attributes such as "not gross" and so forth, which are to be negated, is likewise stated in this Sūtra by means of expansion [of the negation] with the words "and of the cognitions of the syllables. (69)
"The withdrawal of qualities during the knowledge of the reality of the qualityless Brahman would not be logical"— this censure applies only to Vyāsa, but not to me.

If you should be satisfied with the argument that "the qualitylessness [of Brahman] is not contradicted because there is no mention of forms such as those with golden beards or the sun," then let it be so. (71)

If it is argued that because the qualities serve as indicators (lakṣaka), they do not enter into the essence [of Brahman], then let it be so; let the reality of Brahman be meditated upon in this very way.
By means of attributes such as bliss and the like, and non-materiality and the like, one's own Self is indicated here;
thus they meditate: "I am that which is partless and of a single essence. (73)

If it is asked what the distinction between knowledge (bodha) and worship (upāsti) is, listen as it is explained: Knowledge depends upon the reality itself, whereas worship depends upon the agent. (74)
From inquiry arises awakening, which no lack of desire can turn back;
by its mere arising, it burns away all sense of reality within saṃsāra.
Having accomplished his purpose to that extent, he remains yet unsatisfied;
having attained liberation while living, he awaits the exhaustion of his prārabdha karma.
Trusting the instruction of a reliable authority and not doubting it, one should contemplate it with other means of cognition whose operation is uninterrupted. (77)
As long as the conceit of one's own inconceivable nature arises,
one should reflect upon it and thereafter maintain that very state until death.
A celibate student (brahmacārī), engaged in begging while endowed with the Saṃvarga-vidyā,
indeed begs without [the need for] further begging by maintaining the nature of the Absorber (saṃvargarūpa) within his mind.
Since meditation can be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise according to one's own will,
one should therefore constantly maintain a continuous flow of mental conviction.

For one who studies the Veda vigilantly indeed recites it even in dreams, being permeated by it; likewise, one who has performed recitation continues to recite, and so too does one who meditates remain permeated by it.
Having abandoned contrary conditions and cultivating [the object] without interruption,
one attains the state of cultivation even in dreams and the like through the penetration of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Even while eating, one's own [mind] is constantly occupied with intense attachment to what has been begun;
there is no doubt that it is unable to meditate, just like one who is addicted to sensual objects. (83)
A woman who is devoted to another man, even while busily engaged in household chores, internally relishes that very elixir of union with her lover. (84)
Even though she relishes the company of others, her household duties do not become neglected;
rather, they proceed with the mere appearance of being so.
Just as a woman devoted to her domestic duties performs them properly,
so too one who is devoted to another's affairs does not perform them at all in any way.
Thus, even one who is solely devoted to meditation may perform worldly actions to a slight degree;
however, because they do not contradict the state of knowing reality, he should perform worldly actions properly.

"This phenomenal world is composed of illusion, while the Self possesses the nature of pure consciousness"—what contradiction is there for one who understands this while engaged in worldly affairs? (88)
Ordinary worldly discourse does not depend upon the reality of the phenomenal world, nor does it require its own inherent dullness; rather, it merely requires means of accomplishment.
The mind, speech, body, and external objects are the means of accomplishment; one who knows reality does not destroy them, so how could there be no worldly activity for such a person? (90)
If the meditator crushes the mind, he is not a knower of reality;
for one who crushes the intellect is never seen to be a knower of the true nature of a jar.
If the jar appears by means of a single act of cognition alone, then why does this self, which is self-luminous, not appear in the same way as the jar? (92)
If [you argue] that because it is self-luminous, your cognition of it is the knowledge of reality,
then the objection— that cognition perishes moment by moment— is equally applicable to jars and other objects.
If it is argued that when a jar or the like is ascertained, the cognition [of its impermanence] perishes because the jar is then capable of being taken away,
this is equally applicable to the self.

Once the knower of reality has ascertained the Self once and for all, at that very moment he is indeed capable of speaking of it, reflecting upon it, and likewise meditating upon it, according to his need. 95.
If, like a lay devotee, one meditates and should forget the mundane world, that forgetting indeed occurs from meditation, but not from sensation. (96)
Meditation for him, however, is optional, since liberation is accomplished through the realization of [the Self];
for the drums of the scriptures proclaim that absolute isolation (kaivalya) comes from knowledge alone. 97.
If one who knows reality does not meditate, then he would engage with the external world; let him engage at his ease—what obstruction is there to his engagement? (98)

If you say this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), then first state that over-extension. If you claim it is an injunction (*vidhiśāstra*), then it does not apply to one who knows reality (*tattvavid*). (99)
For only he who possesses the conceit of caste, stage of life, and state of age is subject to all prohibitions and injunctions. (100)
"Castes, stages of life, and so forth are imagined within the body by means of Māyā, but not in the Self whose nature is consciousness"—such was his firm conviction. (101)
Whether he practices meditative concentration or performs ritual actions— or whether he does not—
such a person, having cast aside all mental preoccupations through the heart and possessing the highest disposition, is indeed liberated.

For one whose mind is free from latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no purpose served by inaction (naiṣkarmya), nor any purpose served by ritual acts; nor is there any purpose served by meditative concentration (samādhi) or the chanting of prayers (japya). 103.
"The Self is non-attachment; everything other than that is a magical illusion.
When this has been ascertained with unwavering certainty, how could there be any latent impression (vāsanā) in the mind? (104)
Thus, even a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) does not exist; how then could there be an *atiprasañjana* (over-extension) for it?
An *atiprasañjana* should be suspected only for one who has a *prasaṅga*. (105)
Because there is no injunction, no over-extension is seen in the case of a child;
how could there be such an over-extension for him when [the situation] is equal due to the absence of an injunction? (106)
If the fool knows nothing at all, then the knower of reality knows everything;
for all injunctions apply only to one of little knowledge, and not to either of the other two.

If he who possesses the power to curse or favor is a knower of reality, then that power to curse and so forth would not be the fruit of his asceticism; for [the fruit of asceticism is liberation]. (108)
The power of Vyāsa and others is also seen to arise from the strength of austerity;
moreover, the cause of knowledge is austerity, distinct from other causes such as curses and the like. (109)
Only for one who possesses both [austerity and knowledge] does there arise the power and knowledge;
however, performing austerity alone, one obtains only one result.
If one who lacks capability is censurable by ascetics for neglecting the prescribed rules,
then ascetics too are incessantly censured by others who are greedy for sensual enjoyments.

If these [ascetics] were to preserve their alms-bowls, robes, and other belongings for the sake of satisfaction through enjoyment—oh, how their state of asceticism would be slowed by the weight of dispassion! (112)
If it is said that fools devoted to caste and stage of life should revile [him], then let those who pride themselves on their stage of life and hold the body to be the self revile the Buddha. (113)
Thus, because the means of attainment are not sublated by the knowledge of reality, it is possible for the knower to practice worldly activities such as sovereignty in their proper manner. (114)
If there is no desire for that [worldly life] due to the realization of its falsity, then let it not be;
otherwise, whether meditating or engaging in worldly affairs, let this [jīva] abide according to its prārabdha karma.
But the lay follower (upāsaka) should dwell constantly in meditation alone;
by meditation itself, his state of Brahman-hood is established, just like [the attainment of] Viṣṇu-hood and so forth. (116)
That which is derived from meditation dissolves in the absence of meditation;
but true Brahman-hood never dissolves in the absence of knowledge.
Therefore, this [means of knowledge] does not produce a cognition that makes [the object] known as permanent;
for truth does not vanish merely through the absence of a cognizer. || 118 ||
If it is argued that even for a lay follower there exists a real Brahman-hood, then why is real Brahman-hood not also present in commoners and animals? (119)
The lack of the human goal due to ignorance is equal in both cases;
just as fasting is better than begging, so too is meditation better than the other way around. (120)
The performance of ritual actions is better than the conduct of the ignorant;
even better than that is the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa), and better than that is the meditation on the unqualified (nirguṇa). || 121 ||
As long as one remains close to consciousness, excellence continues to increase;
for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman, you should gradually practice the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) directly. 122.
Just as a cognition that is both consistent and erroneous becomes valid knowledge at the time of its result,
so too does meditation become true knowledge at the time of liberation through the completion of its maturation.
If it is argued that for a person who has acted upon a concordant error,
there is valid knowledge (pramā) by means of another instrument of cognition, then let worship likewise become a cause for another instrument of cognition.
Even if the visualization of the form, as well as the mantra and so forth, were to be causes [of cognition], let it be so; nevertheless, in this case, the degree of proximity is distinguished.
When the worship of the attributeless (nirguṇa) has reached maturity, there arises gradually what is called samādhi;
that samādhi known as nirodha is then obtained without effort.
Upon the attainment of cessation, no object remains for the person within;
yet, when this [mind] has been repeatedly cultivated, the knowledge of reality arises from the [teacher’s] words. (127)
The changeless, unattached, eternal, self-luminous, and uniquely full [nature of reality] ascends instantly within the intellect, as taught in the scriptures, without dispute. (128)
The practice of yoga is taught in such works as the *Amṛtabindu* for this very purpose;
and thus, because it serves as a cause even through its perceptible means, it is superior to other methods.
For those who neglect the pilgrimage to that sacred site and perform only recitations and such, the maxim applies:
"Having abandoned the rice-ball, he licks his own hand. (130)
If even for lay practitioners there is an obstruction resulting from the abandonment of such inquiry, then it is said that yoga is practiced when inquiry is impossible. (131)
For those whose minds are greatly agitated, the realization of reality does not arise through discursive inquiry;
therefore, yoga is primary for them, by which their pride of intellect is destroyed. (132)
For those whose intellects are undisturbed but whose selves are veiled by mere delusion, the inquiry known as Sāṅkhya would be primary, as it leads to immediate realization. (133)
The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṅkhya is also reached by the practitioners of Yoga.
He who sees Sāṅkhya and Yoga as one truly sees.
"For its cause is to be attained through Sāṅkhya and Yoga"—such indeed is the Śruti.
However, whatever contradicts the Śruti is a mere semblance of Sāṅkhya and Yoga. (135)
He whose meditation is not yet fully matured is liberated either here,
or in the next world at death, or in the world of Brahmā, once he has realized the ultimate reality.
"Whatever state one contemplates at the time of leaving the body, to that very state one goes; for by whatever the mind is intent, by that one goes—so it is according to the scriptures. (137)
If that were so, future birth would surely arise from the final cognition;
just as there might be a cognition of the qualityless even during the meditation upon that which possesses qualities. (138)

That which is eternally of the nature of being devoid of qualities should be celebrated by name alone; in reality, this is nothing but liberation itself, though it is regarded as a consistent illusion. (139)
By the power of that [practice], the intellect arises which removes root-ignorance, just as the intellect does through the meditation on the Tāraka Brahman in the Avimukta [sacred site]. (140)
For it is heard in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad] that the fruit of liberation is the state of being "with desire" and "without desire," as well as being bodiless, devoid of senses, and fearless. 141.
From the power of meditation (upāsana), the arising of knowledge (vidyā) occurs;
thus, the scriptural teaching that "there is no other path" is not contradicted at all. (142)

Liberation is proclaimed in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad] as resulting from worship performed without desire; the world of Brahmā is proclaimed in the Śaibya-praśna as the result for one who acts with desire. (143)
He who meditates with the three-mora [syllable] is led to the world of Brahman;
from this mass of living beings, he beholds the Supreme Person. || 144 ||
In the section concerning those who do not undergo the rite of cremation (apratīkādhikaraṇa), the principle of "that-which-one-intends" (tatkratu-nyāya) was stated;
therefore, it has been described that for one possessing desire, the fruit is the world of Brahman.
By the power of the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), through the contemplation of reality therein, he does not return; however, at the end of the kalpa, he is liberated.
The meditations on the Praṇava found in the Vedas are for the most part indeed devoid of attributes (nirguṇa);
however, in some instances, the meditation on the Praṇava is described as possessing attributes (saguṇa). 147.
The syllable Om, which is the form of both the higher and lower Brahman, was described by the sage Pippalāda to Satyakāma when he questioned him. 148.
"Having understood this object of focus, whatever anyone desires, that shall be his"—thus it was declared by Yama even to Naciketas when he questioned him. (149)
Whether he dies here, or in this world, or in the world of Brahmā, there shall be the direct realization of Brahman for him who meditates correctly upon the attributeless [Brahman]. (150)
This very point has also been clearly stated in the *Ātmagītā*:
"One who is incapable of [further] inquiry should constantly worship the Self. (151)
Even if one is unable to realize [Me] directly, one should contemplate Me without hesitation;
in time, one will certainly become established in direct experience as a result. 152.

Just as there is no means for obtaining a treasure of great depth except by digging, so too, even for the attainment of the Self, there is no other way apart from contemplation upon one's own nature. 153.
Having removed the stones of the body with the pickaxe of the intellect, and having further dug up the ground of the mind, a person may then seize me, the hidden treasure. (154)
Even if there is no direct experience, one should simply contemplate "I am Brahman.
Through meditation, even that which is non-existent can be attained; how much more so Brahman, which is eternally present? || 155 ||
If one does not meditate day after day while perceiving that the fruit of meditation is the daily weakening of the notion of self, tell me, who else is more of a beast than such a person? (156)
Having utterly destroyed the identification with the body and perceiving the non-dual Self through meditation,
a mortal, having become dead to the world, attains Brahman right here.
The person who correctly grasps this lamp of meditation is indeed freed from doubt and meditates upon Brahman continuously. (158)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Lamp of Meditation."
The Tenth Chapter, titled "The Lamp of Drama.
Filled with the bliss of the non-dual Supreme Self, he first became the world through his own *māyā* and entered it in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). || 1 ||
Having entered into the superior bodies of gods and others, he becomes a deity; residing within the inferior bodies of mortals and others, he worships the deity. || 2 ||
Through the cultivation of many births, one desires to perform self-inquiry;
when illusion has been destroyed by inquiry, the Self alone remains. || 3 ||
The state of having duality where there is the nature of non-dual bliss, as well as suffering, is declared to be bondage; abiding in one's own true nature is said to be liberation. || 4 ||
Bondage is produced by a lack of inquiry and is removed by inquiry;
therefore, one should always inquire into the individual self and the supreme self. (5)
He who conceives the notion "I am" is the agent; the mind is his instrument. His two functions—internal and external—arise in succession.
This inward-turned mental state, "I," delineates the agent; this outward-turned state, "this," delineates this external object. (7)
Whatever specific qualities there may be, such as odor, form, taste,
and so forth, the five sense organs beginning with the olfactory organ distinguish them without confusion.
That which, by a single effort, illuminates the agent, the action, and likewise the objects as they are excluded from one another— this is the Witness here, whose nature is consciousness.
"I see, I hear, I smell, I taste, and I touch"—thus it illumines everything, like a lamp situated in a dance hall. (10)
A lamp situated in a dance hall illuminates the master, the audience, and the dancer without distinction;
even in their absence, it continues to shine.
The Witness illumines the ego, the intellect, and even the objects;
yet even in the absence of the ego and the rest, He shines by Himself just as before.
While the immutable [Self] shines incessantly by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness,
this intellect, being illumined by that light, dances in manifold ways.
The ego is the master, the sense objects are the courtiers, and the intellect is the dancer; the senses hold the rhythm and other measures, while the witness is the illuminating lamp. (14)
Just as a lamp situated in its own place illuminates everything on all sides, so the Witness, remaining firm and stable, illumines both the external and the internal. 15.
This distinction between "external" and "internal" is relative to the body and does not apply to the Witness. Objects reside in external space, while the ego-sense resides within the body. (16)
The internal intellect, together with the senses, goes out again and again;
thus, the flickering of the intellect situated within the objects of perception is falsely superimposed upon the Witness. (17)
Just as a small, steady ray of sunlight entering through a window within a house appears to dance when the hand is moved there, so too does the light seem to move.
The witness, situated in its own place, neither going out nor coming in,
yet due to the flickering of the intellect, appears as if it acts in various ways.
The witness is neither external nor internal, for those two are merely locations of the intellect;
where all [modifications] such as the intellect have completely subsided, there he shines. || 20 ||
If no particular location were to appear, then let it be one that does not occupy a location;
however, its omnipresence arises precisely from the manifestation of all locations, and not inherently.
Whether internal or external, whatever region one may conceive of, the intellect,
as the witness residing in that region, should likewise apply itself to objects.
Whatever form or other quality may be conceptualized by the intellect, manifesting each of those, it remains their witness, being by its very nature beyond the scope of speech and intellect.
If you ask, "How then should that be grasped by me?", let it not be grasped at all; when all grasping has completely subsided, it remains of its own accord.
In that regard, there is no dependence upon means of knowledge, because its nature is self-luminous.
If you require such an explanation, then study the Śruti from the mouth of a guru.
If the renunciation of all homes is impossible, then take refuge in the Intellect; being dependent on that, let this [world] be experienced as both internal and external.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Lamp of Drama. 10.
The Eleventh Chapter, named the Bliss of Yoga within the Bliss of Brahman.
I shall proclaim the Bliss of Brahman; when that is known in its entirety, one abandons the multitude of misfortunes pertaining to this world and the next, and finds happiness. (1)
The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.
Having obtained the essence of Brahman, he becomes blissful, and not otherwise.
When he finds his firm foundation in himself, then he is fearless; but if he perceives a difference within himself, then fear shall arise for him. || 3 ||
Vāyu, Sūrya, Vahni, Indra, and even Mṛtyu— though they understand the Dharma, they move about out of fear of Him, having made room for themselves in another birth.
One who knows Brahman as bliss fears nothing from any quarter;
for him, this anxiety produced by the fire of karma ceases to exist.
Thus knowing, one should always abandon the two types of action and remember the Self;
and when an action has been performed, one perceives it as being of the very nature of one's own Self.
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
Knowing that very [Self], one transcends death; there is no other path.
By knowing the God, there is the severing of bonds; with the afflictions destroyed, one does not undergo rebirth.
Realizing that he is divine, the steadfast man abandons both joy and sorrow right here;
neither merit nor demerit, whether performed or left undone, ever causes him distress.
Many such scriptural passages, along with the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, have proclaimed that through the knowledge of Brahman there is the destruction of misfortune and the attainment of bliss. (10)
Bliss is threefold: the bliss of Brahman, the happiness of knowledge, and the bliss of sense objects; among these, the bliss of Brahman is now being distinguished. (11)
Having heard from his father Varuṇa the definition of Brahman, Bhṛgu’s son abandoned food, vital breath, mind, and intellect, and realized bliss.
From bliss alone all beings are born; by it they live, and in it they dissolve; therefore, this is the bliss of Brahman, without a doubt. (13)
Prior to the emergence of the elements, there is plenitude (bhūman) due to the absence of the duality of the threefold set;
for indeed, during dissolution, the threefold set consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge does not exist.

The knower arises as consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya); knowledge consists of the mind (manomaya); and the objects of knowledge are sound and the rest. These three did not exist prior to their origination. || 15 ||
In the absence of the triad, however, the non-dual is experienced as truly full;
it is full in deep sleep, in swoon, and likewise before the creation of the world.
"That which is plenitude is bliss; there is no bliss in that which is limited and divided into three parts"—thus did Sanatkumāra speak to the deeply grieving Nārada.
Even after learning the five Vedas along with their ancillaries and various treatises,
Nārada grieved intensely because he lacked self-knowledge.
Formerly, she was afflicted by grief through the mere threefold suffering resulting from the study of the Vedas;
later, however, she was afflicted by grief through the loss of practice, forgetfulness, failure, and pride. (19)
"Thus I, though learned, grieve; lead me to the further shore of sorrow.
Being addressed thus, the sage replied to him, "The further shore is indeed happiness. (20)
Considering that sensual pleasure is indeed suffering because it is enveloped by thousands of sorrows, he said: "There is no pleasure in even the slightest [thing]. (21)
Now, it may be argued: "Let there be no happiness in duality; yet even in non-duality, there is no happiness for us.
If it did exist, it would be perceived, and thus there would be the threefold division [of knower, known, and knowing]. (22)
There is no happiness within non-duality; rather, non-duality itself is indeed happiness.
If it is asked what the proof for this is, there is no need for a means of knowledge regarding that which is self-luminous.
Your own statement is the proof for its being self-luminous, since you yourself, having accepted this non-duality, declare that there is no happiness within it. (24)
If you say, "I do not accept non-duality; rather, having repeated your words, I am stating a refutation," then tell me: what existed prior to duality? (25)
Is it non-duality, or duality, or some other final alternative? The second is not established because [duality] has never arisen; thus, only the first remains. (26)
If you say that the proof of non-duality is through reasoning alone and not through experience, tell us:
is it without an illustration or with an illustration? There is no other alternative here for us.
The argument that there is neither experience nor an illustration does not shine.
But if you maintain the position that it must be accompanied by an illustration, then state an illustration according to my view.
If you say that dissolution is non-dual because duality is not perceived, as in deep sleep, then provide an illustration for the claim that deep sleep itself is non-dual. (29)
If you claim that the sleep of another serves as an illustration, oh, what great skill you possess!
For one who does not even know his own sleep—what can be said of his knowledge of the sleep of another? (30)
If it is argued that "another is asleep because of his lack of activity, just as I am," then by that very statement,
the self-luminosity of the one who speaks while in deep sleep would be established by force of logic.
Neither the sense organs nor any illustrative example [establish it], yet you accept that [reality]; this alone is its self-luminosity—that it manifests even without means of proof.
If you maintain that the state of deep sleep is the self-luminous non-duality, tell me: how can there be happiness in sleep?
Listen: at that time there is no suffering; therefore, what remains for you is happiness.
"Though blind, one becomes non-blind; though pierced, one becomes unpierced;
and even if diseased, one becomes free from disease," so says the Śruti, and all people know this to be true.

If it is argued that pleasure does not exist merely through the absence of suffering—as seen in clods of earth, stones, and the like, where both [pleasure and pain] are absent—this statement is inconsistent. (35)
The inference of another's suffering or happiness is made through the manifestation of dejection on the face and so forth;
since such dejection and the like do not exist in a clod of earth, the inference of suffering and so forth in it is impossible. (36)

However, one's own pleasure and pain are not to be inferred; therefore, the existence of those two is to be known through direct experience alone, and their non-existence likewise cannot be known from any other source.
That being so, since the absence of suffering is experienced even in deep sleep, let it be accepted that there is unimpeded happiness due to the lack of its opposite, suffering. (38)
If there were no pleasure in sleep, why would one procure the means for a soft bed and so forth with such great effort? (39)
If you say that this [scriptural injunction] is solely for the purpose of destroying suffering, then let it be so for the sick;
however, determine for yourself that for those who are not ill, it is for the sake of happiness alone. (40)
In that case, because it is produced by a means of accomplishment, pleasure would be merely sensual;
yet this is indeed the case here, such as that which arises from a bed or a seat prior to sleep.
By what cause is that happiness produced in sleep?
First, the intellect, being oriented toward pleasure, subsequently sinks into supreme bliss.
Exhausted by the activities of the waking state, one then rests; once the opposing [state] has been removed, with a mind established in its own natural state, one experiences happiness in the object.
When the mental modification is directed toward the self, one's own bliss is reflected therein;
yet even by experiencing this, one may still incur exhaustion through the threefold division [of subject, object, and act]. || 44 ||
To dispel that fatigue, the individual soul (jīva) should run toward the Supreme Self;
having attained oneness with It, it shall itself become the bliss of Brahman residing therein. || 45 ||
The hawk, the falcon, the prince, the great king, and the great brahmin—these are the examples cited in the Vedas regarding the bliss of deep sleep. (46)
A bird bound by a string, having flitted about in all directions and found no rest, resorts to the hand, a pillar, or some other support as its place of confinement. (47)

The mind is likewise the limiting adjunct of the individual soul; having wandered through dreams and the waking state to obtain the fruits of merit and demerit, it dissolves when its karma is exhausted.
Just as a hawk, longing only for its nest, flies with speed to rest, so too does the individual soul (jīva), longing only for the bliss of Brahman, hasten toward sleep. 49.

Having drunk from the breast of his mother while still an infant, lying upon a soft bed and smiling, he partakes of a nature consisting solely of bliss (*ānanda*) because passion, hatred, and other afflictions have not yet arisen. (50)
The universal monarch, fully satisfied by every enjoyment,
having reached the very limit of human bliss, became the embodiment of pure joy.

The great Brahmin, the knower of Brahman, having attained the supreme pinnacle of the bliss of knowledge— characterized by the state of having accomplished all that was to be done— remains established therein.

In this world, the state of being essentially happy is established for those of simple intellect and those of superior intellect as described; however, others are suffering and do not possess the nature of happiness. (53)
Like a youth and others, this [yogin] is solely intent upon the bliss of Brahman;
like one embraced by a woman, he perceives neither the external nor the internal.
Just as the external world consists of streets and the like, while domestic affairs are internal, so too is waking external, whereas dreaming within the channels (nāḍīs) is internal. || 55 ||
In passages such as "The father also [is] asleep," the status of being a living individual (jīvatva) is excluded;
for when both are asleep, they are Brahman alone, not a living individual, since the characteristics of transmigratory existence are not observed.
For that conceit of being a father and so forth is indeed the source of pleasure and pain;
when that has departed, he crosses over all sorrows.
"When all [the elements] have dissolved during the state of deep sleep, one enveloped by darkness attains the nature of bliss"—thus indeed says the Atharvaṇa Śruti. (58)
"I slept happily here; I was not aware of anything at all"—thus, having awakened, one reflects upon these two: happiness and ignorance. (59)
Since there is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) regarding what has been experienced, there was an experience at that time;
it shines forth by its own nature as the conscious self (*cidātman*), and from that arises the cognition of ignorance (*ajñānadhī*).
The Vājasaneyins recite: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss.
Therefore, Brahman alone is self-luminous bliss, and nothing else.
That ignorance in which both that consciousness and the mind-made [self] are dissolved—
indeed, the state of dissolution of those two is sleep, and that very state is ignorance.
Thereafter, like melted ghee, it becomes a solid mass consisting of consciousness;
this state of dissolution is designated by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).

The mental modification (buddhi-vṛtti) that reflects pleasure in the moment immediately preceding sleep— this very modification, together with its reflection, then becomes the state consisting of dissolved bliss.

Then, turned inward and consisting of bliss, he experiences the happiness of Brahman through mental modifications (vṛtti) born of ignorance that are joined with the reflection of consciousness (cidbimba). || 65 ||
"The functions of ignorance are subtle, whereas the functions of the intellect are distinct"—thus indeed do those who have reached the further shore of the Vedānta doctrine proclaim. (66)
In the Māṇḍūkya, Tāpanīya, and other Śrutis, this is extremely clear:
that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the enjoyer, while Brahman-bliss is the object of enjoyment.
Becoming one, abiding in deep sleep, having attained the state of a mass of pure consciousness,
he consists of bliss, enjoys bliss, and is composed of the functions of the mind.
He who was previously endowed with forms primarily consisting of consciousness has now attained unity through dissolution, like a mass of flour from many grains of rice.
Previously, the various forms of wisdom were the fluctuations of the intellect;
then they became solidified, just as the state of solidity occurs among drops of frost in the northern region.

Ordinary people and logicians alike declare that the state of being a witness, characterized by the density of that [consciousness], is the absence of suffering, as long as the functioning of suffering has been extinguished. (71)
Consciousness reflected in ignorance becomes the mouth for the enjoyment of bliss;
having consumed the bliss of Brahman, it then goes outward through the power of karma.
"Whatever karma existed in another birth, through its connection one awakens again"—thus, in the Kaivalya-śākhā, awakening born of karma is described. (73)
For some time, the latent impression (vāsanā) of the bliss of Brahman realized by the awakened one persists;
therefore, he remains silent, happy, and free from sense-objects.
Driven by their past actions and subsequently contemplating various miseries,
all these people gradually forget the bliss of Brahman.
Even before and after sleep, there is a daily inclination of men toward the bliss of Brahman; therefore, what wise person would dispute this? (76)

Now, if the bliss of Brahman were to manifest while remaining silent, then worldly people would become indolent and their purpose fulfilled; what then would be the use here of scripture or a teacher? (77)
If they should know, "It is certainly Brahman," they would have achieved their purpose by that alone;
for who can know Brahman, which is exceedingly profound, without the teacher and the scripture? (78)
"I know from your words today why I have not attained my goal;
listen to this account concerning a certain person who considered himself wise, yet was like you. (79)
Hearing the words, "It should be given to one who knows the four Vedas," he said:
"I know that there are indeed four Vedas; let my wealth be given to me. (80)
"He knows only Sāṅkhya, but not the Vedas in their entirety;
if that is so, then you likewise do not know Brahman in its entirety. (81)
In the unbroken, single-flavored bliss that is devoid of māyā and its effects,
what occasion is there even for talk of "without remainder" or "with remainder"?
Do you merely recite the words, or do you also perceive their meaning?
When it comes to the recitation of words, the understanding of their meaning is what remains to be accomplished for you. (83)
When the meaning has been explained, direct realization remains regarding the Buddha;
O friend, continue to attend upon the Guru until the conviction that your purpose has been fulfilled arises. (84)
Let this matter rest; know that wherever there may be happiness apart from sense objects, in every such case it is the latent impression of the bliss of Brahman. (85)
Even when sense objects have been obtained, once the desire for them has subsided,
bliss is reflected in the inward-turned activity of the mind.
The bliss of Brahman, latent impressions, and the reflection—these three;
apart from these, there is no bliss whatsoever in this world. (87)
And so, the self-luminous bliss of Brahman exists, generating these two types of bliss: the bliss of sense objects and the bliss of latent impressions. (88)

Since Brahman-bliss, which is self-luminous consciousness by nature, is established through scripture, reasoning, and experience during the state of deep sleep, listen now to what pertains to other times. 89.
That which consists of bliss during deep sleep, having attained the state of the self consisting of consciousness,
undergoes dreaming or waking according to the difference in its location.
In the eyes there is wakefulness, in the throat dreaming, and in the lotus of the heart deep sleep;
consciousness, pervading the body from head to foot, remains awake.
Then, having attained identity with the body like a heated iron ball, one remains fixed in the certain conviction: "I am a human being. (92)
This [Self] attains three states—being indifferent, happy, or miserable;
happiness and misery are the effects of karma, whereas indifference is its inherent nature. (93)
Pleasure and pain are considered to be of two kinds: those arising from external enjoyments and those arising from the kingdom of the mind.
In the intervals between pleasure and pain, there should be a state of remaining in silence.
"I have no concern whatsoever today; I sit in happiness"—by saying this, every person expresses the manifestation of their own bliss within a state of indifference. (95)
Because it is veiled by the general sense of egoism in the form of "I am," this innate bliss is not primary; rather, it is merely a latent impression (vāsanā) of that [bliss]. (96)
The coldness on the exterior of a vessel filled with water is not that water itself; rather, it is a quality of the water, by which the existence of the water is inferred. (97)
To the extent that the ego is forgotten through the yoga of practice,
to that same extent the bliss of one's own nature is inferred by the subtle vision.
Being completely forgotten, it attains supreme subtlety;
because it is not dissolved, this is not sleep, and therefore even the body does not fall [into unconsciousness]. (99)
Where neither duality appears nor even sleep exists—that which is bliss—the Blessed One declared to Arjuna: "That is the bliss of Brahman. (100)
One should gradually come to rest by means of the intellect held with firmness;
having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone. 102.
For supreme happiness comes to this yogi whose mind is perfectly tranquil, whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from all taint. 103.
Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest;
and where, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction within the Self. (104)
That absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and beyond the senses—he who knows that, and being established therein, does not deviate from reality; || 105 ||
Having obtained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it;
established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering. (106)
One should know that disjunction from the union with suffering is designated as yoga;
that yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency.
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi, freed from all taint, enjoys with ease the infinite bliss of contact with Brahman.
Just as the overflowing of the great ocean might be checked by a single drop on the tip of a blade of kusha grass, so too the restraint of the mind is achieved through tireless effort. 109.
To the royal sage Bṛhadratha, the sage Śākāyanya spoke of bliss in the branch known as Maitrāyaṇī, preceded by instructions on meditative absorption.
Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source, so too the mind, through the cessation of its mental modifications, is extinguished in its own source. || 111 ||

For one whose mind has become tranquil within its own source, who desires the truth, and who is deluded regarding the objects of the senses, the [objects] follow the power of karma and are unreal. 112.
The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; one should purify it with effort. Whatever the mind is, of that the mortal becomes; this is the eternal secret. (113)
For by the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma;
with a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable bliss. 114.
If the mind of a living being were attached to Brahman in the same way that it is attached to the realm of sense objects, who would not be liberated from bondage? (115)
The mind is indeed said to be of two kinds: pure and impure.
It is impure through contact with desire, and pure when devoid of desire. || 116 ||
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; free from sense objects, it is known to lead to liberation. 117.
When the mind, its impurities shaken off by meditative concentration,
is established in the Self, the bliss that arises cannot then be described by speech.
It is grasped by itself through its own internal organ. || 118 ||

Although this meditative absorption is difficult for humans to attain even over a long period of time, nevertheless, even in its momentary form, it brings about the certain realization of the bliss of Brahman.
One who is faithful and devoted to this [teaching] will certainly resolve it in every way;
once that has been resolved, he will trust in it even at other times.
Such a person, even during the state of neutrality, disregards the latent impression of [worldly] bliss and,
being intent upon it, meditates solely on the primary bliss.
A woman who is devoted to another man, even while busily engaged in household chores, internally relishes that very elixir of union with another. 122.
Thus, having attained rest in the supreme, pure reality,
the steadfast one experiences that very state within, even while engaging in external worldly affairs.
Steadfastness is the engagement in contemplation of that [object], having set aside all the senses out of a desire to savor bliss, even when the senses are powerful. (124)
Having cast off the burden on his head, the bearer of the load rests, having attained repose; likewise, the abandonment of worldly involvement is what constitutes such repose for the intellect. (125)
Having attained supreme rest in equanimity,
whether in a state of happiness or suffering, you are then solely intent upon that bliss.
Just as the mind is directed toward entering the fire for the sake of the erotic sentiment,
so too does such a mind arise in the wise man regarding [the world], being opposed to further inquiry.
While performing the coming and going between non-conflicting happiness and her own bliss,
she moves here and there in succession, like the eye of a crow.
The vision of the crow is one and the same for both its left and right eyes;
likewise, the mind of the knower of reality moves back and forth between the two states of bliss.

The knower of reality, while experiencing the bliss of the sense objects as well as the bliss of Brahman, should understand both the worldly and the Vedic, just like one who is proficient in two languages. 130.
And there is no agitation upon encountering suffering, as before, because he possesses the twofold vision;
it is like the perception of cold and heat in a man whose body is half-immersed in the Ganges. (131)
In this way, for the knower of reality, the bliss of Brahman shines constantly during wakefulness;
likewise, it shines similarly in the dream state produced by its latent impressions.
Since the latent impression of ignorance also exists,
one perceives pleasure and pain in a dream arising from that impression, just as before.
In this first chapter of the treatise titled *Brahmānanda*, the direct perception of yogins, which illuminates the bliss of Brahman, has been expounded. (134)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, "The Bliss of Yoga," within the *Brahmānanda*.
The Twelfth Chapter of the *Brahmānanda*, titled "The Bliss of the Self.

Indeed, if the yogi thus perceives his own innate bliss as distinct from both the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*) and the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), what recourse remains for the deluded person in this matter? (1)
Let this [self] be born and die again and again by the power of merit and demerit through hundreds of thousands of bodies; tell me, what is the use of our compassion? (2)
If you have a need for courtesy because of a desire to favor us, then tell me:
is that fool one who seeks knowledge, or is he one who has turned his back [on it]? (3)
One should explain the service or the ritual action as is appropriate to one who is averse [to knowledge];
however, one should awaken the seeker of dull intellect by means of the bliss of the Self.
Yājñavalkya enlightened his beloved Maitreyī, saying:
