"Indeed, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear. (5)
A husband, wife, sons, wealth, cattle, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, worlds, gods, Vedas, and all beings—all these are dear for the sake of the self. (6)
When the wife has a desire for her husband, she then brings him pleasure;
but when he is afflicted by hunger, religious duties, illness, and the like, then her husband does not desire her.
That affection is not for the sake of the husband; she acts out of her own self-interest alone.
And the husband is likewise always for his own sake, never for the sake of his wife.
Even when there is mutual instigation, the engagement occurs solely by their own will.
When a child cries from being pricked by the stubble of a beard, the father kisses him;
that is not true affection for the child's sake, but rather for his own sake.
Even though she has no desire for it, she takes pleasure in diligently protecting wealth such as jewels; thus, her concern for wealth is for her own sake, which is not to be doubted. (10)
When one wishes to marry off a bull by force against its will, that pleasure is for the sake of the merchant alone; how could it be for the sake of the bull? (11)
"I possess Brahminhood; I am worthy of worship"—with such thoughts one is gratified by honor.
But satisfaction does not belong to the insentient caste; it belongs only to the person.

"In the statement, 'I am a Kṣatriya, therefore I rule the kingdom,' the quality of being a king [is attributed] to the caste; this has been stated so that it may not be applied to other castes such as the Vaiśya. (13)
The longing "May the worlds of heaven and Brahmā be mine" serves no purpose for those two worlds; it is intended solely for one's own enjoyment. (14)

Gods such as Īśa, Viṣṇu, and others are worshipped for the destruction of sin; it is not for the sake of those gods who are already free from sin, but rather for one's own purpose that such worship is employed. (15)
For the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas are studied for the sake of attaining the status of a true Brāhmaṇa;
that which is not applicable to the Vedas is not applicable to human beings. (16)

The five elements, beginning with earth, desire these [beings] through their respective functions—supporting, thirsting, maturing, drying, and providing space—as well as by means of [the principle of] non-obstruction; they do not desire them for their own sake.
Everyone, such as masters, servants, and others, desires [everything] for their own benefit;
yet no benefit produced by this or that person exists for them [in the ultimate sense]. (18)
One should investigate all worldly transactions in this same manner;
by means of such a profusion of examples, one should settle one's own mind.
Now, what might this "joy" (prīti) be that is heard of in relation to one's own self?

It is passion (rāga) toward objects such as a wife; it is faith (śraddhā) in rituals such as sacrifice; it would be devotion (bhakti) toward the guru, the gods, and so forth; and it is desire (icchā) for an object not yet attained. (20)
In that case, let there be the sattvic state which follows after mere pleasure; yet, because its true nature remains even when pleasure is attained or lost, it is distinguished from desire.

Food, drink, and so forth are dear because they are the means to pleasure; if the Self were likewise dear simply because it conforms to [one's desires], then who here would need to be conformed to by that [Self]? Furthermore, there can be no identity of the object and the agent in a single entity. (22)
In worldly pleasure there is merely affection; but the Self is exceedingly dear.
This affection wavers toward pleasure, yet it does not waver toward the Self.
One constantly abandons one thing and takes up another for the sake of sensory pleasure;
yet the Self is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired—how could one ever deviate from it? (24)

If, in this state, there is equanimity devoid of both rejection and acceptance—like [the attitude toward] grass and such—then because it is the very nature of the one who is equanimous, the self cannot be an object of equanimity. (25)
In some cases, the desire to die is observed in those overcome by disease and anger;
if it follows that the self should therefore be abandoned out of aversion, that is not so.
For the body, which is fit to be abandoned, does not possess the nature of the self; rather, that nature belongs to the abandoner alone.
That hatred does not exist in the one who has renounced; but what harm is there in the object to be renounced? || 26 ||
For everything is dear because it serves one's own self, and thus the self is indeed most dear;
just as a son is more beloved to a father than his other sons or friends, so too is the self. (27)
"May we not cease to exist, but rather may we always continue to be"—this is the blessing seen by everyone; thus, love for oneself is directly perceived. (28)
When joy has been thus established in the self through these three [stages] beginning with "thus," some have asserted that the self exists for the sake of others, such as sons and wives. (29)
With this intention, the Śruti declares that the son is the primary self;
"The self, indeed, is the name of the son"—this is made clear in the Upaniṣad. (30)
Thus, this self of his is assigned to meritorious deeds;
then his other self, having accomplished its purpose, passes away.

Even though the self exists, there is no world for one who has no son; for this very reason, the wise declare that only a son who has been properly instructed is conducive to the world hereafter. (32)
The world of men can be conquered only by a son and not by any other means;
one who is about to die should consecrate his son with the mantras beginning with "Thou art Brahman."
Such scriptural passages declare that one is subordinate to one's son, wife, and others;
even worldly people acknowledge the preeminence of the son.
Just as a son or other relative would live by means of wealth and so forth even when one has died, one exerts effort in that very same way; therefore, sons and others are considered primary. (35)
Certainly, by this much alone, the self does not remain as a remainder for anyone;
this self becomes threefold through the distinctions of the secondary, the false, and the primary. (36)

But in the case of "This Devadatta is a lion," the identity between these two is figurative, because their difference is clearly perceived; likewise is the case with the selfhood attributed to a son and so forth. (37)
There is a distinction between the five sheaths and the Witness, yet this distinction does not appear;
therefore, the sheaths possess a false nature, just as a tree stump may have the nature of a thief [to one in error]. (38)
Difference does not appear, nor does it exist for the Witness who has no counter-correlate;
because He is within all, His alone is accepted as the primary nature of the Self. (39)

This being so, in whatever conventional dealings a thing is appropriately regarded as the self, in those dealings that very thing alone is the principal, while everything else is subordinate to it. (40)
For one who is about to die, only the secondary self (gauṇātman) is useful for guarding the house and such tasks;
neither the primary self (mukhyātman) nor the illusory self (mithyātman) is so. Therefore, the son becomes the residual self (śeṣī). || 41 ||

In the expression "the student is fire," although fire is present, it is not apprehended because of its lack of fitness; rather, it is the student alone who is apprehended here due to his fitness. (42)
In such instances as "I am emaciated; I shall attain nourishment," the identification of the body with the self is appropriate;
however, one does not direct a son to eat food for the sake of one's own nourishment. (43)
In such cases as "I shall go to heaven through austerity," the sense of agency belongs to the self;
therefore, disregarding bodily enjoyment, one should perform penances such as the *kṛcchra*.
At that time, the person is joined with the nature of the conscious self in the thought "I shall be liberated";
he knows this through the teacher and the scriptures, yet he does not desire to do anything at all.
Just as the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others are restricted to specific roles in rites such as the Bṛhaspatisava,
so too are the figurative, the false, and the primary [meanings] applied as appropriate.
In each of those cases, pleasure is found to be most intense toward the self alone;
whereas toward that which is not the self—namely, what remains as its adjunct—there is pleasure, but toward anything else there is neither.
The path, grass, and so forth are of two kinds—either to be disregarded or to be loathed;
tigers, snakes, and so forth are to be disregarded or loathed. Thus, there are four types. (48)

Among these four—self, remainder, that which is to be disregarded, and that which is to be hated—there is no fixed rule regarding their manifestation; rather, they appear in such and such ways according to their respective functions.
A tiger facing one is indeed to be hated, but when turned away, it is to be disregarded;
if it becomes favorable through fondling, it may be treated as a mere pet for amusement. (50)
Let there be no restriction regarding individual instances; rather, the determination [of categories] arises from their defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
Favorability, unfavorability, and the absence of both are the defining characteristics. (51)
The self is the most beloved, the remainder is dear, while those other than these two are objects of aversion or indifference;
thus is the world established, and that is the view of Yājñavalkya. (52)
Elsewhere also, the Śruti declares: "The inner reality is dearer than sons, wealth, and likewise everything else;
let one regard this very reality as the most beloved. (53)
Through the scriptural method of inquiry, this Self alone is the witness, and nothing else;
inquiry is the vision of the reality within, having discriminated the five sheaths. (54)
Since the appearance of the coming and going of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep occurs from that source,
he is the Self, whose nature is self-luminous consciousness.

The remaining [objects], beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa) and ending with wealth (vitta), are proximate in a graduated sequence; accordingly, a corresponding gradation of pleasure is observed among all of them. (56)
A son is dearer than wealth; the funeral oblation (piṇḍa) is dearer than a son; likewise, the sense organs are dearer than the oblation;
the vital breath (prāṇa) is dearer than the sense organs; and the Self is dearer than the vital breath. || 57 ||
Such being the case, a dispute arises here between the enlightened and the deluded;
regarding this, the Veda has declared that the Self alone is the dearest—that is the final determination.
The knower of reality says that the Witness alone is dearer than any other object of perception;
yet the deluded intellect thinks that the son and others are dear because they enable this Witness to experience. (59)
If either the disciple or the opponent speaks of someone other than oneself as being dear,
one should respond to their speech by bestowing either enlightenment or a curse upon them respectively.
"The Knower of Reality gives this reply: 'It will obstruct what is dear to you.
Through discernment, the disciple understands that what he himself called 'dear' was actually harmful. (61)
A son who is not obtained causes his parents long-lasting distress;
even when obtained, he afflicts them through miscarriage and the pains of childbirth.
For one born [under these conditions], there will be planetary afflictions and diseases; for a young boy, muteness;
even when initiated, a lack of learning; and for a scholar, the failure to marry. (63)
Furthermore, there is the sin of adultery with another's wife and so forth, as well as the poverty of one's family members;
there is no end to the suffering of one's parents, especially if the wealthy man then dies.
Having thus discerned this and abandoned affection for sons and others, one determines that supreme affection exists within one's own self and gazes upon it day and night.
For a proponent who does not relinquish his position due to dogmatic attachment or even hatred toward those who know Brahman,
hell is declared as the consequence, along with rebirth in many wombs.
Because he is a knower of Brahman and possesses the nature of Brahman, the Lord has described it;
whatever he says shall be exactly so for both his disciple and his opponent.
But he who serves the Self as his witness, the supreme beloved—for him that dear Self shall never perish. (68)
Its nature as supreme bliss consists in being the object of supreme love;
it is heard in the scriptures that there is an increase in happiness corresponding to the increase in affection, as seen among universal monarchs and others. (69)
If pleasure were the inherent nature of this conscious self, just like consciousness itself, it would persist through all mental modifications (dhīvṛttis), just as consciousness does. (70)

Let it not be so; for a lamp, whose nature is heat and light, pervades the house with its radiance, yet its heat does not do so. In the same way, it is only the consciousness that follows [the object].
Just as even when odor, form, taste, and touch are present, only one object is perceived by a single sense organ and not the others, so it is here.

If you argue that consciousness and bliss are not distinct while odors and other qualities are indeed different, then tell me: is that non-distinction [of consciousness and bliss] in the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) or elsewhere? 73.
In the first case, even odors and so forth residing in a flower are likewise non-different;
yet, when there is a difference [in perception] due to a difference in the sense organs, there is a distinction between those two because of the difference in their modes of functioning.
In the state of sattva, there is the unity of consciousness and bliss because that mental modification is pure;
however, due to the impurity of the rajas-modification, the aspect of bliss is obscured therein. (75)
Just as a tamarind fruit, when combined with salt, slightly excites the digestive fire by suppressing its acidity; so it is in this case. (76)
But surely, since the Self is the supreme bliss due to its being the most beloved, how could it be possible to discern [it] in this way without yoga? (77)

We say that through the application of which one attains that very [state] for the sake of the perfection of knowledge; since yoga has been declared to consist in discernment, why should knowledge not arise? (78)
"The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṅkhya is also reached by those of Yoga"—thus is recorded the identity of the fruit for both yogins and the discerning. (79)
"For some, yoga is the means to liberation; for others, the certainty of knowledge.
Having thus reflected, the Supreme Lord declared two paths. (80)
What excellence is there here in yoga? Knowledge is said to be equal for both;
and the absence of passion, hatred, and so forth is the same for both the yogi and the man of discrimination. (81)
For one who knows that the Self is dearer than anything else, there is no delight in sense objects;
how could there be passion or hatred for one who perceives nothing as adverse? (82)
Aversion toward things contrary to the body and so forth is equal for both [the yogi and the non-yogi];
if one who feels aversion were not a yogi, then even a person lacking discrimination would be such [a yogi]. (83)
The manifestation of duality is equal for both [the dualist and the non-dualist] in worldly transaction;
if you say it does not exist in meditative absorption (samādhi), then it is likewise not so for one who discriminates the state of non-duality.
Indeed, all of that most auspicious matter will be explained by us in the third chapter, titled "The Bliss of Non-duality" (Advaitānanda). 85.
If you say that one is called a "yogi" because they always perceive their own bliss while not perceiving the entire world, then may you yourself be satisfied and prosper! (86)
In this second chapter of the treatise titled *Brahmānanda*, the bliss of the Self (*ātmānanda*) has been analyzed for the sake of bestowing grace upon the dull-witted. (87)
Thus ends the "Bliss of the Self" within the "Bliss of Brahman," [chapter] 12.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Bliss of Non-duality," from the *Brahmānanda*.

That which was previously described as the bliss of yoga should be understood as the bliss of the Self (Ātmānanda). If it is asked, "How can this [Self], which appears to possess duality, be Brahman? listen. 1. If it is asked, "How can this [Self], which appears to possess duality, be Brahman? listen.
From space down to one's own body, as proclaimed in the Taittirīya Śruti, the world does not exist apart from bliss; therefore, there is the non-duality of Brahman.
For it is from bliss alone that this was born, in bliss indeed it remains, and into bliss alone it is dissolved; thus, how can it be separate from bliss? (3)
One should not suspect that the jar is produced from and distinct from the potter;
for this [clay] is the material cause (*upādāna*), not the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) like the potter. (4)
The persistence and dissolution of the jar do not exist anywhere in the potter;
those two are seen in the clay. Likewise, the material cause [of the universe] must be so, according to scripture. (5)

Appropriation (upādāna) is divided into three types: transformative (vivarti), evolutive (pariṇāmi), and productive (ārambhaka). Among these, the last two are not applicable to that which is partless.
The proponents of creation (ārambhavādins) have declared that one thing arises from another;
for indeed, the cloth and the threads are distinct because of the production of the cloth from the threads. (7)
The transformation of a single entity into another state is its being subject to change (pariṇāmitā), just as milk becomes curd, clay becomes a jar, or gold becomes an earring. (8)
The appearance of a different state, however, is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), like a snake in a rope;
even in that which is partless, such an appearance exists, as in the conceptualization of surface-dirtiness in the sky. (9)
Therefore, let the world be considered an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) within partless bliss;
the power of *māyā* would be the agent of this conceptualization, like the power of a magician. (10)

Power is not separate from that which possesses power; likewise, there is no difference between them because it is observed [as such]. Since an obstruction is observed, if power were non-existent, of what would it be an obstruction? (11)
Since power is to be inferred from its effect, there can be no obstruction when there is no effect;
for instance, if a blazing fire does not burn, the obstruction must lie in the mantras and so forth. (12)
Sages have known the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities;
His supreme power is manifold, consisting of action, knowledge, and strength. 13.
Thus spoke the word of the Vedas, and Vasiṣṭha likewise declared:
"Brahman is the supreme all-powerful, eternal, ever-full, and non-dual. (14)
Just as this [consciousness] shines forth and attains manifestation through power (śakti),
O Rāma, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) of Brahman is perceived within bodies.
The power of vibration resides in the winds; likewise, the power of solidity in stones;
the power of fluidity in waters; the power of burning in fire; the power of emptiness in space; and the power of destruction in that which is perishable.
Just as a great serpent exists within an egg, so does the world exist within the Self;
just as a tree— complete with fruit, leaves, creepers, flowers, branches, twigs, and roots—
is contained within the seed of the tree, so is this [universe] situated within Brahman.
In some place, for someone, and at some time, powers arise from that [source],
due to the diversity of space and time, just as rice plants arise from the surface of the earth.
O Rāma, that Self is all-pervading and possesses an eternally manifest, great body;
when it assumes even a slight power of thought, it is called the mind (manas).

First is the mind, then the views of liberation from its attachments, and afterwards the construction of conceptual proliferation known as the world; for this established order has become fixed like a tale told by fortunate children. 20.
Indeed, for the amusement of a child, a nurse tells an auspicious tale:
"O mighty-armed one! Somewhere there are three auspicious princes. (21)
Two were not born, and likewise one did not even remain in the womb;
those endowed with Dharma dwell in a city that is utterly non-existent.
Having emerged from their own empty city, those of pure intention saw trees laden with fruit while traveling through the sky.
"O son! Those three princes who were to become kings in that city are staying comfortably today, engaged in the pursuit of hunting. (24)
O Rāma! Having been told this auspicious tale of the boy by his nurse, the child reached a firm conclusion with a mind free from doubt. (25)
This construction of saṃsāra has come to such a state for those whose minds are devoid of inquiry, just like a story told to children. (26)
Through such narratives, Vasiṣṭha explained the extent of the power of Māyā; that very power is now being defined.
This power (śakti) would be distinct [from its substratum] both by virtue of its effect and its locus;
for when sparks and glowing coals are perceived, the power therein is inferred. (28)
In this context, the clay should be fashioned into the form of a pot with a broad base and belly;
however, the power (śakti) associated with it is of a different nature, being endowed with the five qualities such as sound and the rest.

It is neither earth and so forth, nor sound and so forth; as it exists within the power [of consciousness], so it is. For this very reason, it is inconceivable and does not admit of verbal definition. (30)
Prior to the production of the effect, the power remains hidden, situated within the clay;
through the assistance of the potter and other factors, it undergoes the form of a transformation. (31)
People devoid of inquiry, having unified the earth and its transformations ending with touch and other qualities, as well as the clay, call it a "pot. (32)
Whatever portion [of the process] precedes the potter's activity is not, for us, a jar;
but after that, when it possesses a broad base and so forth, its status as a "pot" is indeed appropriate. (33)
That jar is not different from the clay, because it is not perceived when [the clay] is separated;
nor is it non-different, because it was not perceived previously during the state of the lump. (34)

Therefore, this [universe] is indefinable; like a power (śakti), it is born from that [power]. Power is said to exist in the unmanifest state, while in the manifest state it bears the name of "form" (ghaṭanā).
Even the illusion that culminates in sorcery is not manifested at first;
later, it attains manifestation in the form of the Gandharva army and so forth.
Thus, the Śruti has declared that because it consists of illusion, the modification is unreal in nature, whereas the clay-substance, which is the substratum of the modification, is real. (37)
That which is produced by speech is a mere name, a modification that possesses no reality;
however, the clay alone, endowed with qualities such as touch and so forth, is real. (38)
"The Manifest and the Unmanifest, as well as their substratum"—among these three, there is a synonymy between the first two due to a difference in time, while the third persists [throughout]. (39)
That which appears, though devoid of reality, is manifest and subject to arising and destruction;
upon its arising, its name is produced by men through speech. (40)
Even when the manifest has perished, this name persists within the mouths of men;
because it is defined by that name, the manifest is said to have that as its form. (41)

Because it lacks ultimate reality, because it is subject to destruction, and because it is a mere name based on speech, the manifested form does not possess any true nature of its own, unlike clay or similar substances. (42)
Therefore, prior to and even after the time of manifestation, the clay substance is said to possess reality and be indestructible, maintaining a single uniform nature. (43)
If the object denoted by these names—namely, "the manifest," "the jar," and "the modification"—is unreal, why does it not cease upon the cognition of the clay? (44)
Since your notion of its reality has indeed ceased, such cessation alone arises here from awakening, not the non-appearance [of the object]. (45)
A person reflected in water appears with his face downward, yet he does not exist there in reality;
just like a bystander on the shore, no one has any attachment to him whatsoever.
It is in such an awakening that the non-dualists (Advaitavādins) consider the ultimate goal of human life to consist.
Because the form of the clay is not abandoned, the nature of being a vivarta (illusory manifestation) resides in the jar;
in a pariṇāma (transformation), however, the prior form would be relinquished, as in the case of the form of milk. Indeed, clay and gold do not cease to exist when they become a jar or a bracelet.
When the jar is destroyed, its state as clay does not cease, because the shards are still perceived;
but it is not so in the case of powder, for there the form of clay no longer exists, whereas the form of gold remains perfectly evident. (48)
Let there be transformation in milk and the like, because they subsequently abandon that state;
by this much, the status of clay and other things as examples is not lost. (49)
For the proponent of origination (ārambhavādin), a doubling of the clay would result in the effect;
for color, touch, and so forth are said to be distinct in the effect and the cause. (50)
Āruṇi stated three examples—clay, gold, and so forth—from which one should infer the unreality of all things. (51)
He also spoke of the knowledge of the effect arising from the knowledge of the cause;
how, then, can the knowledge of the unreal occur when there is the knowledge of the real? (52)
From the perspective of worldly experience, every modification of clay possesses the status of an effect;
however, in this context, the realization of its constituent clay-element is the realization of the cause. (53)
The unreal portion need not be understood, because understanding it is of no use;
the knowledge of reality serves the purpose of man, whereas the comprehension of an unreal portion does not. (54)

If it is then argued that the knowledge of the effect arises from the knowledge of the cause, then it would simply mean that by knowing the clay one knows the "clay-ness"; what wonder is there in this? (55)
For one who knows that in all effects the constituent part of the substance is the very essence of the cause, there should be no wonder; for whom, indeed, can such wonder be prevented? || 56 ||

Having heard all these doctrines regarding a single cause—whether it be one that begins anew, undergoes transformation, or is of a worldly nature—they indeed experience astonishment once it is understood. (57)

In this context, through the awakening to one [reality], the awakening to all occurs precisely in order to bring non-duality (advaita) face-to-face; it is not intended by the Śruti to convey multiplicity.

Just as from the knowledge of a single lump of clay, the cognition of all things made of clay arises, so too should the understanding of the world be contemplated through the realization of the one Brahman. (59)
Brahman consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, while the world consists of name and form;
thus Brahman is heard of in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad] as being characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Āruṇi declared that Brahman is of the nature of Being (sadrūpa); the Bahvṛcas [declare] it is consciousness (prajñāna);
Sanatkumāra [declared it is] bliss (ānanda). In this same manner, it should be understood elsewhere as well. 61.
Having reflected upon all forms and having fashioned names, he remains [established], according to the Vedic revelation: "I shall bring forth these names and forms. (62)
Prior to creation it was undifferentiated; thereafter, it is differentiated in two ways.
This Māyā, possessing inconceivable power, is called the "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta) within Brahman.
That which is established in the changeless Brahman undergoes manifold transformations;
one should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial nature) and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā. 64.
The first modification is space; it exists, it shines, and it is dear. Its form is the capacity to provide room (avakāśa); that [triple nature] is illusory, yet not those three themselves.
It does not exist prior to manifestation, nor does it exist after its destruction;
that which exists neither at the beginning nor at the end likewise exists not in the present. (66)
"Beings have an unmanifest beginning, an manifest middle, and an unmanifest end, O Bhārata"—thus did Kṛṣṇa speak to Arjuna. (67)
Being subtle, they always follow along with existence, consciousness, and bliss;
for in the spaceless state, the experience of existence and the other qualities resides within one's own Self.
Now, tell me, what appears to you when that space is forgotten?
If you say it is "merely emptiness," let it be so; for it indeed shines forth as such. (69)
Precisely because it is of such a nature, its existence is characterized by equanimity;
that happiness which is devoid of both favorability and unfavorability is one's own innate happiness.
When there is favorability, there is the cognition of joy; when there is unfavorability, however, there is the cognition of suffering.
In the absence of both, there is innate bliss, and innate suffering never exists at all.
When one abides in innate bliss, there is an instantaneous reversal of joy and sorrow;
since the mind is momentary, let it be understood that these two are merely mental states.
If bliss is thus admitted even in space as its manifestation of existence, let it be contemplated in the same way regarding all things from air up to the body. (73)
Motion and touch are the characteristics of air; heat and illumination are those of fire;
liquidity is that of water; and solidity is that of earth—such is the determination. (74)
Having thus mentally contemplated each respective form as appropriate— in the case of space, as its uncommon [nature], and likewise in the case of herbs, food, and bodies— (75)
Though name-and-form are divided in manifold ways, they abide as one;
there is no contradiction regarding existence, consciousness, and bliss for anyone. (76)
Name and form are devoid of reality; they are both subject to birth and destruction. Behold them within Brahman through the intellect, like bubbles and the like in the ocean.
When this perfect Brahman, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss, is perceived,
name and form gradually vanish of their own accord.
To the extent that contempt arises, to that same extent there is the observation of it;
to the extent that it is observed, to that same extent one should abandon both.
Through the practice of that, once knowledge is firmly established, this person becomes liberated even while living; let the body be as it may. (80)
The wise know that practice to be: reflecting upon That, speaking of That, mutually awakening one another to That, and being solely intent upon That. (81)
When practiced with respect, continuously over a long period of time and throughout many lifetimes, [this ignorance] is entirely dispelled in every way. (82)
The power of Brahman creates many unreal things, just like the power of clay;
or rather, the sleep and dream occurring within a living being serve as an illustration here. (83)
Just as the power of sleep causes impossible dreams within the individual soul (jīva), so too does this Māyā effect the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of Brahman. 84.

In a dream, one might see traveling through the sky or the cutting off of one's own head; likewise, one might see a multitude of years pass in a single moment, or again, the death of a son or other loved ones. (85)
In that state, it is difficult to establish a distinction such as "this is logical" and "this is not";
for whatever is viewed in whatever manner, that very thing appears logical in that very manner. (86)
When such greatness is seen even in the power of sleep, then what wonder is there that the greatness of the power of illusion (māyā) is inconceivable? (87)
Just as sleep creates various dreams for a sleeping person,
so does this [intellect] imagine modifications within the changeless Brahman.

The transformations consisting of air, ether, fire, water, earth, the cosmic egg, the worlds, living beings, stones, and so forth—within these, the shadow of consciousness is reflected in the intellects of sentient beings. (89)
In these sentient and insentient beings, Brahman—characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss—is the same; it is only name and form that differ individually.
These name and form reside within Brahman like a painting on a canvas;
having disregarded both name and form, one's intellect should become fixed upon Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). || 91 ||
Just as one disregards one's own body when it is seen submerged face-down in water, and instead maintains focused attention on one's own body while standing on the bank; so it is here.
Just as that [world] is always disregarded by everyone while thousands of mental constructions persist,
so too is there disregard for name and form.
In every moment, the kingdom of the mind changes from one state to another;
what has passed away never returns, and external worldly affairs are likewise.
Childhood is not found in youth, nor is youth found in old age; once a father is dead he does not exist again, and a day that has passed never returns.
What difference is there between a worldly thing, which perishes in an instant, and a kingdom of one’s imagination?
Therefore, even while such a thing appears, one should abandon the notion that it is real. (96)
When worldly affairs are disregarded, the intellect is free from obstacles in contemplating Brahman;
for, like an actor, one carries out worldly duties while maintaining a state of artificiality.
Just as a massive rock remains steady at the bottom even while the water flows above it, so too Brahman remains immutable despite the transformation of names and forms; it does not otherwise change.
Just as the vast sky containing all things appears within a flawless mirror,
so too does this sky containing the manifold world appear within the solid mass of Being-Consciousness (saccit).
Just as one cannot perceive what is within a mirror without seeing the mirror itself, how can there be the notion of name and form without realizing the True Consciousness-Bliss? 100.
First, while sat-cit-ānanda is manifesting, one should then restrain the intellect by that much alone and not hold it upward toward name and form. (101)
And thus, may people rest for a long time in this non-dual bliss—the Brahman devoid of the world, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. 102.
In the third chapter of the work titled *Brahmānanda*, the bliss of non-duality (*advaitānanda*) itself is described through the contemplation of the falsity of the world. (103)
Thus ends the non-dual bliss within the Bliss of Brahman. 13.
The Fourteenth Chapter, titled "Bliss of Knowledge," from the *Brahmānanda*: Now,
for one who perceives the bliss of Brahman through yoga, through the discrimination of the Self, and through reflection on the falsity of duality, the bliss of knowledge (*vidyānanda*) is described.
The bliss of knowledge, which consists of a modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti), is like the bliss derived from sense objects;
it is said to be of four kinds, including the absence of suffering and so forth. (2)

The absence of suffering, the attainment of desires, the thought "I have accomplished what was to be done," and the thought "I have attained what was to be attained"—thus is the fourfold [nature of liberation] illustrated. (3)
Suffering is thus declared to be twofold: pertaining to this world and pertaining to the next;
and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad speaks of the cessation of that which pertains to this world.
If a person were to know the Self as "This am I," desiring what, or for the sake of whose desire, would he suffer along with the body?
The Self is said to be twofold: the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).
Through identification with the mind, the individual self, being associated with the three bodies, enters into the state of an enjoyer.

The Supreme Self, which is existence-consciousness-bliss, having attained identity with name and form, has become the object of experience; yet upon the discernment of that [Self], neither of these two remains.
Desiring that which is to be enjoyed for the sake of the enjoyer, one should cause the body to suffer;
fevers reside within the three bodies, but they are not the fevers of the Self.

Diseases such as fevers reside in the gross body due to the imbalance of the constituent elements (dhātus); desire, anger, and so forth reside in the subtle body; however, the seed of both resides in the causal source.

When the Supreme Self has been discerned by means of the path of non-dual bliss, what real object of enjoyment could one who knows the Supreme Self not perceive, and thus what indeed would he desire? (10)
When this individual self has been determined according to the method taught by Ātmānanda, there is no enjoyer whatsoever here; how then could there be a secondary fever of the body? (11)
Anxiety regarding the two—merit and demerit—will result in suffering in the next world;
it was stated in the very first chapter that "anxiety shall not torment him. (12)
Just as water does not adhere to this lotus leaf, so too,
for the wise one, there is no adhesion of future karma after the experience [of the present].
Just as the burning of reeds, grass, or cotton by fire occurs in an instant, so too is his accumulated karma consumed through realization. 14.
Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes. 15.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—
even by slaying these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.
The killing of mother or father, theft, the destruction of an embryo, or other such acts—such sin shall not destroy liberation, nor shall the radiance of the face perish. (17)
Just as the absence of suffering has been described for him, so too is the attainment of all desires proclaimed;
for by attaining all desires, he indeed becomes immortal. || 18 ||

Eating, playing, and attaining delight with women, as well as by means of vehicles and other such things, he should not mind his body or his life; he should sustain that [body] through ritual action alone.
One attains all desires simultaneously, not through other births or karmas; enjoyments manifest in the Śrotriya all at once, free from succession.
Young, handsome, learned, free from disease, and firm of mind, he protected the entire earth filled with wealth, accompanied by an army. (21)
The king, endowed with all human enjoyments and having reached the height of satisfaction,
attains that bliss which the knower of Brahman also experiences.
Regarding the enjoyment of mortal pleasures, there is no difference in desire between the two; therefore, their satisfaction is equal.
For one person, freedom from desire regarding enjoyments arises from dispassion, while for the other, it arises from discernment. (23)
By virtue of his learning in the Vedas, King Bṛhadratha examined the defects inherent in objects of enjoyment; he illustrated those defects through these verses.
The defects of the body, the defects of the mind, and the defects of objects of enjoyment are manifold;
just as there is no desire for milk-rice vomited by a dog, so it is for the man of discrimination.
Although the king was equally free from desire regarding the accumulation of his means here,
he was pursued by suffering due to the fear of their inevitable destruction.
Neither of these two belongs to the learned Vedic scholar; therefore, his bliss is greater than the other.
The bliss of the Gandharvas exists for the king, but not for the man of discrimination. (27)
In this kalpa, being a human by virtue of the distinction between merit and demerit,
one who has attained the state of a gandharva is called a mortal gandharva.
If, due to merit performed in a previous kalpa,
one should exist as a Gandharva at the very beginning of that kalpa, such a being is here called a Deva-gandharva.
In this world, the Agniṣvātta and other ancestors who have resided for a long time attained divinity at the very beginning of the kalpa; they are the Ājāna-devas (deities by birth).

In this kalpa, having performed great rites such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and attained the exalted state, those who are worshipped by the gods by birth are the deities of action (karmadevatās). || 31 ||
Yama and Agnimukhya are the deities; Indra and Bṛhaspati are said to be the lords of the Jāti [class];
Prajāpati is declared to be Virāṭ, while Brahmā is named Sūtrātman. || 32 ||
The sūtras beginning with "sārvabhauma" describe those who desire each progressively higher state;
beyond that, however, is this bliss of the Self, which is inaccessible to speech and mind.
Since the learned one is free from desire for all those various pleasures sought after by others, therefore all those joys belong to him.
This is said to be the attainment of all desires, or rather, it is the state of being the conscious Self as witness;
for one perceives enjoyments in all bodies just as in one's own body. || 35 ||
Even for the ignorant, this [knowledge] certainly exists, yet there is no satisfaction due to lack of realization;
"He who knows attains all desires," so says the Śruti. (36)
Or rather, he always sings with the *sāman* his own state of being the self of all;
thus it is studied in the *sāmans*: "I am the food, and likewise the eater of food. (37)
The absence of suffering and the attainment of desire—both indeed have been thus defined.
Let it also be observed that there is the state of having accomplished what was to be done and the state of having attained what was to be attained. (38)
For both [theories] have been correctly set forth by us in the *Tṛptidīpa*;
those very verses should be reflected upon here for the purification of the intellect. (39)

"For the sake of accomplishing the multitude of goals pertaining to this world and the next, and for the sake of attaining liberation, there was much to be done by him previously; all of that has now been accomplished. (40)
Thus, constantly reflecting upon this state of having accomplished all that was to be done in relation to its counter-correlate, he remains eternally satisfied in this manner.

Let those who are ignorant and suffering wander through the cycle of existence at will out of attachment to sons and the like; but I, filled with supreme bliss, wander through the world—what desire could I have? (42)
Let those who desire to go to the next world perform ritual actions;
why and how should I, who am the self of all worlds, perform them?
"Let those who are qualified here expound the treatises or teach the Vedas; for me, however, there is no qualification, because I am inactive."
I have no desire for sleep, alms, bathing, or purification, nor do I perform them;
if observers nevertheless imagine them, what can that imagination of others affect me? (45)
Just as a heap of gunja berries and the like would not be burned by a fire superimposed upon something else, so too I do not partake of the worldly attributes superimposed upon another. 46.
"Let those who do not know the truth listen; why should I, who already knows it, listen?
Let those who are beset by doubt reflect; I, being free from doubt, do not need to reflect. (47)
One who is deluded should practice meditation; for what need is there for meditation when there is no delusion?
I never entertain the delusion that the body is the self. (48)
The conventional usage such as "I am a human" and so forth is possible even without this misconception, due to the habitual tendencies cultivated over a long period. (49)
When the karma that has already begun to bear fruit (prārabdha-karma) is exhausted, worldly activity ceases;
however, as long as that karma is not exhausted, this activity will not subside even through a thousand meditations.
If you maintain that the pervasiveness of conventional usage is what is intended, then let meditation be yours;
seeing conventional usage as uncontradicted, why should I meditate? (51)
Since there is no distraction for me, therefore I have no meditative absorption;
for either distraction or absorption would belong only to a mind that is subject to modification.
For one whose nature is eternal experience, what separate experience could there be for me?
"What was to be done has been done; that which was to be attained has been attained"—such is the certainty.
Whether it be worldly or scriptural activity, or even otherwise,
let it proceed as it has begun for me, who am a non-doer and untainted.
Alternatively, even though my purpose is accomplished, out of a desire to favor the world, I shall proceed by the very path prescribed in the scriptures; what loss is there for me? (55)
Let the body be engaged in the worship of the gods, bathing, purification, begging for alms, and so forth; likewise, let the speech chant the *Tāra* and recite the Upanishads. (56)
Let the intellect meditate upon Viṣṇu, or let it dissolve into the bliss of Brahman;
as for me, the witness, I do nothing at all here, nor do I cause anything to be done.
Satisfied by the sense that all duties have been accomplished, and further satisfied by the realization that all goals have been attained,
he thus reflects continuously within his own mind.
Blessed am I, blessed am I, for I constantly and directly know my own Self;
blessed am I, blessed am I, for the bliss of Brahman shines clearly before me.
Blessed am I, blessed am I; today I do not behold the suffering of worldly existence.
Blessed am I, blessed am I; my own ignorance has fled away somewhere.
I am blessed, I am blessed; there is nothing further for me to do.
I am blessed, I am blessed; everything that was to be attained has been accomplished today.
Blessed am I, blessed am I; what comparison can there be for my satisfaction in this world?
Blessed am I, blessed am I; blessed, blessed—blessed again and again! || 62 ||
Oh, what merit! Oh, what merit! It has truly borne fruit, it has borne firm fruit!
Oh, by the attainment of this merit, oh, who we are! Oh, who we are! (63)
Oh, the scripture! Oh, the scripture! Oh, the teacher! Oh, the teacher!
Oh, the knowledge! Oh, the knowledge! Oh, the bliss! Oh, the bliss! (64)

In the treatise titled *Brahmānanda*, the fourth chapter has been declared; let it be understood that this [chapter] concerning the bliss of knowledge (*vidyānanda*), ending with its arising, constitutes the practice (*abhyāsa*). (65)
Thus ends the bliss of knowledge within the bliss of Brahman. 14.
The Fifteenth Chapter of the *Brahmānanda*, titled "The Bliss of Objects" (*Viṣayānanda*).
Now, herein the bliss of objects—which partakes of the nature of a portion of the bliss of Brahman—is described as being its gateway; that it is indeed a portion thereof, the Śruti has declared. (1)
This is his supreme bliss, which consists of the indivisible single essence;
all other beings enjoy only a mere fraction of it.
The modifications of the mind are threefold: peaceful, terrible, and deluded.
Detachment, forbearance, magnanimity, and so forth are the peaceful modifications. (3)
Thirst, affection, passion, greed, and so forth are said to be states of terrible conduct; delusion, fear, and so forth are called states of foolish conduct. (4)
In all these modes of activity, the nature of consciousness of Brahman is reflected; and when they are stilled, bliss is also reflected.
"He became form after form; he is the counterpart"—this is the Vedic revelation.
The author of the Sūtras has set forth similes such as "the sun and its rays" and so forth.
For the single Self of all beings, residing in every being,
is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water.
Just as this moon, having entered the water, is indistinct in turbid water but distinct in clear water,
so too Brahman appears in two ways within the mental modifications (vṛttis).
In the states of intense delusion (ghora-mūḍha), due to impurity, there is the obscuration of the portion of bliss;
therein, due to slight purity, there is the reflection of the conscious portion.
Or rather, just as heat from fire may be transmitted to pure water but not its light, so too is the manifestation of pure consciousness [transmitted] here.
Just as both heat and light arise from wood, even so do bliss and consciousness manifest when [the senses] have become tranquil. 11.
The formal establishment based on the intrinsic nature of the object is the same for both;
for a restrictive rule is indeed postulated in accordance with direct experience. (12)
The experience of happiness is not observed in states that are either terrible or deluded;
yet, even in those that are tranquil, let it be seen that in some cases there exists a certain excellence of happiness. (13)
Whenever desire arises regarding houses, fields, and the like,
there is no happiness therein because this desire, being rajasic, is terrible.
There is the suffering of whether it will succeed or not; if it fails, that [suffering] increases.
If there is an obstacle, there may be anger, or the one who obstructs may be hated. (15)
If a remedy is impossible, that [suffering] would be poison;
for in anger and the like, there is great misery, and even the suspicion of happiness is far away. (16)

When a desired object is obtained, the state of joy is tranquil; therein lies great happiness. In the actual enjoyment of it, the happiness is even greater; yet when one is merely attached to the prospect of gain, it is indeed only slight.
But the greatest [perfection] is said to be in detachment and the bliss of knowledge;
likewise in patience and magnanimity, because of the warding off of anger and greed. (18)
Whatever happiness may arise, that is Brahman itself due to its reflection; within the mental modifications, the inward-turned state of the Self reflects [Brahman] without obstruction. (19)
Existence (sattā), consciousness (citi), and bliss (sukha) are the three inherent natures of Brahman;
among clay, stone, and other such things, only existence is manifested, not the other two.
In the two mental modifications (vṛtti) that are terrible and deluded, both *sattva* and *citi* are manifest;
in the peaceful modification, all three are manifest. Thus is Brahman described as being mixed. || 21 ||
It is unmixed with the two—knowledge and yoga—which have been previously mentioned.
In the first chapter there is reflection on yoga, and in the [subsequent] two chapters there is knowledge.
Non-existence, insentience, and suffering—these three are the forms of māyā.
Non-existence is found in things such as a man’s horn; insentience is found in wood, stone, and the like. (23)
Thus, through the expansion of Māyā, there is the suffering of those with terrible and deluded intellects;
yet, due to its identity with the mental modifications such as tranquility and so forth, it is proclaimed as the "mixed" Brahman.

This being the case, a person who wishes to meditate upon Brahman here should disregard such things as a human horn and so forth, and should meditate upon that which remains in the appropriate manner.
Having abandoned both name and form in stone and other such objects, one should contemplate pure existence;
having abandoned the terrible suffering of the ignorant and the deluded, one should contemplate Being-Consciousness.
One should likewise contemplate the three—Existence, Consciousness, and Bliss—as peaceful;
these three contemplations are respectively inferior, middling, and superior. (27)

Even for one who is dull-witted, when there is engagement in worldly affairs, the contemplation upon the mixed Brahman is superior; it is precisely to express this that the "bliss of the object" (viṣayānanda) is mentioned here.
But when the mental modification is indifferent, because of its slackness, it is the highest of the high;
thus, meditation (dhyāna) in the bliss of latent impressions (vāsanānanda) is said to be of four kinds. 29.
Meditation is not [the goal] through the practice of knowledge and yoga; rather, it is indeed the knowledge of Brahman itself.
When the mind has attained one-pointedness through meditation, that knowledge becomes firmly established. (30)
In the state of pure consciousness (vidyā), existence, consciousness, and bliss shine forth as a single, indivisible essence;
they do not appear through differentiation, because the limiting adjuncts that cause division have been discarded.

The peaceful, the terrible, and those beginning with the "stone" (śilā) are considered to be limiting adjuncts (upādhi) that cause differentiation. Through yoga and discriminative discernment, there is indeed the removal of these adjuncts.

When the reality of Brahman, which is free from limiting conditions, self-luminous, and non-dual, shines forth, the triad [of knower, known, and knowing] does not exist; therefore, it is called the bliss of plenitude (bhūmānanda).
The fifth chapter has been declared in the treatise titled *Brahmānanda*;
by means of this, let the bliss of the objects be made to enter within. (34)
May Hari-Hara always rejoice in this bliss of Brahman;
and may He protect all living beings who have taken refuge in Him and possess pure minds. 35.
Thus ends the "Bliss of Objects" within the *Brahmānanda*. 15.
Thus ends the work titled *Pañcadaśī*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Vidyāraṇya Muni.
